FOREWORD. 

The aim of this work is to present to students and practitioners a comprehensive view of the art of pleading under the Code of Civil Procedure in Colorado, a statement of what such pleading ought logically to be and of what it is in this state. 

It is my belief that the courts of Colorado, although sometimes they have ignored the spirit and intent of the Code, and, indeed, its express provisions, yet have followed it more closely than have the courts of other states. 

It has been my purpose to restrict the subject to pleading, as distinguished from practice, and to refer to the latter or to the substantive law only as might be necessary. 

As a preliminary I have made a card index digest of all the reported decisions in the Colorado Supreme Court and Court of Appeals on the subject of pleading, having, to that end, read them all and found many which are not otherwise available; e.g., Allison v. Schuber, 74 C. 545, 223 P. 53. Many of these have been cited, and they will occasionally be of use to the practitioner.

It is not to be understood that all the cited cases are decisions or even dicta upon the subject in hand, because, in addition to the attempt to get all such, I have tried to reach many which are analogous or merely consistent with real decisions, or even merely interesting in connection with them. Such cases are not available by means of ordinary digests. 

I have not intended to comment at length upon any part of the Code except Chapter IV, which is devoted to the subject of pleading properly so called, and such other sections as are closely related to it or necessary to its better understanding. 

Among such sections are the first and those immediately following it and those contained in Chapter XII. 

The notes above have been made somewhat full, and when my own opinion has been expressed, it has been, so far as practicable, confined to them, but sometimes it appears in the text. 

Every statement there, however, is intended to be supported by a citation.

The cases cited are practically all taken from the Colorado Reports. No attempt has been made to search for other decisions.

J. H. D. 

Denver, Colorado, October 9, 1935.

NOTE OF EXECUTOR. 

Judge Denison died December 3, 1935, just after his book was in type. He was able, while in the hospital, to look over only a few pages of proof. The checking of the numerous citations, in order that the work might possess the accuracy which alone would have satisfied its author, presented a serious problem to the executor, the family and the publisher. 

With the courteous cooperation of Mr. Courtright, it was happily arranged that this important task should be undertaken by a group of younger lawyers, recent graduate of the University of Denver Law School, who had there taken Judge Denison's Courses in Pleading. Harry S. Silverstein, Jr. organized and directed the group in its painstaking labors extending over a period of eight weeks. Most grateful acknowledgment is given to Mr. Silverstein and to his associates, Richard P. Brown, Miss Dierdre Dunlevy, Ora George, Marvin 

Schwartz, Samuel S. Sherman, Jr., Donald Gilliland and 

H. Leslie Williams, Jr. Miss J. Jane Silverstein and Miss 

Barabel McLean also gave most conscientious and valuable assistance in the revised proof-reading.

Without the intelligent and devoted assistance of these volunteer workers, and the patience and cooperation of Mr. 

Courtright, the publisher, it would have been impossible to publish the book with assurance of its accuracy. 

The Index and Table of Cases were made by William H. Courtright, under an arrangement with Judge Denison, who desired him to Index his Book, to insure completeness. 

Denver, Colorado, February 11, 1936.

What is pleading? Its origin, history and purpose. § 1. Definition: Pleading has been defined in many ways, but the best definition, I think, may be given by a modification of that in our Code of Civil Procedure, viz: "The preliminary statements to the court by the parties of their respective claims and defenses." In common law pleading and in pleading according to the Colorado Code we should add "for the purpose of reaching an issue. 1 

¹Sutton, Pers. Actions at Common Law, 157. Courtright's Mills

Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, Chap. XII, 1 Chit. Pl. 225, 226, 605, 611. 

2 § 2. Anciently: It is obviously most convenient, if not necessary, for a court, when the plaintiff has appeared and has had the defendant brought in, first to try to learn what the trouble is all about. It is, of course, possible to learn this from the evidence, as in claims against estates in our county courts¹ and in cases before justices of the peace, but it is inconvenient, and that inconvenience has caused courts, as far back as there are any known records, before proceeding with the trial, to inquire of the parties concerning the real point in dispute, and their statements then and there made are the pleadings. There are records of the courts of Babylon of about 700 B.C., and I am indebted to Colonel Wigmore, Dean 

Emeritus of the Law School of Northwestern University, for the record of an Egyptian case of 2000 B. C., and for the translation which follows. No doubt there are much older records yet undiscovered. "Court Minutes of Pleadings on File B.C. 2000+ (Translation.) "The party Sebekotep alleges that one 

Usser, now deceased, father of the other party, Thau, made

the said Sebekotep to be guardian of his, the said Usser's wife and children, and to that end delivered all his property to the said Sebekotep, to be applied to the use of the said Usser's family, whether or not the property increased or decreased. But the party Thau denies that his father ever made any such conveyance. "If the said Sebekotep produces credible witnesses who will make oath that the said Usser did in their presence deliver the property on the terms set forth in the said Sebekotep's pleading, then the property is to remain in his possession. But if he does not produce such witnesses, then none of said Usser's property shall remain in Sebekotep's possession, but shall be delivered to the said Thau, son of Usser."

Thus the issue is declared: Deposit in trust vel non, and the method of trial fixed. The burden of proof is put on Sebekotep though he has possession; doubtless because he admits the delivery of Thau's ancestor, Usser, then the owner, and so his defense by allegation of the trust is logically confession and avoidance.

Pleading being thus necessary, or at least expedient and convenient, certain rules are necessary to make it orderly, for without order it would be vain.5

§ 3. At Common Law: The original method of pleading at common law is shown in a most interesting way in the Year 

Books. It was substantially the same as in Egypt three thousand years before. After hearing the statements of the parties and learning the point in dispute the court directed the method of trial.¹

In the times of the Year Books the pleadings were most informal; not much more than colloquies between those present in court, sometimes, it seems, even the clerk joined in.2

The method was to hear from the counsel on both sides, informally and orally. So informal was it that counsel was

PLEARING IN GENERAL 

73 permitted to change his pleading at will whenever the court pronounced against it, which was constantly done, even to the stating of a different cause of action or defense.23 The judge often advised how to plead. This all having been done in Law 

French and the issue and the pleadings agreed on, the record was made up by the clerk in Latin.

Counsel sometimes stated the facts and asked the court how to plead. In Walton v. Latimer, Y.B. Sel. Ed., 2 Edw. II. 81, we have an example of the forcing of a single issue and of the very free and informal way in which counsel and judges conversed and criticized the pleadings. 

So far as such records are found the judge first inquires what the quarrel is about, and, logically, pursues the inquiry until he finds the point in dispute, whereupon the clerk makes up the record in Latin, and this after demurrers and other objections have been heard and immediately decided orally. 

I do not find that demurrers were considered otherwise, though probably they sometimes were.

These matters may be verified with much interest by reading the Selden Society's Edition of the Year Books, which contains not only the report translated into English from the original Law French, but also the record proper translated from the Latin.

§ 5. Transition to Written Pleadings: After the issue was reached, i.e., the point in dispute was discovered, and the clerk had written up the record in Latin, amendments were seldom allowed.¹ These Latin pleadings are not found in the ordinary 

Year Books but are set out in the Selden Edition with translations. 

It seems more than probable that the clerk did not always get the correct idea or did not satisfy the counsel who had conducted the oral altercations; at all events, for this reason or some other or many, the custom changed and the pleadings were drawn by attorneys and put before the court as drawn, with no suggestion by the judge and no opportunity for correction. Amendments, however, were freely allowed even after the pleadings were written if they had not yet been entered of rcord.2

Here began the development of hyper-technicality in pleading. It became rather a game of skill than a real inquiry after the matter in dispute. The free and easy way in which counsel and judge talked the matter over and finally agreed on the point on which the parties disagreed, disappeared. Flexibility was gone and rigidity substituted. By the Acts 1, Geo. IV, and 

9, Geo. IV, however, the law of amendments was liberalized, and our codes, in a way, have done likewise. 

Through all this, however, the one point aimed at was the production of the issue, i.c., the proposition of law or fact which one party affirmed and the other denied. When that was discovered the case was ready for the trial, which was and is an investigation of the truth of the matter affirmed. This idea and theory of issue was the governing principle of common law pleading. Everything else was related to it and directed

to that end, yet in practice, because of frequent injustice, which resulted from the rigidity aforesaid, and because of the rule that there must be but one issue, the "general issue" was allowed to obscure the real issue which, theoretically, was sought. 

¹Charles v. de Bornamville, Y.B., 21 Edw. I, 240, 244, not Seld. Ed. 2Tidd's Prac. 697. 

So called because it was the outcome of the pleadings. When it was reached the pleadings were finished. 

41 Chit. Pl. 225, 226. Sutton Pers. Actions at Com. Law, 157. § 6. Equity: Pleading in equity (chancery) was different in origin, theory and purpose. Every lawyer knows that at some time about the reign of Edward I or earlier somebody wrote a letter to the king saying in substance, "my situation is thus and so, it is unjust and intolerable and your courts of law are so constituted that they cannot help me. I beg your aid."

This was the first bill in chancery. The king, then or later, referred such a matter to his Chancellor, the "keeper of his conscience," (from the importunities of which he was thereby relieved), and the Chancellor thus developed into a court and regularly commanded the person complained of to answer fully the statements made in the complainant's letter, which he did, in writing. The purpose of this letter (bill) and the answer was to inform the Chancellor fully, to disclose to him the full nature of the case so that he could determine it without more. 

The allegations might all be and always some were of evidential facts, improper to be stated in legal pleadings. 

Indeed, in their origin these papers were not mere pleadings but were and still are, where the old chancery practice is in use, regarded as evidence; hence the practice, not yet wholly abandoned, of the hearing on.bill and answer, without further evidence. In time further evidence was more and more resorted to and the bill and answer, with sometimes a replication, became more and more to be regarded as preliminary statements like pleadings, till at last it grew into a system of preliminary statement and subsequent proof; still retaining, however, its original characteristics, that the bill and answer were evidence, and were intended to give information, to disclose evidential details, and not to find the point in dispute. § 7. Codes: The purpose, then, of equity pleadings being to disclose the whole situation in fullness and detail, and to spread the statements as widely as necessary to that end, and that of common law pleading being to make the statements as narrow as possible with the purpose of reaching a single point

PLEADING IN GENERAL 

77 in dispute, the framers of the code stepped in and said that the two systems should be one.

One of the stock arguments in favor of the adoption of the code was that it would do away with the absurd fictions of the common law system and permit the actual facts to appear. For example, the ancient action of ejectment was held up, and rightly so, as a thing to be remedied, although, as a matter of fact its principal faults had already been remedied by statute.¹ 

Less was said about equity, in which equal absurdities were permanently intrenched.

The further development of the codes is considered more fully elsewhere. 

1S. L. 1861, p. 368. R. S. 1868, Ch. XXVII, p. 272. In other states likewise. 

§ 8. Modern English Pleading¹: By the Act of 1873, the 

English courts were reorganized and a supreme court was empowered to make rules of practice, which they did. These rules are in many ways not unlike the codes in use in the United States, but in one respect especially they greatly differ and that is with reference to pleadings. 

They prescribe forms for "statements of claims," (complaints), "defenses" (answers), and "replies" (replications), and, by Order XIX, Rule 5, their use, wherever applisable, is required. These are forms of pleading, not forms of action as earlier at common law; forms of statement, not categories of legal liability as in the older system. 

It will be seen that such a system is radically different from our code which permits the use of any form of expression and only restricts the pleader to "ordinary concise language." 

The consequences of this difference are referred to in other places.

§ 9. Common Law Forms: The division by the common law of rights of action into "forms of action” was a classification of causes of action. The term "form of action" at common law meant a category of legal right and liability; e.g., the form of action "trespass" was the remedy for injury by force. "Assumpsit" was the proper form of action for breach of a promise, i.e., a simple contract.

Rights are no longer determined by "forms of action," and the complaint need not name the form of action, the substance of which it states.2 The complaint, however, and every pleading, must be expressed in some form, though the "form of action" has been eliminated."

While the code permits a plaintiff to state his case in any way he likes so long as it is in English, ordinary and concise, yet it is desirable and much more efficient to use forms of statement which have been found sufficient, and their use commended,* and "inartificial pleading" is deprecated. The term "form" is often misused, e.g., an omission to allege certain facts in the complaint said to be an error of "form" only." 

1Zinn v. Denver Co., 68 C. 274, 275, 187 P. 1033. 

2Ramsay v. Meade, 37 C. 465, 471, 86 P. 1018.

860. Even an ordinary business letter is more efficient if expressed according to well-known conventional form because more readily understood and less liable to be misunderstood. "Scott v. Stutheit, 58 C. 540, 542, 146 P. 766. "Sch. Dist. v. High Sch. Dist., 25 C. A. 510, 516-17, 139 P. 1089. 

See discussion of this case in Chapter on Complaint. § 10. Designation: It matters not, legally, what you call an action, but the law cannot much resemble a science unless it employs definite terms. In an attempt to do that we often use

the terms of the common law but the names of the forms of action are not used with their exact common law meaning. 

An action is, for example, called an action of debt,¹ but the court means that the facts are such as would justify an action of debt at common law. An opinion says the court cannot tell whether the action is replevin, detinue, trespass de bonis or trover, but the court does not mean to say that any of those "forms of action" are in use. It is immaterial what we call an action. It matters not whether you call an action one for false imprisonment or for malicious prosecution. Yet the common law actions still exist in substance; legal and equitable rights are measured as before. If trover would not lie then it will not now." The distinction between causes of action or the nature of actions cannot be abolished." 'Doyle v. Nichols, 15 C. A. 458, 63 P. 123. So an action for deceit is called case.

La Poudre Co. v. Water Co., 74 C. 1, 8, 218 P. 739. § 12. Variations: There are cases which, inconsistently with the foregoing, hold or seem to hold that the principle of forms of action is still in force. The following are some of the instances of such decisions.

It was held that a demurrer was properly sustained because a judgment for damages was prayed when the facts justified only mandamus.¹ Though the facts justified a judgment for salary, a judgment for plaintiff was reversed because the proceeding was mandamus. So mandamus and replevin seem to be recognized as different forms of action. 2 A complaint for injunction was held subject to demurrer though it stated sufficient facts to justify quo warranto. And 7724

81 a like decision because the plaintiff claimed under a statute when his facts gave him a cause if any at common law. § 14. Origin and Development: The Code of Civil Pro cedure of Colorado was enacted by the first legislature of the 

State and took effect October 1, 1877. Until that time the civil procedure of the territory and state had been that of the common law and chancery modified by various statutes.¹ 

Beginning with Goss v. County Commissioners, 4 C. 468, 471, which is the first reported case wherein the code is mentioned, its construction and interpretation has been one of our supreme court's principal labors, and their decisions to the present time, with the code itself and the rules promulgated by that court under the act of 1913, S. L. 1913, Ch. 121, constitute our present law with reference to that statement in court of causes of action and defenses thereto which is called pleading. 

Our code is what it represents itself to be, a code of civil procedure, and includes much more than mere pleading, which is the particular subject of these notes. 

Its purpose has been said to be "to assist the parties in obtaining justice." This is obvious but such is the purpose. of all remedial law, and so the proposition is of little avail. 

Section 1 of that Code is as follows: 

"The distinctions between actions at law and suits in equity, and the distinct forms of actions and suits heretofore existing are abolished, and there shall be in this state but one form of civil action³ for the enforcement or protection of private rights, and the redress or prevention of private wrongs, which shall be the same at law in equity, and which shall be denominated a civil action, and which shall be prosecuted and defended as prescribed in this act. 

In Goss v. County Commissioners, 4 C. 468, the opinion says: "While the code abolishes form of action it cannot obliterate the distinctions between the causes or nature of actions, as, for example, actions ex delicto and ex contractu." This proposition was not then as clearly understood by the bar or bench

as it is now, though it is evident upon any careful thought. 

The nature of a cause of action, i.e., that which is manifested by the facts which constitute the cause of action, exists independently of law and cannot be controlled by law, all the law can do is to say whether those facts amount to a cause of action. Smith sells a piano to Jones, and Jones promises to pay him five hundred dollars for it: The law cannot control those facts but it can say and does say that Smith has a cause of action if there is a breach of that promise. This is a function of what we call the substantive law, which is that part of the law which relates to men's rights and duties to each other, and is distinguished from the remedial law which tells how to enforce those rights and duties to secure compensation for their denial or breach. So if I enter my neighbor's garden and trample his crops the law cannot control those facts, and no law that could be framed could make the transaction the same as the sale of a piano. The law can only say that whoever is in the position of my neighbor shall have damages or some other remedy and provide a means to enforce it. It is impossible to make these cases alike because they are what they are and are not alike. One is a violation of a right and duty which the parties themselves created and justifies an action ex contractu; the other of a right and duty which the law establishes between all men under like circumstances and justifies an action ex delicto, and here is the basic difference between actions ex delicto and ex contractu. The reasoning is the same when we compare two forms of action ex delicto, say trespass and case. These actions are based on different rights and duties, trespass on the duty to refrain from forcibly injuring another man's person or property, and case, in its larger sense, on the duty to refrain from injury without force. This distinction may not be very reasonable or scientific but it is one of substance and no law can change it. What the law can do, however, is to say that the statement of the fact of forcible wrong or of wrong without force shall be sufficient without naming the action trespass or case, and that is what Section 1 of the Code does. It will, of course, be trespass or case, and an action ex contractu may be assumpsit, covenant, debt, etc., and these names, because of their convenience, are still used to describe actions"; furthermore, even under the code one cannot bring an action for a forcible injury and prove one without force, unless he is permitted to amend, because, there as elsewhere a plaintiff must prove the case he has stated; by virtue of this Section 1, however, he is relieved of the necessity of labelling his action trespass, case, assumpsit or at all.

The abolition of the distinction between actions at law and suits in equity may be the subject of similar comments. The same facts will produce the same results since the code as before it. The formalities of neither of the old methods are adhered to nor do we say in the pleading itself that a complaint is at law or in equity, but we do, and must, constantly, recognize the distinction in argument and through the whole proceeding to decree.

The art and science of pleading under the codes has developed on somewhat different lines in different states. The chief difference being in the views of the courts of the several states on the methods of pleading in action at law and suits in equity, or rather what would have been called such before the code, and are still distinguished by those terms. 

One purpose of this book is to show the direction of that development in Colorado and to compare our methods with others.

Our code, which was enacted by the first General Assembly of the State, took effect, as above stated, October 1, 1877. It was nearly a literal copy of the California Practice Act and is said to have been patterned after the Montana Code which was a copy of the California Act. Like the codes of other states it was a sort of descendant or heir of the codes of New York, and suffered, as they did, from hostile and ill-considered construction, whereby the benefits of its provisions were partly lost. 

The code is simpler than lawyers have made it. If carried out as it reads it would make pleadings concise, logical, and simple, and therefore easily understood, but some of its rules have been misconstrued and some ignored."

409, 414, 277 P. 299. § 15. Modern English System: As we have noticed, the 

English have escaped many of our difficulties by prescribing brief forms for all ordinary cases. The facts pleaded under the provisions of our code, being stated in any terms satisfactory to the pleader, are subject to misunderstanding by others, but there can be little danger of misunderstanding when the terms of the statement are prescribed.

To illustrate: Our code and most codes say that only material facts may be stated. What is a material fact? One that is essential to the right of action or defense.¹ How shall we determine what is essential? The English rules specify, our codes leave it first to the attorneys and finally to the courts. 

How shall we state them? With us the nisi prius courts determine because questions of method of expression do not often reach the courts of last resort, and the nisi prius courts differ, so practice becomes diverse, un-co-ordinated and uncertain. 

One of the principal purposes of the codes was to get away from the complications caused by the distinction between. pleadings at law and in equity. The form in which they expressed this was unfortunate. The Colorado Code says: "The distinction between actions at law and suits in equity" is abolished. This was, of course, impossible in substance and

impossible in form without adopting in law suits the remedies and methods peculiar to equity or vice versa. So far as the mere statement of causes of action and defenses was concerned either alternative was possible, and, perhaps, reasonably practicable. Other distinctions such as the restriction to equity of the enforcement of specific performance, regulation of trusts, etc., had to be and have been maintained, together with much of the terminology peculiar to the two old systems. We still constantly use even the old terms "law" and "equity" and distinguish cases as of one or the other of those categories, e.g., Danielson v. Gude, 11 C. 87, 93, 17 P. 283, holds that a suit to foreclose a mortgage is a suit in equity. These matters, however, do not now principally concern us. What we wish to study is the mode of statement.

The Colorado Code by its own terms reveals a clear intention not to maintain the two methods of statement. Having provided that there shall be but one form of action with respect to private rights and wrongs, every code proceeds to direct what the pleadings shall state and how they shall state it, making no distinction between the two systems, as indeed they could not consistently, because they had abolished it.³

16. Early Views: New York was the first state to adopt a code of civil procedure, and the codes of other states have been modeled, more or less closely, upon it. It was enacted in 

1848, principally through the influence of Cyrus W. Field, whose brother, Stephen J. Field, probably influenced the adoption of California's "Practice Act" which was the original code of California and was copied by Montana. Our code, as we have noted, was substantially a copy of the latter. 

When the codes came up for interpretation lawyers and judges were, of course, men who had been trained in the old order. Few felt favorably toward the new system' and if they had they would have been unable to overcome their old habits

2 of thought and customary methods of action. They were used to plead not by logical statement but by rule of thumb: "This is the way to do it because this is the way it is done." They could not wholly cast this aside, and, because some of the common law ways of statement were to be avoided, they naturally looked toward equity for an example to be followed. 

The code directed them to state a cause of action in "ordinary concise language" and thence it was sometimes inferred that in the statement should be used not only the ordinary words which men would use in their dealings with each other but that the methods of statement, the construction of sentences, should likewise be such as a man would ordinarily use in telling his own story. Since a large number, perhaps a majority, of pleaders are not clear thinkers, the pleadings were discursive and verbose, and the requirement that the statements of the complaint which were to be controverted should be denied and that some might be admitted made it apparently necessary or advisable to admit or deny every allegation in the complaint however trivial. This made the pleadings look somewhat like pleadings in chancery; especially the answer to look like the series of admissions and denials in an answer in chancery, and so, for this and for other causes, principally that it required much less capacity to reason and less mental effort, it became common, almost a habit, in many states, including Colorado, to state facts in great detail and with many allegations that were purely evidential. Some judges sanctioned this, especially in actions equitable in their nature. The theory was that such pleading was necessary in equity (as perhaps it was under the old practice), but the code required pleadings to be conducted "as prescribed in this act and not otherwise," and this they ignored. 

The late Hon. Victor A. Elliot, the first judge of the district court in Denver after the adoption of the code and afterward on the supreme bench, was an advocate of this method, saying from the bench that he would not strike out an evidential allegation in an equity case. To say this he, of course, had to abandon 

Chapter XII and the code's definition of material fact. Since at that time he had before him many more cases than any other judge in the State, his influence was great. His dissent in 

Elder v. Schumacher, 18 C. 433, 33 P. 175, shows something of his ideas and mental attitude. 

The result of all this was that both in equity matters and in those which we still call law-suits the code provisions for the statement of material facts were ignored. It could hardly be otherwise. The court said pleading in equity should be thus and so, and the code said there should be no distinction between pleading in law and equity, the consequence was obvious. 44

Pleaders must follow court or code and to follow the court was safer. These results still largely influence pleading in this state. Notwithstanding that the supreme court has repudiated this idea and in many ways indicated the contrary, yet the bar and the nisi prius courts were slow in noticing the higher court's decisions on this point, but have kept without much. change in the path marked out for them by custom. 

¹One old practitioner said the complaint ought to be called a disease.

3The word "concise" was thus ignored, and its purpose disregarded. 

Denver v. Bossie, 83 C. 329, 330, 266 P. 214.

§ 17. Motion to Make More Specific: After the enactment of the so-called Code of 1887, in which the motion to make a pleading more specific¹ and certain was authorized, matters became worse. The motion was a very convenient weapon for delay and was quickly and constantly used for that purpose, generally with no substantial reason. Before 1887 the objection of uncertainty had been made by demurrer, and had to be made with all other grounds of demurrer or it was waived, so the new motion enabled the defendant to delay the case one more step, first moving and then demurring. Judges became careless about the matter. It was easier to grant the motion than to think about it, and so, since the harm of granting it seemed, in any particular case, less likely to do harm than its denial2 some judges, ignoring the baneful general effect of such a habit, granted the motion almost of course. This still further obscured the main purpose of the code with respect to its pleading, viz, the issue, because more often than not it forced the parties to plead evidential and immaterial facts; facts the denial of which would form no issue.

Our supreme court has never sanctioned this, but, on the contrary has condemned it in many cases. 3 Real indefiniteness, however, is a serious defect and has been severely criticized.* It is cured by bill of particulars and is waived by answer.

§ 18. The Several Pleadings and Issues: The Colorado Code does not permit indefinite accumulation of one pleading upon another until an issue is reached, which was in vogue at common law, and permits only complaint, answer, replication and demurrer to each.

The complaint corresponds to the declaration at common law and to the bill in equity. By it the complaining party, called the plaintiff, states to the court the facts which he claims give him a right to some judicial relief against the opposite party called the defendant.

The defendant then answers. He may deny one or more material facts which plaintiff has alleged and may add any new fact which he claims avoids the conclusion that plaintiff has a right against him.

The plaintiff then replies. He may deny some material allegation or allegations of the plaintiff, and may allege any new matter which he claims will avoid the force of the matter alleged by defendant. 2 Each denial of a material allegation forms an issue, which is called an issue of fact. Every new material allegation in the replication is taken as denied and an issue is thus formed. The defendant may demur to the complaint or replication and the plaintiff may demur to the answer. A demurrer is, in substance, a statement that the pleading to which it is directed is insufficient either in substance or form to merit consideration. 

Such a pleading forms an issue called an issue of law.¹ 

1Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, Ch. XII. 

2Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 77. 

§ 19. The Purpose of Code Pleading: The code¹ defines pleading: "The pleadings in any action are the formal allegations by the parties of their respective claims and defenses for the judgment of the court. ""2

It further says: "The mode of pleading in civil actions, and the rules by which the sufficiency of the pleadings shall be determined, shall be as prescribed in the act, and not otherwise. ''8

The code intends that the aim of pleading shall be to find an issue or issues as at common law, and not, as in equity, to disclose details.

This will appear more fully as we go on but it is well to make it plain here.

The complaint must state "the facts constituting the cause. of action. 994 Immaterial allegations may be stricken out,5 and therefore should not be in. "A material allegation is one essential to the claim or defense and which could not be stricken from the pleading without leaving it insufficient."

The answer must deny every material allegation intended to be controverted."

Those not controverted are taken as true.8 

The Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, in 

Chapter XII, treats of issues and their disposition. It says that "an issue arises when a fact or conclusion of law is maintained by the one party and controverted by the other." Issues are of two kinds, of law and fact." "An issue of law arises upon demurrer to the complaint or answer or replication or some part thereof.''10

An issue of fact arises upon a material allegation by one party denied by the other.11

And thereupon Chapter XII goes on to prescribe the method of disposition of issues as at common law; issues of law by the court and, unless a jury is waived, issues of fact by a jury in a lawsuit, and, in equity cases by the court or by jury if so directed by the court.

It cannot be denied that, by these sections, the code requires the formation of issues both in actions at law and suits in equity; and it must be said that there are issues of law and of fact as at common law, that the determination of the issues determines the case and that the purpose of pleading under the code is to discover these issues and to formally express them.12 

It is, of course, true that one purpose of pleading is to tell each party what his opponent claims, but not to the extent of alleging any fact the denial of which would not be a defense. 

Only material facts are to be alleged.13 A material fact is one essential to the cause of action or defense. It follows logically and is enacted in Section 190, that a denial of a material allegation will make an issue and be a complete defense and that the decision of that issue, if it be the only issue, will decide the case.

The decisions and opinions of our upper courts have upheld these propositions with uniform consistency. For example it is held that the code and the rules of the Supreme Court are intended to provide and do provide for orderly procedure to make up issues,14 that the ultimate object of all written pleadings is to formulate issues to be tried,14 that an issue of law

arises only upon demurrer,15 that a judgment should be reversed because the case was tried on an issue not made in the pleadings.16 

And, of course, a denial of an immateriál allegation, i.e., one not essential to the claim or defense, will make no issue, because its decision will not decide the case.¹7 

So Hutton, Pers. Act. at Com. Law, p. 158, says of the issue: "It was very important that it should be material, that is one which really disposed of the dispute between the parties,' and 1 Chitty Pl. 225-6, 611.

So in California, an issue is said to be immaterial unless it presents a point which will decide the case.18 

And a demurrer does not admit a conclusion of law¹º nor can counsel bind the court on a question of law.20 

So of an issue of law. A demurrer raises an issue of law which determines the case if nothing more is done.21 

The necessity of issues is adjudged,22 and this is inconsistent with the old equity system; and the evidence must be confined to the issues 23 which is also inconsistent with it because there were no issues in equity pleading. And so of the instructions.24 

It is sometimes asserted that the purpose of pleading is to inform the adverse party, and that as we have noted above is true25; but it is necessary to remember that that is not the principal purpose, 26 that it never was the principal purpose, that the code says nothing about such a purpose and that neither party is required or permitted by his pleading to inform his adversary of his evidence, nor is he permitted, in pleadings, to inform him of conclusions of law, but only of the ultimate facts on which he, the pleader, relies. This later will be shown more fully. 

To make use of pleading to attribute corrupt motives to parties, counsel and court is reprehensible.27 Pleadings must be free from scandal and it is a matter of contempt.28 When it is necessary to allege the use of vile language it should be alleged in general terms.2

§ 22. In General: The method of pleading under the codes, as at common law, is by alternate statements by the plaintiff and defendant until an issue is reached, and these statements are required to be in writing and to be filed in court,¹ and they thereby become a part of its record. The names of the pleadings under the old system were declaration, plea, replication, rejoinder, surrejoinder, rebutter, and surrebutter, with demurrer to each. This was the common law system; the code, however, in terms, stops with the replication, though in fact with the rejoinder, since all matter in avoidance in the replication is taken as denied, an automatic traverse, and a demurrer to the replication is permitted.¹ 3 The names of the several pleadings under the code are complaint, answer and replication, with a demurrer to each." 

The complaint takes the place of the declaration at common law, and of the bill in chancery, the answer stands for the plea at common law or the answer or plea in chancery, and the replication for the replication at law and in chancery. The demurrer, in most respects, resembles the demurrer at law rather than in chancery, but is governed by statutory rules. 

¹Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 54. But only in actions begun in courts of record, Joss v. Hallett, 39 C. 392, 89 P. 809. 

2See Chapter 1 herein. 

3 Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 77. 

The character of a pleading, however, is determined by its substance, not its name, and a so-called demurrer was held an answer, Perkins v. Peterson, 67 C. 101, 103, 185 P. 660; so it is not necessary to say whether a defense is fraud or want of consideration. The only question is: Do the facts constitute a defense? Mastin v. Bartholomew, 41 C. 329, 333, 92 P. 682. "What amounted to a motion to dismiss a writ of error in the 

Supreme Court was miscalled a “plea in bar." Fischer v. Hanna, 8 C. A. 

471, 481, 47 P. 303. 

§ 23. Cardinal Rules: The result of this method is, as at common law that there are two inexorable rules, which, because they are based on logic, cannot be abrogated while we adhere to reason.

First: At every state of the proceedings in any action one party or the other is shown by the record to be entitled to judgment and must have it if nothing more is done.¹ 

Second: After every pleading by either party the opposite party must demur, traverse, confess and avoid or suffer judgment.

The necessity for these rules and for their rigidity can best be shown by illustration. 2 The complaint states plaintiff's cause of action, that is, the facts which he claims give him a right to some sort of a judgment against the defendant. If the law, by virtue of these facts, will give him any judgment, then, upon filing his complaint, the record shows him to be entitled to such judgment and he will get it if nothing more is done, but if the law, by virtue of these facts will not give him a judgment then the defendant will be, ipso facto, entitled to judgment against him; but to one or the other, on the record, judgment must be given. 

By a demurrer the defendant says that the facts alleged by plaintiff give him no right; that is, on the record the plaintiff is entitled to no judgment, and the defendant therefore is. 

This raises an issue of law, viz: Does the record show a right in the plaintiff to a judgment, or not? The court decides this issue and gives judgment accordingly."

But suppose the complaint shows sufficient facts, how can defendant avoid a judgment against him? Manifestly there is no way in reason but to traverse, i.e., deny, some fact or facts essential to the sufficiency of the complaint, or to add some new fact which avoids the effect of those therein alleged. 

¹McMillen v. Hayman, 74 C. 300, 301, 221 P. 893; Williams v. Smith, 76 C. 151, 230 P. 395; Swanson Co. v. Pueblo Co., 70 C. 83, 86, 197 P. 

762; Fort v. Demmer, 91 C. 285, 14 P.(2d) 489. 

2See Chapter 12 on Complaint. 

3For simplicity we do not here notice matters of form, but only matters going to the merits. Errors in the record may be corrected by an action for that purpose, but the better way is by motion or petition in the original case. Shattinger v. Shattinger, 73 C, 573, 574, 216

P. 1057. The case made by the record is sometimes misconceived. 

Parks v. Bucy, 72 C. 414, 417, 211 P. 638. 

4The judgment for defendant is "that he go hence without day." He has been required to come into court and answer and if there is nothing to answer he may go. The same result occurs if he answers successfully. 

5For simplicity we here disregard amendment and pleading over. 

§ 24. Material Allegations: An allegation of a fact essential to a complaint, or to any pleading, that is, an allegation without which the pleading would be insufficient, is called a "material allegation""; if not denied it is taken as true² but if denied there is an issue of fact which must be tried and determined, at law ordinarily by jury, before any judgment

METHOD OF CODE PLEADING 

97 can be rendered. The denial, traverse, removes an essential to plaintiff's right to a judgment, and, on the record, the plaintiff is no longer entitled to a judgment and therefore the defendant is, unless the plaintiff is able to prove his material allegation.

If at the trial the court or jury determines the issue of fact in plaintiff's favor a judgment is then due the plaintiff'; if not, it is due the defendant. 

¹Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 78. 

2Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 77. 

Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Ch. XII. 

4Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, § 243, or C. L. '21, § 244. 

§ 25. New Matter: If all the material allegations in the complaint are true and sufficient to justify a judgment the only other defense possible is confession and avoidance, that is, the defendant, by failure to deny, tacitly admits all that plaintiff has said, but adds some allegation which destroys its force, refutes the conclusion which the law would otherwise consider to be the result of the facts alleged in the complaint. 

The code usually terms such allegations "new matter," but sometimes refers to them as "in avoidance," but, of course, to be effective the "new matter" must be "in avoidance.'' This new matter shows, or is intended to show, on the record, that the defendant ought to have judgment. The plaintiff may, however, then demur to the answer and test its sufficiency and there is then an issue of law as in case of a demurrer to the complaint.* 

1Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, §§ 62 and 77. 

2Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, § 77. So in. Coe, et al. v. Coryell, 27 C. A. 61, 146 P. 791. 

See Ch. 27 on Confession and Avoidance herein. 

4Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, Ch. XII. 

§ 26. The Replication: The plaintiff may traverse, deny, any material allegation in the matter in avoidance in the answer, and so raise an issue of fact, and thereupon defendant is no longer entitled to a judgment on the record, but, if nothing more is done, the plaintiff must have it, unless the issue is tried and determined in defendant's favor. The plaintiff, however, may, by replication, avoid the defendant's new matter by adding further facts, which, as above stated, are taken as denied, but after the replication there can be no further confession and avoidance.

Since the defendant may plead more than one defense there may be several issues. The following will illustrate the foregoing propositions:

A sues B. His complaint alleges a sale and delivery of goods to B at B's request and B's promise to pay. 

B answers: (a) that the goods were not delivered, and: (b) that A by deed under seal released his claim.

A replies that the release was obtained by duress. 

The duress is automatically denied. 

The issues are then, delivery vel non and duress vel non.¹ 

1The matter of issues and the requirements of the several pleadings are more fully treated elsewhere. See Issue, Ch. 28, Answer, Ch. 19, Replication, Ch. 20, Demurrer, Ch. 17. 

§ 27. Logic of Code Pleading: It is clear from the foregoing that the pleadings follow the only course possible in reason. 

Every cause of action is a logical syllogism. The law is the major premise, the facts are the minor, and the judgment is the conclusion. 

The only ways to attack a syllogism, are 1. The major premise is not true-Demurrer. 

2. The premises are unrelated-Non Sequitur, Demurrer. 

3. The minor premise is not true-Traverse. 4. 

There are other facts which avoid the conclusion from the premises-Confession and Avoidance.

This is true of every attempt at reasoning; political, scientific, commercial, social or what not. "Jimmy, you struck Johnny." "There is no law against striking," a demurrer; "I didn't strike him," a traverse; "He was kicking my dog," justification, i.e., confession and avoidance. 

"Roosevelt ought to be elected President because he has been a good governor. "That's not a sufficient reason,' a demurrer; "He has not been a good governor, a traverse; "He's a great invalid," confession and avoidance. 

Roosevelt's protagonist would probably say that he was not invalid enough to hurt,-substantially a traverse-but the parties would have no way to try the issues except by the election which would not determine them. 

Another example is the Egyptian case, Thau v. Sebekotep.¹

§ 28. Definition: Jurisdiction is power to hear and deter mine. 1. The "subject matter,' i.e., this kind of a case; 2. For or against this plaintiff and defendant, i.e., jurisdiction of the person; 3. To render the particular judgment, sometimes called jurisdiction of the case. It is held that to render a valid judgment the court must have these three powers.¹ 

1Newman v, Bullock, 23 C. 217, 222, 47 P. 379. The court has no jurisdiction in this case over matters not involved in it. They belong in some other case.

It seems to the writer that although this case was rightly decided, for no court can adjudge matters not before it, yet really there are but two classes of jurisdiction, viz., of the subject matter and of the persons, i.e., the parties; that the reason why a court cannot render a judgment on matters not in the case is because it has no jurisdiction of the person of either plaintiff or defendant for that purpose. The plaintiff has submitted to the jurisdiction for one purpose, the defendant has been summoned and appeared for one purpose, and although the court of general jurisdiction has jurisdiction to try any sort of a case and render any sort of a judgment, yet it must first acquire jurisdiction of the persons who will be affected thereby, consequently it cannot, in an action, for example, on a promissory note, give judgment for damages for assault and battery. In other words, premising jurisdiction of the persons (parties), it has power to hear and determine the issues in that case (i.e., jurisdiction of the case), if not, not; therefore, it is only the determination of the issue of law, jurisdiction of the person vel non, which determines the so-called jurisdiction of the case. If jurisdiction of the parties, then of the case; if not, not; and there is no other alternative. The truth of this proposition is recognized in substance in Hume v. Robinson, 23 C. 359, 361, 47 P. 271, which holds that if the defendant "appears and takes part in the actual litigation of the matter determined," he will be bound by the judgment, although outside matters put in issue by the pleadings. The same thing appears in Franklin v. 

Burris, 35 C. 512, 518-9, 84 P. 809, and in Sowers v. Johnson, 59 C. 258, 149 P. 248, but jurisdiction of the subject matter cannot be conferred by consent, Id. 260. The rule that jurisdiction of the subject-matter and the person is all there is to it is stated and approved with citations in Camplin v. Jackson, 34 C. 447, 451, 83 P. 1017. The Courtright's

Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, § 50, speaks of "acquiring" jurisdiction "by filing a complaint" or "service of summons" and this may be called jurisdiction of the case; but what it means is merely that that particular court has acquired the right to control the proceedings when a complaint has been filed.

§ 29. Definition, continued: We elsewhere notice that there is much confusion of thought in regard to the term "jurisdiction." The Supreme Court has found it necessary to hold, what seems too obvious to question, that want of facts in the complaint does not deprive the court of jurisdiction. A court has jurisdiction to render a wrong judgment. Inconsistently with these propositions it is said that a court of equity has no jurisdiction to try the right to a public office, it must be by quo warranto,¹ and that that court has no jurisdiction to grant a new trial as a matter of right."

§ 34. Question, How Raised: If the lack of jurisdiction appears in the complaint the question of jurisdiction is raised by demurrer,¹ if not, then by answer.2 Such an answer is regarded as in abatement. The mere statement that the court has no jurisdiction is a conclusion of law, the facts which show that the court wants the power must be alleged, but, however the lack is made known, as soon as the court perceives that it has no jurisdiction over the subject matter it will dismiss the case. When the jurisdiction depends on a question of fact, e.g., the residence of some person, the question must be tried, and, to that end, must be raised in apt time and in the right manner."

51. Against Executors and Administrators. § 36. Real Party in Interest: The first question for the plaintiff's pleader is whom to make plaintiffs and defendants. 

Ordinarily the question is so simple that it needs no thought and is decided without a realization that it has been raised, as in case of an action on a promissory note, payable to the plaintiff, with one maker; but in some cases the question is difficult.¹

The code has many express regulations on the subject with a net result not very different from the combined rules of chancery and law.

Section 3. Every action shall be prosecuted in the name of the real party in interest except as otherwise provided in this act.

This is an enactment of the general rule in equity; true it applies to all actions, legal as well as equitable, but, since most. legal actions are brought in the name of the real party in interest anyway and since other sections greatly qualify the effect of the general clause, the effect of this section is not drastic but rather narrow. 

1Board of Supervisors v. Mineral Point R. R. Co., 24 Wis. 93. 

§ 37. Assignees: The principal effect of Section 3 is to enable an assignee of a chose in action to sue in his own name. 

He is regarded as the real party in interest because he will get the fruits of a victory, but, rather inconsistently with this view, it is held that the real party in interest is he in whom the legal title to the claim in suit is vested, and this although a third party will share in the proceeds of success.¹

Since it would seem that he who gets the proceeds is the real party in interest, these cases leave no general premise upon which to base an answer to the question, "Who is such party?"

If we say: "He who has the legal title," we have adopted 

Chitty's common law rule. If we say: "He who gets the benefit of the action," we exclude, e.g., the assignee for collection. Evidently, in Colorado, either may maintain the action. 

This seems to be considered in an action by an alimony creditor on a ne exeat bond where she is held to be the real party in interest though the bond runs to the sheriff.³ 

An action is maintained by the assignee of the surviving joint tenant of a savings account.*

§ 42. Adoption of Equity Rules: In Allen v. Tritch, 5 C. 

222, one of the earliest cases in which the Supreme Court of Colorado considered the new code, the old rules as to parties in equity were expressly adopted, and, substantially, chancery's threefold classification, proper, necessary and indispensable, was set out and the classes were clearly defined. 

It was there said (p. 227), quoting from Williams v. Bankhead, 19 Wall. 573: "The general rule as to parties in chancery is, that all ought to be made parties who are interested in the controversy, in order that there may be an end of litigation. 

But there are qualifications of this rule arising out of

PARTIES 

109 public policy and the necessities of particular cases. The true distinction appears to be as follows: "First: Where a party will be directly affected by a decree he is an indispensable party, unless the parties are too numerous to be brought before the court, when the case is subject to a special rule. "Second: Where a party is interested in the controversy but will not be directly affected by the decree made in his absence, he is not an indispensable party, but he should be made a party if possible and the court will not proceed to a decree without him if he can be reached. "Third: Where he is not interested in the controversy between the immediate litigants but has an interest in the subject matter which may be conveniently settled by the suit, and thereby prevent further litigation, he may be a party or not at the option of the complainant. 

§ 43. Equity Rules: These definitions are, perhaps, as accurate as possible and are very much like many others, but they are not easy of application to every concrete case. When will a party be "directly affected" by a decree? When are the parties "too numerous to be brought before the court?" If one is indispensable why are five hundred in the same condition dispensable? If one is indirectly interested so as to be subject to a decree and injuriously affected by it should it be wrong, why is he not as indispensable as if he were directly affected to the same degree?

These, and many other questions occur to anyone upon a little thought and they suggest, what is true, that the rules must be qualified and sometimes illogically qualified in particular cases. Indeed this is so true that it may almost be said that they are not rules but merely suggestions to guide, but not control, the courts.

The equity courts of England will not allow themselves to be paralyzed by the omission of a party beyond their jurisdiction, but the court will proceed to decree and save the rights of the absentee if it can, yet, in an extreme case, will grant a full decree and let the omitted parties reopen it, if, when they return, it is found to be erroneous.¹ The court cannot compel the absentee to do any act, but it can proceed against the other parties, and, if the disposition of the property is in their power, the court may act upon it. So if the court cannot do all that equity requires it will go as far as it can."

These cases and others like them were approved by our Supreme Court and the district court was required to go on with a case for an accounting by a fraudulent trustee though not all the beneficiaries under the trust could be reached.^

These cestuis que trustents were conceded to be necessary parties and would ordinarily be regarded as indispensable, yet the court could not allow itself to be palsied and its powers over those within its jurisdiction to be atrophied by the act of one in absenting himself. Yet the objection that an indispensable party is wanting is not waived by answering over.5 

Williams v. Whinyates, 2 Brown Chan. 399; Smith v. Hibernian

§ 44. Defect of Parties: "Defect or misjoinder of parties" 

is one of the grounds of demurrer to the complaint provided by the code. The expression "defect or misjoinder" is universally taken to mean misjoinder or nonjoinder; misjoinder, the inclusion of an improper party, and nonjoinder, the omission of an indispensable or necessary party. 

The general rules concerning joinder of parties are in the sections of the code already mentioned in this chapter, but for the reasons already stated, our higher courts have done little to elaborate or construe them. 

It is held that if a separate cause of action is stated against each of several defendants there is a misjoinder of parties,2 but, if an action be against several, plaintiff may have judg ment against those against whom a cause of action is proved," and may dismiss as to those improperly joined. A case against several, against one of whom no cause of action was stated, was discussed on the theory that there was a misjoinder of parties; but see above and notes.³ 4 The question of misjoinder of defendants cannot be raised by a joint demurrer of all the defendants, if a cause is stated against one. Some decisions are hard to reconcile." 

The burden of including all necessary parties is said to be on the plaintiff.8

56. Consistency in a Cause of Action. 

§ 52. What is a Cause of Action: The complaint must state facts which "constitute a cause of action." It is obvious that such facts are the cause of action, yet there are decisions which betray some confusion on this point and others which clarify the question.¹ "Cause" is the correlative of "result." The result is the judgment and the cause is the facts which justify it. It would have been better if the code had said "facts which constitute a right to a judgment" in favor of the plaintiff. 

There is, however, no confusion of thought on this point. Cause of action was regarded by the court as distinct from kind of action.2

It is held that the prayer for relief does not determine the cause of action. The test whether causes are one or more than one is "would a recovery on one bar the other?" Consistently, it is held that it is not a change of cause to strike out an illegal alternative promise, leaving a legal one. In an action for death of husband the administratrix may be substituted for the widow as plaintiff," and it does not change the cause to add a party."

³Mullen v. McKim, 22 C. 468, 474, 45 P. 416.

The reason recovery on one bars the other is because they are the same. We must first conclude that they are the same before we can say that recovery on one bars the other. § 53. What is a Cause of Action, continued: It is said that an amendment in a personal injury case which "adheres to the injury originally declared upon an alteration simply of the manner" by which it was caused does not change the cause of action. The decision was right because the negligence charged in the amendment was still the premature starting of machinery, but the dictum is too broad. If "injury" is used in its technical sense of violation of a legal right the dictum is true, but if in its ordinary sense of hurt or pain the dictum is not true. The truth is suggested on page 394, by the words "facts to establish the same act of negligence." We should apply Pomeroy's Analysis. The primary right was due care in the operation of the machinery, lack of care in starting it was a violation of that right.2

One violation of one primary right makes one cause of action, two violations of one primary right make two causes of action,s An action cannot, against defendant's objection be changed from contract to tort, but where a complaint showed both contract and tort an amendment which showed only tort was held proper."

§ 56. Consistency in a Cause of Action: A cause of action must be consistent. A plaintiff cannot have relief inconsistent with the contract he has alleged as the basis of his action.2

allegations, be made a defendant but no cause of action is thereby stated against him and there is but one.¹ Where contractors with the State gave a bond to the people of the State conditioned to pay their bills, an action on the bond by the people for several creditors stated but one cause." 

The opposite of joinder of causes is splitting them. One cause of action is divided and two actions brought thereon or an action brought for but a part of one cause. The question has seldom arisen in Colorado, but it was once held that where a fire insurance company was subrogated to the right of the insured to recover for the negligence of the railway company which had caused the fire, the fact that the insurance company's claim covered but a part of the damage did not amount to dividing the cause of action."

§ 63. Counts at Common Law: At common law it was the usual practice to state the cause of action in several ways in order to avoid a non-suit for variance at the trial. If the proofs did not fit one statement, the hope was that they would fit some one or more of the others. These causes of action were stated as if they were distinct, composed of different facts, as they sometimes, though rarely, actually were, and the declaration read as if several causes of action were joined in it. These separate statements were called "counts. The latter count, for example, in trover, would be for "other goods, chattels, etc., " that is, would appear to be of a separate matter. In assumpsit a common practice was to allege in the first count a special set of facts as nearly as possible what it was hoped the evidence would prove and then to add several counts in general assumpsit to cover the case of a possible failure of proof of the first count. Thus in an action on a promissory note, if proof of the note should fail a count for money lent might meet the proof and save the case. 

11 Chit. Pl. 226-7; 2 Chit. Pl. 887, or might be a cause of action in case, 1 Chit. Pl. 199. 

§ 64. Counts Under Codes: In pleading under the code the 

Supreme Court of Colorado has been less strict toward the practice of adding counts on the same transaction than some other courts, and the later attitude of all our courts has been more liberal than the former; the Supreme Court, however, always showing more liberality than the others.

The only direct statement unfavorable to the allowance of repeated separate statements of the same cause of action that I have found is a dictum by Reed, J., in Manders v. Craft, 3 C. 

A. 236, 238, 32 P. 836, that a count on an express contract cannot stand together with one on quantum meruit; on the other hand both the court of appeals and the Supreme Court has repeatedly approved such practice¹, but have sometimes qualified their approval.2

§ 65. Term "Count" in Colorado Reports: The term 

"count" is often used in our reports, sometimes to denote causes of action really separate; for example: An action on several separate contracts for printing and publishing,' and sometimes to indicate variant statements of the same transaction, as special assumpsit and quantum meruit², or simply statements in somewhat different ways of the same transaction.³ 

The term is too convenient to be discarded and probably never will be. The note below shows some additional cases in which our higher courts have used it in one sense or another. 

At least twice it has been used to denote a separate defense.5 It is safe to say, from these cases, that counts may be used to avoid variance wherever it is reasonably convenient, but the Supreme Court would hardly sanction the common law custom of adding to a count in special assumpsit a dozen or more formal counts in general assumpsit on the mere chance that some one of them might be met by the evidence.

§ 66. 

Counts in Assumpsit: The use of counts at common law, especially in assumpsit, progressed so far that forms were published containing a space for a count in special assumpsit followed by all the possible counts in general assumpsit in pearl or diamond type, a mere formality, never intended to be read, but sufficient many times to avoid a variance. Of course this method frustrated pleading's main purpose, because, when the general issue was pleaded to such a declaration, nobody knew or could learn, from the facts set forth, what the issue was, and also well nigh emasculated the pleadings for their secondary purpose which was to inform the opponents of the facts which constituted the cause of action and the defense.¹ 

Under the code pleaders have never yet been permitted to go so far, but the Supreme Court has held a refusal to compel plaintiff to elect between his counts to be no error,2 and, conversely, cases have been reversed because election was compelled."

The question is elaborately discussed in C. & F. Lumber Co. v. D. & R. G. R. 

Co., 17 C. A. 275, 282, 68 P. 670, and it is there said, quoting from Follett v. Ry. Co., 36 N. Y. Supp. 200, "The only motive conceivable for urging such a motion (to elect) is the hope that the party might make an unwise election to the detriment of his rights," and, indeed, that is doubtless always the chief, if not the only motive for such proceeding. Another purpose,

sometimes, is delay. The ostensible reason always is that defendant does not know the case; but he always does. It is usually true, however, that the election narrows the issues.

§ 69. Election of Remedies: Closely related to election of counts is election of remedies. If one has two inconsistent remedies he must choose between them and his choice of one

SEPARATE CAUSE OF ACTION 

127 2 destroys his right to the other. Having sued for fraud and deceit one cannot, after defeat, maintain an action ex contractu on the same facts. So an action for rescission destroys a right of action on the rescinded contract. Otto, 4 Sandf. 668, that no allegation is material unless an issue on it will decide the case.2

§ 73. What Allegations are Material: In every class of action, upon what principle soever they may be classified, there must be certain allegations without which any given pleading will be insufficient, but this insufficiency must be of substance because Ch. XII defines an issue as a denial of a material allegation and a denial of a matter not of the substance of the cause of action or defense could not create an issue because a determination of it would not determine the case.¹

The cases which definitely decide whether an allegation is a material allegation by that term are few, but those which decide in effect whether this or that allegation is essential to the pleading which contains or omits it are many; indeed every demurrer for want of facts and every motion to strike and sometimes one to make more specific calls for such a decision.

We cite some such cases in the note below.2

§ 78. In General: Before we take up the formation of pleadings it is well to consider the rule of construction of their language.

The general rule for the construction of pleadings under the code is that the pleading is to be taken in its entirety and receive a liberal construction. "No matter how clumsily or loosely a complaint may be put together or what unnecessary matter it may contain, if the facts can be found in it that would authorize a recovery, then, against a general demurrer, it must be upheld." It is also held that indefinite and equivocal pleadings, when capable of any interpretation, are to be "construed most strongly against the pleader." It is said that on general demurrer, prior to trial, a complaint is "construed most strongly against the pleader.""

Pleadings to restrain proceedings to incorporate a town were construed as quo warranto.5

§ 83. Function: The function of the complaint is to state a cause of action';

to allege the facts which give the plaintiff

a right to some sort of a judgment against the defendant, and a judgment without a complaint is void. As has been said, the substantive law tells in every case what those facts must be. It says that he who buys goods and receives them must pay for them what they are worth, and so if a grocer delivers goods to his customer who receives them, he has a right to receive and the customer a duty to pay what the goods are worth; the complaint, then, must show the sale, delivery and value. It says that he who forcibly enters the land of another must pay damages, and so if you break your neighbor's fence and trample his crops you must recompense him. The complaint, then, must allege a forcible entry into his land and the damage.s 

1See "Cause of Action," Ch. 7. 

2 Beckett v. Cuenin, 15 C. 281, 285, 25 P. 167. 

Equitable Co. v. M. & D. Canal Co., 20 C. A. 465, 79 P. 747. $ 84. Pomeroy's Analysis: Professor Pomeroy has stated a most useful analysis of a cause of action. Every cause of action is made up of a primary right and duty and a violation thereof which produces a secondary right and duty, the result of such violation, and every violation of a right has its remedy, i.e., secondary right.

In the case of the sale and delivery of goods the primary right is in the seller to have the price and the corresponding duty is in the purchaser to pay it, the violation is failure to pay and the secondary or resulting right is to have damages+ for that violation. In the case of the trespass on the owner's land the primary right is the exclusive enjoyment of the land and the duty is to respect that right, the violation is the entry and the resulting right is to receive and the duty is to pay damages.

Actions at law as distinguished from suits in equity are commonly divided into two classes called actions ex delicto and actions ex contractu or tort and contract. The classification is reasonable but the terms are unfortunate because not correlative. A tort is the correlative of a breach of contract. not of the contract.

The confusion of thought caused by these inaccurate terms. will be remedied if we apply the Pomeroy analysis.

§ 85. Pomeroy's Analysis, continued: In actions ex delicto the primary right is one given by the substantive law to every man in a like situation, without action by the parties. The simplest case is assault and battery. Every man has a right to his person free from assault. It is a primary right given by the substantive law to him and everybody else. A blow violates that right and he may maintain an action for damages. So in an action for trespass on land: The law gives to every man the exclusive possession of his own land, which is a primary right, and a right to damages results from a violation of it. A violation of such a right is called a tort,¹ and an action for such damages is an action ex delicto.2 In an action ex contractu, however, the primary right is created by some act of the parties themselves. Goods have been sold, purchased, delivered and received; the vendor has a primary right to be paid. Jones agrees to build a house for 

Smith and Smith to give a parcel of land in payment; either has a primary right to the fulfillment of the other's agreement and the other a duty to fulfill it, and a failure on the part of either gives rise to the secondary right to damages, but neither these rights nor duties existed until the parties had done. something which amounted to what the law calls a contract, that is, until the parties had conferred each upon the other a primary right the violation of which would create the seeondary. We shall refer often to these matters.

§ 86. Pomeroy's Analysis, continued: The secondary right is always the conclusion of a logical syllogism of which the substantive law is the major and the facts to be alleged in the complaint the minor premise.

Thus, in an action for conversion of goods; the major premise may be stated: He who converts the goods of another must pay him damages; the minor, the defendant has converted the goods (automobile) of the plaintiff; the conclusion, the defendant must pay the plaintiff damages.

The major premise, however, should never be alleged.¹ The complaint states the minor premise, and leaves the court to apply the law, the major premise, and asks for a judgment which shall establish the conclusion. 

The substance, then, of the complaint for conversion must be: "The defendant converted the (watch) of the plaintiff."

This is followed by a demand for judgment. Further particulars are required to be stated, which we shall consider later, but they are not necessary to illustrate the substance of a complaint. 'Denver v. Bossie, 83 C. 329, 330, 266 P. 214. 

§ 87. What Facts Must Be Stated: The Courtright's Mills 

Anno. Code, and C. L. '21, Code, § 55, requires the complaint to state "the facts constituting the cause of action." 

You may say that the law, the major premise, is a constituent of the cause of action, and there is something to be said in favor of that proposition, but the view of the old pleaders, both at common law and in equity was, and that of the framers of the code was, that the cause of action was the facts because of which the plaintiff wanted relief, or, in other words, men look to facts to explain or justify rights and claims, and seldom state the major premise of their syllogisms. If we say a passenger fell overboard and was drowned we do not state the natural law, that persons who fall overboard are likely to be drowned. Everybody is presumed to know that, and the court is presumed to know the law and only needs to be told the facts, so the facts only should be stated, and for our present purposes they do constitute, i.e., are, the cause of action.¹

They are regarded as the cause and the right to a judgment pursuant to an action as the effect, so we ignore the proposition that without the law there would be no such effect, and consent to the implication of the code that facts constitute a "cause of action," that is: Give a right to a judgment of a court for something. The code then, requires a statement of the facts, not the law, which constitute the cause of action,2 and all additional facts are forbidden.³

It follows from what we have said, does it not, that, under the code, the definition of a cause of action is "those facts which justify a judgment against the defendant in favor of the plaintiff?"4

When, therefore, your client brings you a statement of facts your first duty is to consider whether they justify any judgment in his favor, and, if they do, you must know how properly and against whom to state them.

§ 91. 

Forms of Action: The code, as we have seen, abolishes forms of action but not forms of statement; that would be impossible, because statement must assume form of some sort and established forms are recommended.¹ In addition to that, however, we cannot understand the category "causes of action" without analysis, and, to analyze it we must divide into sub-categories or classes. These are sometimes referred to as forms of action, but, of course, this term does not denote form according to the common law idea, but denotes categories according to classification which has been found necessary in practice according to the code. The form is never stated in pleading under the code. The plaintiff states his ultimate facts and has such judgment as they justify.³ 2 The first and most important are the classes, legal and equitable. These classes are distinguished for the same reasons, by the same terms and by the same rules as before the code. 

Equitable relief will not be granted where there is an adequate legal remedy and will be where there is not, and the other conditions which will justify equitable relief are the same now as then, e.g.. administration of trusts, injunction, bills quia timet, of interpleader, etc., but under the code the method of statement of a cause of action in equity is the same as at law and is governed by the same rules, moreover those rules are approximately those which were theoretically followed in the common law system. This is shown by Ch. XII and the other sections already referred to, which impose rules inconsistent with the course of pleading in chancery but based on the fundamental theory of the older system, viz., that there is always an issue the determination of which will determine the case.

2Gutheil v. Montclair, 32 C. 421, 425, 76 P. 1050.
