Dudley, 69 C. 560, 195 P. 649. § 92. Equitable Actions: Actions in equity, that is actions for relief which before the code have been brought only in a court of chancery, were never governed by rules as to "forms

THE COMPLAINT 

145 of action."

There was never any such thing as a "form of action" in chancery. Authors on the subject have sometimes classified causes of action in equity for the purpose of a clear understanding of chancery jurisdiction, and those classifications are still used by both bar and bench for that purpose. 

For example, we say of a bill in chancery, this is a "bill for an injunction" or "creditor's bill" or "bill to quiet title," as the case may be, and, under the code, we say the same, sometimes not even substituting "complaint" for "bill." In alleging the facts constituting a right to equitable relief we must allege the same facts¹ as in chancery, and they have the same effect. 

In nearly every case the facts bring it within one of the recognized classes and the pleader is required, as at law, to determine to what class the action belongs, if he would plead intelligently. The classifications in equity were and are based on the nature of the relief desired, while those of the common law had sometimes one basis of distinction and sometimes another, and the classes were not mutually exclusive.

§ 94. Divisions of Actions at Law: The main divisions of these actions are ex delicto and ex contractu. As has been said, these terms are not happy ones. They are not correlative. A tort is the correlative of a breach of contract. If we follow Prof.

Pomeroy's analysis of a cause of action, that it consists of a primary right and a corresponding duty, a violation thereof and a resulting right and corresponding duty, we can detect

the fundamental, logical difference between these two classes of actions. The difference is in the primary right. In an action ex delicto the primary right is given by law to every man in a like situation'; while in actions ex contractu the primary right is created by the parties. Attention to this distinction is of advantage when drawing a complaint on facts which justify an action in tort or contract, that is, in either of the two classes in question. 

1Ante: In General, § 82. 

§ 95. Actions ex delicto: These actions, under the code, are not, as at common law, divided into definite classes, called forms. An action is described, often by its purpose: e.g., "for possession and damages, or by its cause: e.g., "action for personal injuries," more often, however, the common law terminology is used, e.g., "trespass," "trover," "replevin." 

§ 96. Actions Ex Contractu: This class of actions is sub divided only as are actions ex delicto. Though the term "assumpsit" is occasionally used, yet more often the action is denoted more specifically, as "an action on a promissory note, or "an action for goods sold and delivered." Indeed, the common law terms for forms of action ex contractu are less in use than those ex delicto. "Assumpsit," "covenant," "debt"" are, however, not uncommon, but "account" is never used, probably because actions for accounting are viewed and treated as equitable. 

1City ordinances are usually enforced by a fine recoverable by an action of debt. An example is Peo. v. Drug Co., 10 C. A. 507, 51 P. 1010. 

§ 97. Primary Right, How Exprssed: Since matters of law are not to be alleged,' and the primary right in actions ex delicto is a matter of law, nothing need be said about that in pleading except to show the relation of the parties to the legal proposition. In the simplest case, assault and battery, not even that need be stated, because every man's relation to his own body is a matter of common knowledge, judicially known, and requires no allegation; but in an action for an injury to property the relation of the plaintiff to the property must be alleged, and for such purpose the words, "of the plaintiff" are usually enough."

In actions ex contractu it is necessary to state the facts which will show that the defendant by a transaction called a contract has given the plaintiff some primary right which he, the defendant, has violated, and that some secondary right has resulted.

§ 100. Things Judicially Known: As to pleading law we have said enough, and matters judicially known are classed as matters of law,' and should not be alleged. 

What matters are judicially known? Of what matters does the court, as the saying is, "take judicial notice"?

All matters of common knowledge: The sun rises in the morning, summer is hotter than winter, men are stronger than women, dogs sometimes bite, horses are apt to be frightened;

These four classes of facts, law, common knowledge, geography, and history and tradition, include, broadly considered, all matters which the court will notice without allegation or evidence. All are considered matters of law and no issue of fact can be raised on any of them. More detailed classification is often made," but this is enough for present purposes. All matters in the record of the case in hand are of course judicially noticed because already alleged. This includes original pleadings on consideration of amended ones, and record in the same court in actions between the same parties on the same issues'; but not generally in another case. It is manifest that the facts judicially known vastly outnumber those facts which must be alleged in any single case. 

Except things judicially noticed, things unalleged are assumed not to exist."

§ 102. Legal Conclusions: The basic and logical reason for the exclusion of the allegation of a conclusion of law in pleading is that it begs the question. The substantive law is the major, the facts alleged are the minor premise and the conclusion follows and is thus demonstrated; but if you state the conclusion it stands without support. So of the final conclusion; the law is presumed to be known, the facts are made known by the pleadings and the conclusion of law logically follows. The statement of the conclusion of law, if permitted, would permit the allegation of the final conclusion which would dispense with pleading altogether and frustrate its principal purpose, because the court would know no more about the precise matter in dispute after the pleadings than before.

This is illustrated in our procedure before justices of the peace, where there are no pleadings, and the summons states merely what the plaintiff claims; i.e., the final legal conclusion. 

Various allegations have been held not to be conclusions of law. A statement of the principles upon which complainants (mind healers) proceed in their business.¹ Ownership and conversion. By virtue of two chattel mortgages is owner.³

§ 103. Evidential Facts: One reason for the inhibition of evidential matters in pleading is that if any is permitted then all, and we have no limit but the whim of the judge or the vocabulary of the pleader, and there is no standard of sufficiency; but the logical reason is that evidential allegations confuse the issues. They hide or blur the real issues by presenting false ones, and by their tendency to immaterialty and irrelevancy. The denial of an allegation merely evidential raises no real issue because the decision of the question thus raised will not decide the case. (* Take, for example, the plea of the statute of limitations. 

The proper plea is: **action did not accrue within six years," etc.; or "defendant did not promise within six years **'' etc.; or as the case may be. An allegation that the action accrued on such and such a date though more than six years before the suit was begun would be evidential and insufficient.2

The reason for such a proposition is evident if we suppose a traverse of the evidential allegation. The issue would then be: "promise on (the specified date) vel non." If the jury finds that the promise was made on that date the case is determined and defendant wins, but if that it was not then made there is no determination. The apparent issue, therefore, is not an issue because its decision will not decide the case.³

It follows, of course, since evidential allegations are barred, that an amendment which changes evidential facts only is of no avail.¹ 

1Sweet v. Barnard, 66 526, 534-5, 182 P. 22; Adams v. Tucker, 6 C. A. 395, 397, 40 P. 783. 

2Sweet v. Barnard, 66 C. 526, 182 P. 22.

The plea that the promise was made "more than six years before" action was commenced would seem to be logically good, notwithstanding the dictum in Sweet v. Barnard, 66 C. 526, 535, 182 P. 22, because an issue on that allegation would determine the case.

§ 106. Adoption of Allegations: At common law it was customary in any count of the declaration after the first, instead of repeating an ultimate fact, alleged in any previous count, to refer to it by the phrase, "as in said first count herein stated" or the equivalent. The original code of Colorado,¹ and all since, have required each of the several causes of action to be stated "separately in the complaint" and this was regarded as an inhibition of the common law practice, consequently long paragraphs and pages were often repeated, and re-repeated in complaints. To remedy this the Supreme Court, under the Act of 1913, which authorized the regulation of practice by rule, provided that allegations "need not be repeated but may be incorporated in other counts * reference. This was done to enable a pleader to so incorporate those parts of a previous count which were material to the subsequent one, but pleaders immediately began, in the statement of a later cause of action, to say, in substance, that by

THE COMPLAINT 

153 the plaintiff "adopts the allegations in the first cause of action," thus taking them all in, relevant and irrelevant, a practice which confused the issues irremediably, and often made a later count state several causes of action. 

The Supreme Court has corrected this misapplication of the rule by several decisions which point out the faults of the practice and condemn it. The right way is to refer only to the relevant part of the previous cause by the words "as in the first cause of action alleged."

2Sec. 76 of Courtright's Mills Anno. Code and C. L. '21, Code. 

3Supreme Court Rule 2, Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, p. 653. 

4Fulton Co. v. Farmers Co., 76 C. 472, 476, 231 P. 61; James v. 

McIntyre, 81 C. 548, 550, 256 P. 657; Hicks v. Cramer, 85 C. 409, 412, 277 P. 299. 

Fulton Co. v. Farmers Co., 76 C. 472, 476, 231 P. 61. For example: "The plaintiffs are partners and the defendant a corporation as in the first cause of action alleged." 1 

§ 107. Partnership, How Alleged: The fact of partnership, whether of plaintiffs or defendants, should be specifically alleged. The form of such allegations is fixed but the usual form should be used. To name the partnership in the title "a partnership composed of A, B and C" does not make A, B or C a party to the action, but "P and H, partners doing business under the firm name and style of P & Co., defendants, in the title, is a sufficient allegation of partnership.* 

Allegations which show that defendant corporation was jointly and severally liable with the corporation with which the contract in suit was made, leave it unnecessary to show they were partners."

§ 111. The Prayer: The code¹ requires a "demand for the relief which the plaintiff claims." This in equity cases is commonly called the "prayer" and seldom in any case the demand. Here we use the term to include the statement of the plaintiff's claim in any action. 

It was early held that "the office of the prayer for relief * *'' is "that of indicating the relief allowable where no answer is filed." The code, Section 187, says that "the relief granted 446

A. 76, 127 P. 241. § 112. Prayer, continued: With respect to the first clause of this sentence two principal questions arise: 

1. When does "the relief granted" exceed that demanded?"" And, 2. What is the effect of the prayer for general relief?

Upon the first question it was said that the code "necessarily implies that in case no answer is filed the judgment rendered must be of the character prayed for in the complaint," and it was held that a joint judgment instead of a several as prayed was not of such character, the opinion at the same time saying that it was not in excess of the prayer.2 

It is said that "relief" is the judgment and the means of enforcing it.

¹One instance of a judgment greater than the amount prayed for in an action for unliquidated damages. Ruth v. Smith, 29 C. 154, 68 P. 278. 

2Russell v. Shurtleff, 28 C. 414, 420, 65 P. 27. The case also holds that neither an appearance nor a demurrer constitutes an answer; but, since it is said that the judgment did not exceed the prayer, this point seems irrelevant to the decision. What the decision really does is to add to the word "exceed" the words "or differ in character from." It is also noticeable that although the second opinion (the first was withdrawn) is on the ground that the judgment did exceed the prayer (p. 

419-20), yet the final opinion (p. 420) asserts that it did not. The remarkable and farreaching thing about this decision, however, is that it decides that, although a judgment in excess of the prayer would be a mere error, a judgment which differs in character (whatever that may mean) from the prayer is void. The reasonableness of this seems doubtful. If the facts alleged and proved justify the judgment, what more is necessary? In Brown v. Bilton, 34 C. 135, 137-8, 81 P. 758; a demurrer to the complaint was overruled and a judgment was rendered which the allegations justified, then upon the objection that such a judgment had not been prayed, it was held that that was immaterial because what was omitted from the prayer was already in the body of the complaint of which the prayer was not a part. This reasoning is hard to follow. If, a demurrer cannot take the place of an answer, there was no answer, and the judgment therefore could not exceed or according to Russell v. Shurtleff, 28 C. 414, 420, 65 P. 27, differ in character from that prayed. The decision was right but the right ground for it was that the prayer was sufficient. The complaint contained a general prayer but the opinion does not notice it, yet even without it, the prayer seems sufficient. 

3Jahl v. Lewis, 57 C. 109, 139 P. 1113; but, of course, no one prays for execution. 1

Although it is held that a demurrer is not equivalent to the answer mentioned in Section 187,3 yet the proposition that the prayer will be disregarded and relief given according to the facts was asserted in a case where there was a demurrer to the camplaint sustained, but no answer.*

There seems to be no case in Colorado which affirms a judgment which exceeds or differs in character from that prayed unless there was an answer.

§ 114. Anticipated Defenses: Some pleaders find it impos sible to resist the temptation to anticipate defenses and the defect is common. The example of most frequent occurrence is the statement of fact or facts to negative contributory negligence. The reason for the rule that defenses must not be anticipated is the reason which lies at the root of all inhibitions in pleading, viz: It confuses the issues. It may be, and often is, true that there was no contributory negligence, and that the defendant would not attempt to plead or prove it. Then the statement in the complaint is immaterial, surplusage, and, at its best, useless, and therefore should be stricken.2 

For these reasons the anticipated defense, whenever it is recognized as such, is regarded as null, and a denial of it raises no issue. It is not admitted by failure to deny, and is often criticized and condemned.5

§ 120. In General: It is necessary for the complaint to show injury in jurem, i.e., violation of a right¹; damage, that is harm to the plaintiff, and the damages claimed. 

Injury and injuries are often confused with damage, and damage with damages.²

The allegation of damage is subject to no fixed rules and cannot be. It is customarily exaggerated in order to permit full proof. In Colorado the tendency has been to require a more specific statement of the damage than at common law, though there is nothing in the code which requires it. 

The measure of damages is a matter of substantive law and will be noticed here only incidentally. Our subject embraces the allegations with reference to them, so of the question for what damage one may have a judgment. 

1See Pomeroy's Analysis, herein. 

217 C. J. 698. We speak of personal injuries to denote hurts to the body, which is properly damage. Thus in an action for assault and battery, the blow is the injury, and a broken nose is the damage, though often called injury, and the compensation sought is the damages. These terms are constantly misused. The distinction between damage and damages must always be kept in mind. A plaintiff's leg is broken by defendant's act; the damage is the breaking of the leg, the damages is the sum for which he asks judgment therefor. The former was always stated with some detail, the latter with none. 

17 C. J. 710. At common law it was ad damnum; under the code it is the demand for judgment; 

Silverberg v. Kiesler, 74 C. 21, 23, 217 P. 70. They are much confused in text books and reports, which causes some confusion of thought, yet

are distinct in substance.

See Damages, Ch. 13. The common law recognized the distinction between the terms injury and damage by the expressions damnum absque injuria and injuria sine damno. 

81 Arch. Nisi Prius, 551. § 121. In General, continued: It is common to add to the statement of damage the allegation that plaintiff has thereby suffered damage in the sum of $.......... ....., and this is regarded as a part of the statement of damage. The code,¹ seems to regard the requirement of a statement of the amount of damage as satisfied by the demand of judgment,' but the cases leave the matter so that the omission of the allegation is questionable. The objection that the amount of damage is not stated cannot be made if defendant goes to trial without it.³ 

¹Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. I.. '21, Code, § 55, Third. 

2Tucker v. Parks, 7 C. 62, 67, 1 P. 427; D. & R. G. v. Klaes, 40 C. 

126, 90 P. 60. Yet Silverberg v. Kiesler, 74 C. 21, 23, 217 P. 70, seems to settle the matter. 

3D. R. & G. v. Klaes, 40 C. 125, 129, 90 P. 60. 

§ 122. General and Special: Damage is either general or special. General may be compensated on a general allegation of the amount, but special must be particularly alleged.' But it seems that any damage may be proved under a general allegation if there is no motion to make more definite.¹ General damage is the usual and natural consequence of the defendant's act, all other is special. The class of cases in which this distinction is most definite is libel and slander. There the accusation of a felony or slander in respect to plaintiff's business or calling, is "actionable per se.' 

Another example is an action for beating a servant where the allegation of special damage "per quod servitium amisit" is necessary. Although a motion to make the complaint more specific might have been sustained the complaint as it stood was sufficient to let in proof of special damage.* 

¹Denver Elec. Co. v. Lawrence, 31 C. 301, 314-15, 73 P. 39. The court here uses the word "damages" to mean "damage"; and if physical or mental pain is natural and inevitable result of the injury it need not be specially alleged. Colo. Spgs. v. Marr, 26 C. A. 48, 141 P. 142. 

2Tucker v. Parks, 7 C. 62, 69, 1 P. 427. General damage is presumed to result from defendant's act. 1 Chit. Pl. 338, 395, 398. Pueblo v. 

Griffin, 10 C. 366, 15 P. 616. On pages 395 and 398 of 1 Chit. Pl., it is said that special damage must be the "legal and natural consequence." 

81 Chit. Pl. 396; Coulter v. Barnes, 71 C. 243, 205 P. 948; Switzer v. 

Anthony, 71 C. 291, 296, 206 P. 891. 

Farrer v. Caster, 17 C. A. 41, 45-6, 67 P. 171. The action was for breach of contract to deliver cattle, the item of damage in question, was rent of a pasture to receive them, "the complaint set forth in a general way the expense and loss to which the plaintiff testified." Since the report does not show how general this setting forth was, the decision is not very instructive.

§ 127. Special Damage, How Alleged: Although the code was intended to simplify the allegations of pleadings yet for causes which are hard to discover the courts have compelled more elaborate statements under it than at common law and this is true in the allegation of special damage. The Supreme 

Court, however, as we have noticed elsewhere, has not gone so far in this direction as the lower courts. No definite rule can be stated, but the decisions may be correlated and that may prove worthwhile.

§ 129. Damages in General: The term "damages" is plural in form and so treated in ordinary use, but in mental conception is singular, and denotes the sum of money for which one party, usually the plaintiff, claims judgment against another for the violation of a primary right. They are the legal consequence of damage.¹ The law of the measure of damages is another branch of the remedial law but must be incidentally noticed here. 

To justify a judgment for damages the action must, of course, be for damages, and a proceeding for adjudication of water rights cannot be converted into an action for damages,² but a claim for the wrong measure of damages will not vitiate a complaint where under the allegations, plaintiff is entitled to general damages, and a court of equity will sometimes award damages to do complete justice.* 

¹See Damage. Tidd's Pr. 870. 17 C. J. 698.

Aetna Co. v. North Sterling Dist., 75 C. 185, 190-1, 225 P. 261. 

421 C. J. 141. 

§ 130. Ex Delicto: The damages in tort are usually unliquidated and subject to the estimation of the jury. In an action for conversion the general measure of damages is held to be the value of the goods at the time of the conversion.2 

1Nielson v. Hansford, 78 C. 456, 242 P. 677. 

2Barkhausen v. Bulkley, 90 C. 558, 560-1, 11 P.(2d) 220. 

§ 131. Ex Delicto, continued: The rules as to measure of damages are a matter of that branch of the law. The general rule is "those which result directly and proximately from the wrong complained of."" In deceit in inducing plaintiff to exchange notes the measure of damages is the difference in value of the notes.2

In the case of false representations as to land the damages are the difference between the value of the land as represented and as it is.8 The statement of the damages should be followed by a demand for judgment. This demand is not, it must be remembered, a statement of damage." 

Damages for annoyance and inconvenience are not recoverable.Ⓡ 

In Chandler v. Ziegler, the damages would be stated in substance, "that the value of said land if there had been restrictions as represented by defendant would have been ($2,000.00) and that its actual value does not exceed ($1,000.00)." 

In the case of false warranty (of a horse) that he was sound, kind and gentle in harness, the allegation of damage is that he is worthless and has (kicked and injured another horse, and has run away and injured plaintiff and his wagon, or according to fact'); i.e., the consequences of the fact that he was not "kind" and "gentle in harness." § 134. Amount Issuable: At common law the amount of damages was regarded as not issuable.¹ This was logically correct because a traverse of merely the amount of damages would not raise an issue which would decide the case. amount of damages, however, was always regarded as in question and evidence was always admissible upon that question. The modern English rule is the same. In most of the code states the practice is the same but in Colorado it was early held that on account of the absence of a Section of our code which appears in others an undenied allegation of the amount of damages was admitted.¹ The conclusion from these decisions is that it is unsafe to leave the amount of damages undenied ; the common use, however, of the general denial will prevent the frequent rise of the question.

'21, Code, § 186, which, inconsistently with the opinion, requires proof of damages in case of default and it ignores the fact that the common law of England is law in Colorado, and, above all, ignores the fact that § 55, on which it relies, does not require the allegation of the amount but only the demand. § 136. Exemplary Damages: At common law the jury in certain cases ex delicto were allowed to enlarge their verdict beyond mere compensation to plaintiff, by consideration of the grossness of the wrong done him. Such damages were called exemplary, vindictive or punitive damages and sometimes, colloquially, smart money. The Supreme Court of Colorado originally followed this law,' but afterwards repudiated it.² 

It was later restored by statute. Exemplary damages are held to be inconsistent with an action on contract, but survive to the administrator or executor. In one case the court said that the exemplary

should not exceed the actual damages, but the opinion was later construed, and qualified." 

We are here concerned with the allegation of such damages

§ 138. Mitigation: Mitigation of damages is logically miti gation of damage, in consequence of which damages are reduced. The facts which mitigate, lessen, the damage are pleaded as if in confession and avoidance, and are in substance a partial defense.¹

62, 1 P. 427), any facts tending to show mitigation could not be confession and avoidance, but evidence in support of a denial, that is, argumentative traverse. Payne v. Williams, 62 C. 86, 160 P. 196. This position was taken in Bijou Dist. v. Cateran Co., 73 C. 93, 96-7, 213

P. 999.

§ 140. In General: The motions which directly affect the pleadings are: 

1. The motion to strike; 

2. The motion to make more specific and certain; 

3. The motion to amend; 

4. The motion to elect; 

5. The motion to separate.

There are other motions which are based on the pleadings, but which do not directly affect them: 

1. The motion for judgment on the pleadings; 

2. The motion for judgment non obstante veredicto; 

3. The motion in arrest of judgment. 

There are others which, while not directly based on the pleadings, are sometimes affected by them: 1. 

The motion for dismissal or non-suit; 

2. The motion for a directed verdict; 

3. The motion for a new trial.

There are other motions which require no notice here. 

Motions are not pleadings, nor subject to the rules of pleading, but are sometimes treated as demurrers.2 1 

¹Hanson v. McCann, 20 C. A. 43, 48, 76 P. 983. 

2Dunphy v. St. Mary's Hosp., 60 C. 196, 153 P. 89. See Mills Dig.

There was a rule in the Denver district that a motion decided by one judge could not be renewed before another, but it was held that the

rule did not forbid a new motion against an amended complaint. Sch. 

Dist. v. Stone, 14 C. A. 211, 218, 59 P. 885. 

§ 141. The Motion to Strike: This motion has its sanction in Section 60. "Sham and irrelevant answers and defenses, and so much of any pleading as may be irrelevant and redundant, immaterial or insufficient may be stricken out, on motion,

This motion was not unknown to the common law. 1 Arch. N. P. 393. The striking out is a fiction, not a fact and the stricken pleading is still a part of the record for review. Henry v. Montezuma Co., 55 C. 182, 133 P. 747.

It has been determined that the purpose of the motion to strike parts of a pleading is to clear away rubbish.¹ It was often used in place of a demurrer, the Supreme Court, however, has never approved that practice but has held the contrary, always declaring, nevertheless, that irrelevant and immaterial matter should be erased.³ 2 

Of course a sufficient defense may not be stricken, nor a material allegation, and if a material allegation has been stricken the Supreme Court will not consider a demurrer. An evasive or irrelevant answer should be stricken." It is error, however, to strike a whole complaint though full of useless and unnecessary matter, if it states a cause of action. 

A sham pleading is one good in form but false in fact. Not in good faith.10 Its character must appear aliende,¹º because if the truth is really in dispute the issues must be tried.¹¹

§ 142. The Motion to Strike, continued: Surplusage is always irrelevant or immaterial or both. It was stricken out on motion at common law, and is also under the code,' but neither there nor under the code will mere surplusage vitiate a pleading and so a denial of a motion to strike it is error without prejudice. Both evidential matters and conclusions of law are disregarded in determining the sufficiency of a pleading,* but both are bad pleading and are condemned. Some examples of surplusage may be found in the reports, generally, however, such matters do not reach the upper courts. Surplusage does not constitute a separate cause of action." "There is no excuse for confusing an issue and encumbering a record by allegations which are wholly irrelevant, but which, in the pleader's mind, may tend to excite sympathy, or arouse prejudice in the minds of the jury. Such should be stricken out. "A failure to do this increases the burden of the trial court as well as that of the reviewing court."' 

But the motion is said to be in the sound discretion of the trial court.⁹

§ 143. The Motion to Strike, Waiver: The code, while it provides for waiver of certain grounds of demurrer, says nothing about waiver of motions, but the courts have held that the motion to strike may be waived in various ways.¹ 

By failure to object, Foley v. Coon, 41 C. 482, 436, 93 P. 13.

By amendments, Rawlings v. Casey, 19 C. A. 152, 154, 73 P. 1090. By a subsequent stipulation as to merits, Sweeney v. Amphlett, 67 C. 366,

176 P. 748. To strike parts of answer waived by reply, Bollen v. Woodhams, 68 C. 322, 190 P. 427. By delay till trial begun, Martin v. 

McLaughlin, 9 C. 153, 10 P. 806. By delay to move to strike amended complaint till case was at issue, Johnson v. Cummings, 12 C. A. 17, 20, 55 P. 269. A motion to strike is referred to, after answer, as if it were not waived, no comments, Burrell v. Masters, 65 C. 310, 312, 176 P. 316.

By filing a replication plaintiff waives the granting of defendant's motion to strike parts of complaint, Hartford Co. v. Bank, 96 C. 127, 128, 40 P.(2d) 254. 

§ 144. The Motion to Strike, Amendments: A motion to strike an amended complaint is proper if it was filed without opportunity for the defendant's attorney to examine it,¹ but an amended answer should not be stricken if it contains a defense even though mingled with irrelevant matter. If in substance the same as an original which has been stricken it is properly stricken.2

Although a motion to strike an amended complaint has been overruled by one judge, defendant may move before another judge to strike part of it.³

An amendment which does not amend an insufficient complaint may be wholly stricken, but not if it states a cause of action.*

A plea in mitigation of damages was stricken out and, when evidence in mitigation was nevertheless admitteed, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment for defendant because mitigation of damages had not been pleaded.5

§ 146. Motion to Make Specific and Certain: This motion has been briefly noticed in that chapter on the Demurrer. Its sanction is in Section 66: "When any pleading is too general in its terms to be readily understood, the court may, on motion require the same to be made more specific and certain." As stated in that chapter, it was used to compel the statement of evidential details, a use not yet wholly abandoned, but the Supreme Court's insistence on ultimate fact has altered the attitude of the nisi prius tribunals on that point and the practice is fading. The rule is that a pleading is good against this motion if it can be readily understood and is not misleading. Such use is subject to two objections; First: There is no limit which can be set to the requirements for details but the opinion or even whim of the judge who hears the motion, therefore all the courts in the world could not, by any series of precedents, establish rules to tell us what ought or ought not 2 1

to be alleged; Second: The pleading of minute details confuses the issues and often hides them. The supreme court finally held that the motion could only compel compliance with the rules of certainty, i.e., time, place, quantity, quality, value, names of persons and clearness of statement in general, never to compel allegations of evidence, or of matters in confession and avoidance of one's own complaint. The omission of such allegations does not justify a general demurrer.* 1The question is not often decided by an appellate court because it is so largely discretionary. Seeing Denver Co. v. Morgan, 66 C. 565, 566-7, 185 P. 339; Spaulding v. Porter, 94 C. 496, 499, 31 P.(2d) 711; Mulligan v. Smith, 32 C. 404, 407, 76 P. 1063; Lacey v. Bentley, 39 C. 449, 452, 89 P. 789; there is no error but through abuse, Sheridan Co. v. 

Davidson, 75 C. 584, 227 P. 553; Commonwealth Co. v. Nunn, 7 C. A. 

117, 119, 67 P. 342. 

2Fox v. D. C. Tr. Co., 57 C. 511, 517, 143 P. 278; Dubois v. First N. 

B., 43 C. 400, 96 P. 169. So of description of land, Bay State Co. v. 

Jackson, 27 C. 139, 142, 60 P. 573. 'Attempted to get aboard" the street car “in the usual manner" is a good allegation, Fox v. D. C. Tr.

§ 155. Motion to Elect, continued: The court of appeals considered this kind of motion at some length and cited many cases and also criticized the practice strongly.¹

In an action with two counts one to pay a specified sum and the other to pay a reasonable amount, trial to court, it was held that a denial of the motion was without prejudice.2 In a like action the plaintiff at the conclusion of his case elected to stand on the quantum meruit."

Where the breach of contract is also a trespass, plaintiff is not called upon to elect, or even declare whether the action is tort or contract, but a defendant who has won on the theory that the action is ex contractu cannot, in the court above, win on the theory that it is ex delicto.5 

When several causes are mingled the motion should be to separate. When there is really but one cause an order to elect is a nullity, and though the plaintiff elects contract, if the cause was really tort he may prove the tort."

§ 157. Motion to Separate: The code requires causes of action to be separately stated; i.e., stated in separate counts. 

They may be joined: i.c., stated in one complaint, but each cause must be stated by itself.¹ 3 A convenient term for the violation of this rule is "mingling causes." The remedy is not demurrer but a motion to compel the plaintiff to state the causes separately, commonly called the motion to separate.2 The fault should be always distinguished from misjoinder. Two causes that might properly be joined if separately stated, are, when in one count, mingled, and a motion to separate them must be granted. A motion to elect is not the remedy. This motion cannot be sustained if the complaint states no cause of action, nor, logically, unless it states two. The denial of the motion may or may not be prejudicial error,' but is reversible error if prejudicial,' and is not waived by answer. Yet it seems to be held that the objection must be made at nisi prius."

Pomeroy's analysis is most useful in the determination of the question whether there are two causes.10

§ 161. Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings, In General: 

The motion for judgment on the pleadings is an anomaly under the code, which nowhere expressly authorizes it. The only reference to it is in Section 66: "When any motion in writing * for judgment on the pleadings shall be filed **"' it "shall be taken as a part of the record without bill of exceptions." This first appeared in Section 60 of the code 1887, the motion, however, was in use previously. We shall see that the authorities on it are in confusion and its distinction from a general demurrer has not been made clear.¹ 

It was early used by attorneys for defendants with the understanding that if it should be granted the plaintiff could not amend, but later it was held that amendment could not thus be barred, and that the motion was not a substitute for a demurrer, and could not be converted into a demurrer," and if the complaint lacks a material allegation defendant should demur." 2 

¹A defect of form will not support it, Griegerson v. Weddingfield, 70 

C. 494, 202 P. 709; Richards v. Stewart, 53 C. 205, 207, 124 P. 740; 

Highlands v. Raine, 23 C. 295, 297, 47 P. 283; e.g., that the replication does not designate the "count" in the answer where it intends to deny; 

Orman v. Mannix, 17 C. 564, 30 P. 1037; Rice v. Bush, 16 C. 484, 485, 488, 27 P. 720. It is hopelessly confused with a general demurrer in 

Steinhauer v. Colmar, 11 C. A. 494, 497-8, 55 P. 291. This opinion says that Ch. 10 is authority for the motion, but in fact holds that it merely does not forbid it. It would follow from this opinion that every judgment not based on the determination of an issue of fact is a judgment on the pleadings. It is on the merits. Id. 

2It has been recently so held. McLaughlin v. Niles, 88 C. 202, 206-7, 294 P. 954. This is, of course, consistent with the rule that the motion

should not be granted where an amendment is possible, and this case so declares. § 159.

The paragraph contains a contradiction in terms. An issue of fact is raised only by the denial of a material allegation, not otherwise. (Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, or C. L. '21, Code, Ch. XII). 

But a material allegation is essential to plaintiff's case, § 78. Therefore, it could never be true that "where an issue has been joined" either party could be "entitled to a judgment no difference what the findings might be upon the issues of fact joined." On the contrary, the findings upon the issues of fact must invariably determine the judgment. Similar cases are Jackisch v. Quine, 62 C. 72, 75, 160 P. 186; Moore v. Kline, 26 C. § 168. Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings, Comments: 

It will be seen from the foregoing that if any rules with reference to the motion for judgment on the pleadings can be learned from the decisions they are so inconsistent, in such confusion and so indefinitely expressed that none of them can be said to be unquestioned. Some of them, however, seem to be based on sound reasoning.

So far as such a judgment for a plaintiff is concerned it is said that it "should not be rendered unless upon the admissions in the answer it is impossible for the court to render any other judgment than that prayed for in the complaint."" Many of the decisions, however, approve the motion in cases, for example, for unliquidated damages, in which the court cannot know, without evidence, what judgment to render. 

¹Roberts v. C. S. & I. Ry. Co., 45 C. 188, 194, 101 P. 59; Richards v. Stewart, 53 C. 208, 124 P. 740. See also Hoover v. Horn, 45 C. 288, 101 P. 55; Mills v. Hart, 24 C. 505, 52 P. 680. 

§ 169. Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings, Comments, continued: If the motion cannot take the place of a demurrer, when can it be used? It always takes the place of a demurrer if it is used at all. It will not lie where a demurrer will not. 

Of what use is it then when it takes the place of a demurrer? Why not use the demurrer? The result is the same unless the motion bars amendment which it is held not to do if an amendment is possible¹; so the result is always the same. 

If it is made during a trial, orally, it is equivalent to a demurrer ore tenus.

The motion is said to be in the nature of a demurrer² and equivalent to a demurrer and motion,2 which is manifest; but of what avail? A demurrer would accomplish the same thing in the same time." 4 It has been said that it has many advantages, and perhaps that is true under some systems of practice, but with the Colorado rule which permits a demurrer for want of facts at any stage of the case none of the advantages mentioned in the note in C. J. is apparent. 

149 C. J. 668, N. 3(b), and above. 

249 C. J. 668. But the demurrer needs no motion. 

Johnson v. Watkins Co., 66 C. 458, 182 P. 879. 

449 C. J. 667. N. 84. Only one case and that in an inferior court. 

§ 170. Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings, Comments, continued: There is one situation where it may be of value, in some cases, e.g., an action for a liquidated sum when there is but a partial defense. Plaintiff may acquiesce and take judgment for the undisputed balance; but there it is a matter of mere form, and substantially a default or nil dicit.¹ 

The motion is somewhat analogous to the hearing on bill and answer in the old chancery practice, but the differences are such that the precedents under that practice afford us no guide. 

The cause of the confusion in the decisions on this subject is the expression "on the pleadings" by which every one is led, naturally and surely, to the conclusion that whenever the pleadings show one party entitled to a judgment the motion should be granted, but to reach such a judgment is the appropriate function of a demurrer. Always the record shows one side or the other entitled to a judgment, a demurrer searches the record, i.e., requires consideration of the whole of it, to determine which. The motion for judgment on the pleadings can do no more.2

Since a demurrer will always answer the purpose and a decision upon it be free from the uncertainties which surround the decisions on the motion, a prudent practitioner should choose the former. 

Briggs v. Bruce, 9 C. 282, 11 P. 204. 

2The motion may be of use when there is a perfect defense undenied and without reply. There is then nothing to demur to, yet defendant is entitled to judgment on the record, or, if plaintiff has put in his evidence, to a nonsuit. Allenspach v. Wagner, 9 C. 127, 182, 10 P. 802. 

§ 171. Motion Non Obstante, In General: This is a motion for a judgment for plaintiff notwithstanding a verdict for the defendant. In many states, however, either party may have this judgment if the pleadings show his right to it. It is,

2 logically, a judgment on the pleadings, because it depends on nothing else. It need not be called a motion non obstante.³ 

The rule in Colorado is that when the complaint states a cause of action and the verdict for the defendant is solely on immaterial issues on an invalid plea of confession and avoidance a judgment is due the plaintiff. The reasoning is unanswerable, because the defendant is as if he had made no answer. So in replevin, where the defendant denied plaintiff's ownership and proved only a special property in himself, a judgment non obstante was upheld."

A judgment non-obstante must rest on the pleadings and the evidence is irrelevant to it.5

The suggestion is made that this motion if filed within the time allowed for a motion for a new trial will retain the trial court's jurisdiction," so that the motion for a new trial may be filed later."

The motion is not for the defendant. His motion is for arrest of judgment. Quimby v. Boyd, 8 C. 194, 6 P. 462; Floyd v. C. F. & I.

§ 172. Motion in Arrest of Judgment, In General: This motion is not expressly authorized by the code but is mentioned in Section 422. It is the defendant's motion, after a verdict against him, when the pleadings show no right in the plaintiff to any kind of a judgment. The motion must be based only on the record proper.¹

It seems that want of jurisdictional facts will justify the arrest. On this motion all the plaintiff's allegations are taken as proved, and it must be granted if the defect is fundamental and shown by the record.¹ There can be no motion in arrest after a demurrer to the complaint has been overruled. The motion will not be granted because of departure. The remedy for that is demurrer."

§ 173. Motion for Dismissal or Non-Suit, In General: Dis missal was the final judgment for defendant in chancery; it is a term often used in code practice by the court to indicate a final judgment for defendant in any kind of action. The non-suit is a judgment for defendant when the plaintiff's evidence fails to prove a cause of action, or fails to prove the cause he has stated, i.e., variance. If the action is equitable the judgment is then called a dismissal, and the code, Section 184, seems to regard it so. The basis of such a judgment is evidential and the pleadings have no direct effect upon it,¹ yet because the evidence must conform to the pleadings their indirect influence is often great.

The ordinary instance is the case of a variance. The evidence fails to prove the case stated by the complaint; then, unless there is an amendment, there is a non-suit. The proceeding is not exactly within the scope of our subject.2

The judgment on this motion formerly was no res adjudicata and another action for the same cause could be maintained,³ but Rule 5 of the Supreme Court now reverses this practice and unless the non-suit or dismissal is expressed to be "without prejudice" no new action is permitted. It has been said that a good defense, undenied, entitles a defendant to a non-suit,' but the statement is inaccurate; it entitles him to a judgment on the pleadings, i.e., the record shows him entitled to judgment without demurrer.

The other grounds for non-suit or dismissal have no relation to pleadings. Sec. 184. In James v. McIntyre, 81 C. 548, 551, 256 P. 

657, a refusal to permit the plaintiff to dismiss against one defendant was upheld by the Supreme Court and in Phares v. Don Carlos, 74 C. 

356, 221 P. 883, such a dismissal was declared erroneous. 

2See Foreword. If, in such a situation, it appears that the complaint states no cause of action, the defendant's course is to demur for want

of facts. The motion for judgment on the pleadings is also sometimes used here. 

Allen v. Steiger, 17 C. 552, 31 P. 226.

§ 175. Non-Suit, Variance, General Principles: The general proposition is that the plaintiff must recover upon the case he has alleged,¹ the defendant may defend only on the defenses he has alleged, and variance defeats the party guilty of it if the objection is in time. A variance which does not affect the substantial rights of the parties may be disregarded. If, taking the whole complaint together it appears that the proof conforms to it there is no variance.5 A variance which neither surprises nor harms is not fatal. Where defendant is not misled nor his rights prejudiced the variance is disregarded'; the court is bound so to do or to permit amendment to conform to the proof, saving the rights of the objecting party. So when evidence is rejected for variance amendment should be allowed, and the objection should be on the ground of variance so that the plaintiff can amend."

§ 181. Variance, Sundry Cases: The doctrine of variance was applied to a claim in probate against a decedent's estate.¹

§ 182. Motion for a Directed Verdict, In General: This motion is upon the same grounds as the motion for non-suit. 

It has been viewed with favor by some courts and disfavor by others. 

Judge Hallett, formerly of the Federal Court in Denver, would not grant a non-suit, because that permitted another suit to be brought and he thought it right to end the controversy. Other courts have thought that wrong and some have refused to direct the verdict unless the moving party, who is usually the defendant, would rest, and thus submit the case to the court on the plaintiff's evidence alone, having the verdict directed for or against him as the judge might decide. This he seldom dared to do. In such courts the motion is seldom made. 

Since Rule 5 of the Supreme Court, the advantages of a directed verdict over a non-suit or dismissal have diseappeared. 

Unless the latter is expressly "without prejudice" the cause is res adjudicata and no subsequent suit can be maintained, and if the court should consider that unjust it would not direct a verdict, so the net result of either course must be the same. 

The relation of this motion to the pleadings is like that of the motion for dismissal or non-suit.

In this motion the reasons or grounds for it must be stated.¹ 

1Southern Surety Co. v. Peterson, 86 C. 350, 352, 281 P. 746.

It should be remembered that a motion for a new trial is for a new trial of issues of fact only, not of law.¹

§ 184. What Governs: Since the grounds for demurrer are specified in the code¹ it is not necessary to look so constantly to the rules of pleading at common law or in equity when considering demurrers as when considering methods of statement of fact, which are prescribed by that statute in general terms only.

Grounds of Demurrer: The code specifies six grounds, any of which, if it appears on the face of the complaint, will support a demurrer to it. They are as follows:

First: That the court has no jurisdiction of the person of the defendant, or the subject of the action; or, or, Second: That the plaintiff has no legal capacity to sue; 

Third: That there is another action pending between the same parties for the same cause; or, Fourth: That there is a defect or misjoinder of parties plaintiff or defendant; or, Fifth That several causes of action have been improperly united; or, Sixth: That the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action; or,

Seventh That the complaint is ambiguous, unintelligible and uncertain. (L. '87, p. 110, § 50, Code '08, § 56, Č. L. 

'21, Code, § 56, C-M A. S., § 56.)

§ 185. To the Various Pleadings: The code does not specify the grounds of demurrer to an answer or replication, except it is said that the plaintiff may demur to the answer "for insufficiency" but it is uniformly assumed that they are the same as in the case of the complaint. Thus, if an answer is believed to state no defense, the plaintiff may demur on the ground "that the answer does not state facts sufficient to constitute a defense to the complaint of the plaintiff herein"; and perhaps on other grounds. And in like manner the defendant may demur to the replication¹; it has been held, however, though it does not seem reasonable, that a statement in the replication that the answer does not state facts sufficient to constitute a defense is not to be regarded as a demurrer.² It is held that in mandamus the alternative writ may be attacked by demurrer, though the orderly method is a motion. to quash; and the same in prohibition.*

Every ground except one and six must be specified in the demurrer or disregarded," but a demurrer should never state fact or contain argument."

§ 188. Want of Jurisdiction: This demurrer may be used to attack the complaint because of lack of jurisdiction of the person of the defendant or lack of jurisdiction of the subject of the action.

Lack of jurisdiction of the person can seldom appear on the face of the complaint; indeed, it is difficult to see how that is possible. If it ever should appear, it would, of course, destroy the power of the court to go farther in the case.¹

It sometimes, however, though rarely, happens that a complaint shows that the court before which the action is brought has no power to hear and determine the case, that is has no jurisdiction of the subject of the action. For example, it might appear that a judgment for more than $2,000 was sought in the county court, or a judgment, let us say, for but $1,000 was sought in the United States District Court, and whenever such a thing happens, as soon as the court learns it, by demurrer or otherwise, it has no course but to dismiss the action. 

The demurrer is the proper and orderly way to call this to the attention of the court and other methods should not be used unless it is unavoidable.2 

1Fischer v. Hanna, C. A. 471, 47 P. 303. 

2Sec. 1 herein. 

§ 189. Want of Jurisdiction, continued: Lack of jurisdic tion of the subject matter cannot, of course, be waived, for such jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, but lack of jurisdiction of the person may be waived, and is waived or, more accurately, jurisdiction of his person is yielded by any act of the defendant which constitutes an appearance.¹ We treat waivers of demurrers more particularly below in this chapter. 

It rather frequently happens that this ground of demurrer is confused with the sixth ground, that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. The idea in such cases seems to be that because the court cannot lawfully render a judgment for the plaintiff upon the facts stated in the complaint, it has no power to render any judgment, and that since jurisdiction is power to hear and determine, that it follows that the court has no jurisdiction.

It seems hardly necessary to answer this reasoning. If the court has power to hear and determine the case, it has power

THE DEMURRER 

207 to hear and determine it erroneously. It must, in fact, exercise jurisdiction to determine the sufficiency or insufficiency of the complaint. 

¹Peo. v. Dist. Ct., 74 C. 48, 51, 218 P. 912. 

2The position is made clear in Buckmaster v. Williams, 72 C. 593, 595, 212 P. 977; see also Jurisdiction, Ch. 5. 

§ 190. Capacity to Sue: The second cause for demurrer is that the plaintiff has no legal capacity to sue. It can seldom occur in this country. Coverture no longer constitutes incapacity and infancy did never, since the infant could always sue, and in his own name, but by his next friend or guardian.¹ 

The fault is possible in some cases where a plaintiff corporation has failed to pay an annual license tax, but that can seldom appear in the complaint.

So, logically, of citizenship in adverse mining cases, the alien, though he cannot win because he has no power to acquire the property in question, has a right to sue. It is held, however, that where a taxpayer only is given right to "institute an action" on a county commissioner's bond, the issue, taxpayer vel non, is one of capacity to sue, is in abatement and not raised by general denial, which seems clearly according to reason.

The principal or commonest reasons for incapacity were that plaintiff is an outlaw or an alien enemys or an official of a foreign state acting in his official capacity. Outlawry is unknown to us in Colorado. There can be alien enemies only in time of war; and then only under extraordinary conditions, and for these and other reasons such defenses rarely, probably never, appear on the face of a complaint. Capacity of aliens to sue is often regulated by statute."

It ought to be held sufficient to allege that "it appears from the complaint that the plaintiff has no legal capacity to sue because he is an alien enemy,' "but the following might be added, "to-wit: a citizen of (The Empire of Germany, with whom the United States is at war) and a subject of (Wilhelm 

II, Emperor thereof)." If more is required, as in a plea of alien enemy at common law, it is scarcely possible that it should appear in the complaint. The commonest, yet uncommon, occasion for this defense in Colorado is against a plaintiff corporation to file its reports with the Secretary of State."

7Watson v. Empire Co., 66 C. 284, 180 P. 685. § 191. Capacity to Sue, continued: Capacity to sue, like jurisdiction, has sometimes been confused with right to recover or right to maintain the action, i.e., sufficiency of facts. 

Lawyers, and even the courts, have made this mistake. It was held in Beshoar v. Chapell, 6 C. A. 323, 332-3, 40 P. 244, that a stockholder who sues to protect the company in bad faith and for ulterior purpose has no capacity to maintain the suit, which is correct, but the distinction between capacity to sue and capacity to maintain should always be kept in mind.¹ If he cannot maintain the suit it is because something is the matter with his facts or his allegations or proofs. If he cannot sue, it is because something is the matter with him. The word "maintain" is properly used in Pinney v. Bank, 71 0. St. 173, in the beginning of the opinion.2 

In Smith v. School District, 88 C. 309, 311, 313, 2 P. (2d) 238, counsel was urging the proposition that the district had no capacity to sue because it had never been incorporated, but the opinion notices, what is obvious, that that is a question of entity, not of capacity. There was no plaintiff and the question of the plaintiff's capacity to sue could not arise. There being no plaintiff, no cause of action was stated or could be stated, and, in such case, there was, of course, a defect of parties, a total want of a plaintiff. 

1The court notices this in Goldfield v. MacDonald, 52 C. 143, 147-8, 119 P. 1069, but the attorneys for defendant, in their demurrer, claimed the plaintiff had no capacity to sue because he could not maintain the action, 147. See also Page Co. v. Joslin, 38 C. 162, 88 P. 142. 

2The point is made clear in Funk v. Funk, 76 C. 45, 46-7, 230 P. 611, and in Hoyt v. Trustees, 96 C. 442, 449-50, 44 P. (2d) 513, though the syllabus seems to misunderstand the opinion. 

§ 192. Capacity to Sue, continued: In Woodmen v. McCue, 

88 C. 209, 210-11, 1 P. (2d) 99, the question whether members of a fraternal insurance society could maintain an action to enjoin the enforcement of a void amendment to its constitution, and whether only the Attorney General could do so, was discussed as a question of capacity to sue, but the point was not before the court because it had been waived by answer.¹ 

In Underhill v. Whitney, 88 C. 609, 610, 5 P.(2d) 581, the question of plaintiff's right to maintain the action is treated as a question of his capacity to sue. This was evidently an inadvertence. The plaintiff sued as trustee and the claim was

THE DEMURRER 

209 made that he, by certain transactions, had lost all right as trustee in the property in question, and so had no capacity to sue. Of course if he had no such right, he could not maintain the suit but he had capacity to sue and have a trial of the question whether he had any such right, and that is what he did. The decision was that he had capacity to sue and had such right, and so the final result of the case was the same as if the question of capacity to sue had not been raised, but here again the question was not before the court because the defendant had answered. The demurrer was not to the complaint but to the evidence which was a proper way to question plaintiff's right to maintain the action but not to question his capacity to sue.

One may sue whether he be the right person to have a judgment or not; thus one may bring ejectment, although another has the right of possession, or a bill to quiet title, though another is in possession. He cannot maintain the action, cannot win, but whether he can or not is a question he has the right and capacity to litigate."

It has been said that the objection that the plaintiff has no capacity to sue cannot be cured by amendment and, rather inconsistently but according to the statute, that it is waived by failure to demur."

§ 193. Another Action Pending: The third objection "that there is another action pending between the same parties for the same cause "is as rare on the face of the complaint as the second. It could not appear in any ordinary law action, but it is conceivable in some complicated state of facts in equity. 

I have never heard of a case in which such a fact appeared in the complaint. It need not be said that a demurrer will not lie on this ground unless the complaint shows it.¹ 

¹Elkins v. Milliken, 80 C. 135, 142, 249 P. 655. 

§ 194. Defect of Parties: The fourth ground of demurrer, defect, that is, non-joinder, the omission of a necessary party or misjoinder, the inclusion of an improper one, is not an

uncommon ground of demurrer¹ but the question seldom reaches the Supreme Court because whether a demurrer on that account is sustained or overruled, the defeated party usually acquiesces and so proceeds as to waive the point. 

We shall discuss this waiver more fully below. There may, too, be other defects, e.g., total want of a party, as in Smith v. School Dist., 88 C. 309, 311, 313, 2 P.(2d) 238. A master cannot be joined with his servant if his liability is merely by respondeat superior, but may be if personally negligent. While an answer over waives non-joinder,* yet, it does not waive want of an indispensable party'; and, of course, failure to demur does not waive the point if it does not appear on the face of the complaint."

§ 195. Misjoinder of Causes: The fifth ground of demurrer, misjoinder of causes of action, appears often, especially in equitable suits. It often occurs together with misjoinder of parties, and often misjoinder of causes results from the fact that some of the parties to one of the causes of action are not concerned with the other.¹

With respect to the joinder of causes of action the code. abandons all rules of the common law and equity, and specifically prescribes just what may be joined.² 

Of three classes causes in each class may be joined. The following is a sufficient synopsis of each class: 

First: Actions to recover specific real property, with damages, rents, profits and waste of and from occupation thereof. 

Second: Actions to recover specific personal property with damages for detention, taking, conversion, and, in proper cases, exemplary damage. 

Third: All actions sounding only in damages.

But every cause must affect all of the same parties, both plaintiff and defendant, and affect them in the same character and capacity and must require the same place of trial.

§ 196. Misjoinder of Causes, continued: Because of the provision that the parties must be the same it is said that a cause of action by Smith against Johnson cannot be joined with one by Jones against Johnson, and the court of appeals and the Supreme Court have so held¹ and such a joinder amounts, also, to a misjoinder of parties. So also if defendants are not all the same there can be no joinder.2 The same section also says that each cause must be separately stated, a matter which we treat under the head of mingling causes. This fault is frequently mentioned as misjoinder but it is on a different basis.2 Misjoinder is a violation of the limitations upon the right to join, (i.e., state separately in one complaint), mingling (failing to separately state) is a violation of a rule of method of statement. They have no logical relation to each other. Misjoinder is met by demurrer; and mingling by motion to separate.³ 8 4 And so, where defendant demurred only on the ground of mingling, he was held to have waived the ground of misjoinder of causes. It is always waived if defendant fails to object."

§ 197. Misjoinder of Causes, continued: The parties must all appear in the same character and capacity; so it was held that it is a misjoinder of causes to bring mandamus against one person who is secretary of several companies to compel him to permit an inspection of the corporate books of more than one of them, because his capacity as secretary of one company is distinct and different from that as secretary of another.¹

The common example of inconsistent causes is a complaint on an express contract containing a count on an implied one, e.g., quantum meruit. That they are inconsistent is clear and is noted in Manders v. Craft (note below). It cannot be true, then, that mere inconsistency between causes of action constitutes misjoinder.

§ 198. Want of Facts: The sixth ground of demurrer is that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.

In pleading this ground of demurrer it is enough to state it in the words of the code. The usual way is: "The defendant demurs to the complaint on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action," or similar words in respect to an answer or replication, mutatis mutandis. 

In substance this is the ordinary ground of general demurrer at common law. It is often called a general demurrer in code practice. It raises a question not of remedial but of substantive law. Does the law, assuming the facts to be true as stated, give the plaintiff any right to demand anything of the defendant; or, conversely, do the facts cast on the defendant any legal duty toward the plaintiff? In every case the answer to these questions is found only in the law which declares the rights and duties of men toward each other, that is, the substantive law, and not in the remedial law, of which the present subject is a branch.

A demurrer to the whole of a complaint of several counts cannot stand if any count is good.2

A motion for judgment on the pleadings cannot be substituted for a demurrer so as to prevent amendment.³ 

And, of course, it is error to sustain a demurrer to an answer which contains a general denial or a denial of a material allegation.*

It is held that a general demurrer must be sustained to a complaint which shows contributory negligence," but not if it

THE DEMURRER 

213 also shows that defendant had the last clear chance. And such demurrer cannot be sustained to a complaint which shows a right to any kind of relief. A demurrer which does not specify grounds will be treated as a general demurrer." 

And this demurrer searches the record and must be sustained to the earliest insufficient pleading."

On review of a judgment upon a demurrer sustained, the court should confine itself to the sole question: Does the complaint state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action?" 

This demurrer does not raise a question of jurisdiction or of proper procedure,10 and it has been held that a judgment will not be reversed for overruling it unless substantial rights are affected. And it is held that the omission of a material allegation is harmless if it does not "prejudice" the defendant.12

Sometimes a motion is treated as a general demurrer.13

§ 199. Uncertainty: The seventh ground of demurrer is that the complaint is "ambiguous, unintelligible, and uncertain." The code itself does not explain or construe this term. 

Lawyers generally, until the enactment of the code of 1887, paid no careful attention to it, and so far as it was by the courts considered at all it received no definite interpretation. 

Most nisi prius judges contented themselves with overruling the demurrers if they thought they understood the complaint pretty well and sustaining it if they thought otherwise. The 

Supreme Court seldom met the question and established no rules about it. After the enactment of the code of 1887, which provided for the motion to make more specific and certain, that motion was used pretty generally, and was and still is used principally for delay.¹

There is an apparent tendency in the early opinions to apply the common law rules of certainty, time, place, manner, number and amount, in alleging any traversable fact, but it was not laid down that those rules controlled the meaning of the terms above quoted. Later cases, however, leaned the same way, and it was finally said, in substance, that the common law uncertainty was denoted by that term in the code.2

In Price v. Kramer, 4 C. 546, the complaint, which is there with the demurrer set out in full, was said to be uncertain, and the demurrer held to have been properly sustained, but principally, if not wholly on the ground of want of fact. The objection of uncertainty is properly raised by demurrer, but cannot be raised by a demurrer for want of facts.5 

This seventh ground may be used in an election contest."

546, the action was against two counties to prevent their double taxation of plaintiff's cattle which were on the range in both.

215 there and the opinion said that certainty required that he should allege in his complaint the number so returned in each county. The court, therefore, would seem to be following the common law on that point; but the action was equitable, so, it seems, the common law rule was carried into equity. However, the number assessed in each county was in that case necessary to a proper decision. It may likewise be noted that the uncertainty mentioned in the opinion was not among those mentioned in the demurrer.¹ The case, therefore, does not take us far. 

In Manning v. Haas, 5 C. 37, Elbert, J., discusses the question of uncertainty, and quotes from Bliss on Code Pleading, that the common law rule for alleging the time of every traversable fact may be disregarded except where time is necessary to a clear understanding of the facts, in which case it should be alleged, and except also a case where it is material, as in time contracts, where it must be stated or no liability will be shown. 

If we take this case with Catlin v. Hinderlider, 80 C. 522, 527, 253 P. 389, we must conclude the rule to be that the common law rules of certainty are the only rules of certainty that govern code pleading, and that they are to be enforced, not as at common law, under all circumstances, but only where they are material or necessary to a clear understanding of the facts. 

Any objection on the seventh ground is waived by failure to demur or move. So of uncertainty in a petition of intervention, and in answer.* 2 ¹It appears, then, that the court ignored the code's requirement that the demurrer must specify its grounds.

§ 201. Uncertainty, continued: Where time is material, its omission, of course, puts the compaint within the sixth ground of demurrer, as would the omission of any other material allegation.

A clear understanding of the facts, however, is held to be all that is necessary for certainty, and when a complaint can be readily understood and is not so general in its terms as to be misleading it will stand against either a demurrer for uncertainty or a motion to make more definie and certain. 

This matter of certainty is treated further under the subject of complaint, and the motion to make more specific. 1 It is held that a demurrer on the ground of ambiguity must state wherein the ambiguity consists. The same is true of uncertainty and unintelligibility.2

The custom is, in demurrers on the seventh ground, to say in substance, "the complaint is ambiguous, unintelligible and uncertain in this " and then proceed to specify the reason why it is subject to those objections. We thus regard ambiguity and unintelligibility as species of uncertainty, which seems reasonable.

The only complete remedy for this perplexity is the modern English method of pleading by fixed forms prescribed by rule of court. § 203. Waiver of Demurrer: There are three sections of the code which provide for the waiver of demurrers or demurrable objections.

Section 58: "The defendant may demur to the whole complaint or to one or more of the several causes of action stated therein, and answer the residue, but demurrers must be disposed of before any other pleading to the same cause of action shall be filed, or they will be deemed waived.'' 

Section 61: This section follows 60 (which is that if the 

"matter" 'demurrable" does not appear on the face of the complaint the objection may be taken by answer), and is as 

"If no such objection be taken by demurrer or answer the defendant shall be deemed to have waived the same, except only"-numbers one and six-"which objections. may be raised at any time.''2

Section 79: “*** A demurrer shall be deemed waived by filing an answer or reply to the same cause of action or defense."

The appellate courts of Colorado have never considered the relation of these three sections, 58, 61 and 79, to each other.

They have decided many questions of waiver of demurrer and waiver of grounds of demurrer and have cited these sections or some one or more of them in support of their decisions, but they have never compared them with each other. 

¹At common law in Colorado a demurrer, undisposed of, was waived by going to trial. Anderson v. Sloan, 1 C. 484, 487-8, citing Evans v.

Gee, 11 Pet. 85; and a demurrer and plea could not be joined, Walton v. Latimer, Y. B. 17, Sel. Ed. 2 Edw. II, 81, 82. And the same was held in San Juan Co. v. Finch, 6 C. 214. The corresponding section 53, of the code of 1877 said "or may demur and answer at the same time." 

20tis Co. v. Maryland Co., 95 C. 99, 107-8, 33 P.(2d) 974. § 204. Waiver of Demurrer, continued: It is impossible to harmonize these sections perfectly, but it should be noted that no two of them refer to exactly the same situation. A careful reading makes this so clear that it must have been intended. 

Section 61 refers to the case where the "objection" available as a ground of demurrer has not been raised by either demurrer or answer. Section 58 to the case where such objection has been raised by a demurrer but an answer has been filed before the demurrer is disposed of. Section 79 relates to the case where the objection has been raised by demurrer, whether it is disposed of or not.

There seems to be no way perfectly to harmonize Sections 58 and 79 because by 79 an answer waives a demurrer whether disposed of or not.¹ It evidently makes the provision of Section 

58 as to waiver superfluous. We shall find it simpler, therefore, to compare Sections 61 and 79, for what we say with reference to 79 will apply equally to 58; and we shall also find it simpler to refer only to objection by demurrer, ignoring for the present objection by answer.

We must conclude that Section 79 refers to a "demurrer" which has been filed, not to an objection which might have been made by demurrer, that is to say, a ground of demurrer, because otherwise we find these two sections hopelessly inconsistent, Section 79 saying that all objections including one and six are waived by answer; Section 61, saying that one and six are not. This difficulty is avoided if we say that Section 79 refers to a case where a demurrer has been filed, and Section 61 to a case where it has not. These sections then become harmonious. If there is no demurrer every objection except one and six is waived, but one or six "can be raised at any time" thereafter (after answer?). If a demurrer is filed without making the objection one or six the same result occurs. If a demurrer is filed making those objections, an answer will waive the demurrer but not the objection, which may be raised by other means, e.g., arrest of judgment or motion for nonsuit, etc.

It was considerations of this sort that led to the decisions of Stanbury v. Kerr, 6 C. 28; Gillett v. McAllister, 1 C. A. 168, 169, 27 P. 1013; Kyes v. Best, 8 C. A. 129, 131-2, 45 P. 227; 

Cochrane v. Parker, 12 C. A. 169, 177, 54 P. 1027; Williams v. 

Smith, 76 C. 151, 230 P. 395; Erisman v. McCarty, 77 C. 289, 236 P. 777; and the same idea seems to have controlled the court in Rosebud Co. v. Hughes, 21 C. A. 247, 121 P. 674. 

¹And see Courtright's Mills Anno. Code, § 191, or C. L. '21, Code, § 

192. "When there are issues both of law and fact to the same complaint the issues of law shall be first disposed of." But under § 58 there could not be "issues both of law and fact to the same complaint." Yet in 

Metzger v. Baker, 93 C. 165, 166, 24 P. (2d) 748, the answer contained a general demurrer and the opinion regards the general findings for the defendant as a determination of an issue of law and issue of fact, which seems a violation of § 79, and inconsistent with § 58. Possibly 79 could be construed with C-M A. C. § 191, or C. L. '21, Code, § 192, by assuming that the latter refers to the case of an issue of law as to one cause of action or defense and an issue of fact as to another.

Peck, 33 C. 421, 80 P. 1063, that the omission of an indispensable party defendant was not waived by answer without demurrer. The opinion cites Homestead Co. v. Reynolds, 30 

C. 330, 70 P. 422; Allen v. Tritch, 5 C. 222; Colorado State

The decision was doubtless right, but it should be noticed that the question in such a case is not merely one of defect of

THE DEMURRER 

223 parties, but of jurisdiction of the person. If in any decision that can be rendered the rights of one not a party must be determined the court cannot act because it has not acquired jurisdiction of his person. This point was not made clear by the court in Peck v. Peck, but the distinguished counsel for appellant in that case made it clear in written objection 15, quoted on page 423. To regard the case as an authority that a mere defect of parties is not waived by answer is to charge the Supreme Court with a violation of the code. 

Homestead Co. v. Reynolds, supra, contains only a dictum on this point, for it was there held that the omitted party had no interest. In Allen v. Tritch, the question of waiver was not raised. Bank of Durango v. Davidson, however, is directly in point. 

The case of Conroy v. Cover, 80 C. 434, 252 P. 883, illustrates the rule that a party ordinarily regarded as indispensable may be omitted if beyond reach of the court, provided the court can grant any sort of relief by saving his rights. 

§ 211. Repugnancy: The repugnancy may be immaterial and leave enough material allegations to justify some relief.' 

Words of a complaint cannot be taken as stating a contract when others show there was none.2 It is said that a complaint which is entirely consistent with a state of facts, which would defeat a recovery is bad. In an action on a bond of indemnity, which requires three months' notice to the obligor, it was held that an implication that the plaintiff discovered the loss more than three months before notice did not vitiate the general allegations of full performance. Inconsistency between separate causes in one complaint is not a ground for demurrer, but for a motion to compel election. Where the complaint on a note alleged that the defendant was a guarantor but set out the note which showed him to be comaker the inconsistency was held to be harmless. 

¹Wanamaker v. Reno, 79 C. 153, 155, 244 P. 602. The action was to quiet title, and the complaint showed defendant in possession, but showed enough facts to justify other relief.

§ 212. Effect of Demurrer: The demurrer is a pleading and the hearing on it is a trial of an issue of law; it follows that judgment is due the successful party if his opponent makes no further move, and that, if a defendant elects to stand on his demurrer to the complaint he cannot move for a non-suit on the hearing to determine damages. At any time before the hearing of the first demurrer to a complaint, however, the plaintiff may amend without leave. 2 If a complaint shows a right in plaintiff to any part of what he claims, a demurrer cannot be sustained.*

Apparently forgetting that a judgment would follow the decision upon a demurrer, counsel agreed that a demurrer should be regarded as a motion for judgment on the pleadings." 

There has been much confusion of thought on this matter. It has been held that the motion and the demurrer amount to the same thing, and that the motion cannot be substituted for a demurrer, and that failure to rule on a demurrer to the answer was error without prejudice, because the same result was reached by a motion for judgment on the pleadings and the right to amend after a demurrer was sustained cannot be taken away by substituting a motion for judgment on the pleadings."

It seems reasonable to consider that the motion for judgment on the pleadings in a law suit should be restricted to the case where the plaintiff admits a partial defense (e.g., by setoff) and asks judgment for the undisputed balance; and in equity cases to the chancery hearing on the bill and answer, where the chancellor, without further evidence, decrees such relief as the facts in those documents may justify, or the case of a good defense with no reply. A final adjustment of the law to that effect would clear the air.10
