§ 213. 

Demurrer Searches the Record: The demurrer is said to "search the record.'' This means that a demurrer to any pleading after the complaint is regarded as a demurrer to the whole record and the judgment goes against the first bad pleading. This rule goes only to demurrers for want of facts or jurisdiction, because all other grounds are waived by previous pleadings. The rule is one of logic. A bad answer cannot make a complaint good, and if the complaint shows no right in the plaintiff he can have no judgment even though there be no defense. If the complaint says that defendant promised to build a house but does not say that he has not done it, an answer that George Washington is dead is good, and a demurrer to it will be sustained against the complaint.

§ 216. Statute of Limitation: It seems in accord with reason that if the bar of the statute of limitations appears from the complaint that a demurrer to it ought to be sustained, and it is so held.¹

It seems clear enough that this objection belongs under the sixth category of grounds of demurrer, want of facts. The facts stated in the complaint do not justify any judgment in favor of the plaintiff, do not constitute a cause of action. If the defendant did not promise within six years no judgment can be rendered against him; if, then, that fact appears in the complaint, it appears that no judgment can be rendered against him; then the facts stated in the complaint do not constitute a cause of action, or, in the words of the code, "the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.' 

¹Arkins v. Arkins, 20 C. A. 123, 126, 77 P. 256; Bush v. McMann, 12 

C. A. 504, 509-10, 55 P. 956; Peo. v. Barton, 4 C. A. 455, 36 P. 299;

Bank, 43 C. 400, 403, 96 P. 169; Foot v. Burr, 41 C. 192, 194, 92 P. 236; 

Ballard v.

§ 217. Statute of Limitation, continued: Pipe v. Smith, 5 C. 

146, holds that if the statute of limitations appears on the face of the complaint to have run, a demurrer will lie. This was an equity case. We see no reason why the same would not be true in an action at law. The demurrer specified that the statute had run. This case also holds that a general demurrer will not lie to a complaint which shows that the statute of limitations has run. That such a matter must be pleaded specially "whether the pleading be by demurrer or answer" (sic). This decision seems illogical: If the complaint showed that the fraud, the ground of complaint, was discovered three years before the action was begun, there was no right of relief from it, i.e., no "cause of action," and if so, a general demurrer should be sustained. If, on the other hand, we follow the common law rule, and require the statement in the answer of the fact that the fraud was not committed within three years

THE DEMURRER 

227 next before, etc., the complaint is good and no demurrer will lie, because no new fact may be alleged in a demurrer. Further, no specification is required for the sixth ground, want of facts, beyond the statement that the facts are insufficient, yet this decision requires it, although there is no ground for this demurrer but the sixth. It comes within the scope of neither jurisdiction, capacity to sue, another action pending, defect of parties, misjoinder of causes or ambiguity, unintelligibility or uncertainty. 

The cases, however, seem all to hold that a mere statement that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action is not enough to cover the objection of the statute, that the demurrer must state that the complaint shows that the cause is barred by the statute, and it is called a "special demurrer." Reason, however, seems to the contrary. 

¹Arkins v. Arkins, 20 C. A. 123, 126, 77 P. 256; Hunt v. Hayt, 10 C. 

278, 15 P. 410; Jennings v. Rickard, 10 C. 395, 15 P. 677; Evans v. 

Rep. Pub. Co., 20 C. A. 281, 78 P. 311, and elsewhere.

Curiously enough, this is unconsciously recognized in the opinion in 

Arkins v. Arkins, 20 C. A. 123, 126, 77 P. 256, which says: "The complaint must disclose a subsisting cause of action," and holds that it does not, because it does not "allege matters which avoid the bar raised by the special demurrer"-meaning "the statute of limitations." 

This opinion, thus contradicting itself, shows better than any extended argument that the objection in question is within the category want of facts.

There is, however, the further point, to which there seems no answer, that there is no ground of demurrer provided by the code, other than the sixth, want of facts, which can be said to include this objection. 

The rule, then, must be regarded as an exception to the general rule that a demurrer for want of facts need not specify of what that want consists. 

It is doubtless a distorted relic of the well known rule of the common law that the statute of limitations was not a subject of demurrer but always a matter of confession and avoidance. 

The probable cause of this confused reasoning is the inaccurate use of terms. "Pleading the statute of limitations," "pleading the statute of frauds" are misleading terms. We never plead statutes. We plead the facts which bring the case within the scope of the statute, but if they already appear they should not be repeated. 

The question whether a complaint shows that the statute of limitations has run is one of substantive law, but one or two cases are noted here.

In an action on a note a demurrer will not lie to a complaint which shows a payment within six years. Du Bois v. First National Bank, 43 

C. 400, 403, 96 P. 169.

A complaint to recover land is not subject to this demurrer unless it shows seven years possession by defendant, under claim and color of title. Ballard v. Golob, 34 C. 417, 425-6, 83 P. 376. 

And a plea of the wrong statute is invalid. Ahart v. Sutton, 79 C. 

145, 149, 244 P. 306.

Harmless Error: The courts have not been entirely consistent on the question of harmless or prejudicial error in pleadings but in general the rule is that the defeated party must have been misled or the error will be harmless.¹ We note two or three instances.

The court of appeals refused to reverse a judgment which was claimed to be erroneous because in an action for wages the plaintiff had not mentioned damages.2 The omission in a complaint of a fact which is proved without objections will be disregarded, and striking out a defense is harmless if defendant proved all he might have proved under it.¹ 3

266. Miscellaneous Allowances, continued. § 224. Generally: We treat amendment immediately after demurrer because it usually appears there in practice. 

The code provides liberally for the amendment of pleadings.¹ 

Upon demurrer before the trial of the issue of law, the pleading demurred to may be amended once by filing the same as amended, and serving a copy. Other amendments must have 1

leave of court. Plaintiff may amend once after demurrer is sustained, and a motion for judgment on the pleadings cannot prevent him." Although in most jurisdictions an amendment may state a new cause of action," in Colorado it may not, but plaintiff may add a cause' but may not change the "theory," whatever that may mean. Yet a plaintiff was allowed to change ejectment to mortgage foreclosure."

The case of the amendment to the answer, however, is different, and new defenses are freely permitted on almost any sort of a case.10 The reason for this distinction is that the defeated plaintiff in this situation can bring a new action, but the defendant is defeated finally. This argument, however, reveals no reason for denying the leave to the plaintiff, but only an additional one for granting it to defendant.

§ 225. At Common Law: The common law courts, notwith standing the ordinary impression to the contrary, were liberal in the allowance of amendments,¹ even after judgment. Indeed,

AMENDMENT 

235 in the year books, amendments, until the record was entered, were at the will of the pleader. The Colorado precedents are mostly liberal³ but the judges of the lower courts differ greatly in their views and rulings upon the subject. It is a matter of discretion, wherefore the cases which reach the Supreme Court, though numerous, form but a small part of those actually decided. Amendments during trial are not uncommon, and it is held their allowance is not an abuse of discretion. It has been held an abuse of discretion to deny an amendment to set up a complete defense discovered after the trial had begun."

Many decisions advocate great liberality' where there is no surprise or injury. It was even held error to dismiss a bill which stated no cause of action without giving plaintiff an opportunity to amend."

§ 226. Change of Cause: The rule that a new cause of action may not be stated by amendment¹ makes it necessary, of course, for courts constantly to decide the question "What is the cause of action?" which often is difficult, and consequently the decisions are not always consistent. The precedents

go so far as almost to nullify the rule, yet they are nearly all in the furtherance of justice, and they thus lead toward the conclusion that the rule is a bad one. Indeed, it can seldom be wholly just unless in the case of a foreign defendant who appears in one case and then has another thrust upon him, one in which he never would have appeared. The objection, however, that an amendment changes the cause cannot be first made in the Supreme Court.2

The function of the amendment is to state accurately the same cause which has been stated inaccurately.³ 

Change from negligence to willful wrong was held not an entirely different cause of action. A promise to pay the "regular commission usual and customary" is not a different cause from a promise to pay a specified sum.5 Employment as a "special prosecutor" is not a cause different from employment to "assist the district attorney. 196 The second amended complaint may return to the cause inaccurately stated in the original.'

But there may be no change from ex contractu to ex delicto, or from a basis of express trust to one of constructive trust. 

1Givens v. Wheeler, 6 C. 149; D. & R. G. Co. v. Iles, 25 C. 19, 53 P. 

222; Anthony v. Slayden, 27 C. 144, 150, 60 P. 826; Anderson v. Groesbeck, 26 C. 3, 55 P. 1086; Mullen v. McKim, 22 C. 468, 45 P. 416.

If this case is followed it will stand as an exception or qualification of the rule as to change of cause by amendment; somewhat similarly an amended complaint which alleges a sale and delivery of stock does not state a cause of action different from a written contract with explanation of its uncertainty. § 227. Change of Cause, continued: Change from a legal to an equitable cause is not permitted';

but it is hard to see

AMENDMENT 

237 a sound reason for this in a system which allows both legal and equitable relief in one action. The reason for the rule is said to be that "the defendant finds himself in court to answer a charge concerning which he has never been summoned"; but a moment's thought shows that to be no reason. 

If a plaintiff adds a cause as in Engert v. Orr, the defendant is in the same situation. In the year books the practice was constant. The defendant never knew, presumptively, what the trouble was till in court and the plaintiff's counsel "declared." 

So in our probate courts and in cases before a justice of the peace. It is held, however, that a complaint in equity may be amended so as to show a right to damages. But this is not an absolute right. A complaint for specific performance may be amended to an action for damages for breach of the same contract, and both specific performance and damages may be adjudged in a proper case." 2 In an action for work and labor and for board furnished, an amended complaint which merely alleges more facts but shows the same balance does not change the cause of action." In an action by the payee of a draft against the drawee an amendment which added to the complaint the allegation that the plaintiff had paid the drawer the amount of the draft did not change the cause of action. The opinion says that the amendment merely perfected the original statement, and that such cannot be a new cause, which is clearly right, but may we not go further and say that whether the amendment merely perfects the original is the final and only test that can determine whether it changes the cause? At all events we may say that this will ordinarily be true. "The real purpose is to supply omitted material allegations."'

§ 228. Change of Cause, Contracts: A cause is not changed if it is still for the breach of the same contract to pay money.¹ 

A somewhat similar case involved an original complaint for taking and conversion which alleged a contract by which plaintiff was entitled to the goods and an amended complaint which alleged ownership and conversion, and it was held that there was no change of cause²; but an action on a different contract is a different cause³; so an amendment that asserts a right by assignment does not state the same cause as the original which alleges a right as trustee for the assignor.* 

It does not change a cause of action to strike out an allegation of an illegal alternative promise."

A change is without prejudice if the judgment would be justified with or without the amendment. Change from a claim of a resulting to an express trust does not change the cause. So of the addition of an allegation of fraud to sustain a resulting trust. 8

§ 229. Change of Cause, Torts: A complaint to recover money obtained by deceit cannot be changed to one for money obtained by mutual mistake.¹ 2 It is said that if the ultimate facts are the same, the cause is the same, and that a prayer for different relief does not change the cause."

Substitution of an administrator for the widow in an action for death does not change the cause. That a railroad company killed cattle by neglecting to fence is the same cause as by negligently operating a locomotive.5 

If the amendment is made without objection it may change the theory of the case."

An amendment of a complaint against an employer charging unsafe appliances, which alleges that machinery was started while plaintiff was cleaning it, does not change the cause."

Change of Cause, Torts, continued: Even though the description of the land in controversy is changed the cause of action is not changed,¹ and so of the source of plaintiff's title.2 It is said that an action to quit title and one to remove a cloud are different causes, and that an amendment that substitutes one for the other changes the cause of action, but that the defendant cannot object if his evidence of title would be the same in either case. It is said that facts in an amended complaint which establish the same ultimate fact as did the original complaint do not make a new cause, but a change of evidential facts does not make a bad complaint good."

§ 235. Effect of Amendment: An amended pleading cancels the original and renders it void. It cannot then be considered in a question upon the amended pleading.2

§ 249. To Conform to Proofs: Many amendments, perhaps a majority, are requested to conform to proofs, that is, to avoid a variance, or add a material allegation, but the reports of some cases illustrate the proceeding better than others, and I have selected a few examples of that sort. 

An amendment which does not conform to the evidence is properly rejected.¹

In an action by a vendor of land against the vendee for specific performance it was held that plaintiff should be allowed to plead a waiver which defendant's evidence had proved.2 

After an amendment enlarging the ad damnum to conform to the proof and judgment thereon, plaintiff cannot complain that the amendment was wrong.³

An amendment to conform to proof should not be cut off by failure to object till motion for new trial. But it was error to allow an amendment to conform to proof long after trial when the plaintiff then knew all the facts."

When defendant has not claimed a variance below the higher court will regard an amendment to conform to the proofs as made, but, even though he claimed at the trial that certain evidence should be stricken because no allegation justified it (i.e., because it was irrelevant) yet if by objection he prevented amendment to conform to proof he cannot claim that the complaint did not justify the proof." 

¹D. Tr. Co. v. Johnson, 66 C. 50, 179 P. 143. 

2Doyle v. Miles, 74 C. 182, 183, 219 P. 1068. 

3 West Elk Co. v. Telck, 71 C. 79, 82, 205 P. 270. 

4Perkins v. Russell, 56 C. 120, 128, 137 P. 907. "Atchison Co. v. Baldwin, 53 C. 426, 128 P. 453. "Merritt v. Hummer, 21 C. A. 568, 580, 122 P. 816. "Boltz v. Bonner, 95 C. 350, 355-6, 35 P.(2d) 1015. This condition is often met by considering the amendment as made. 

§ 250. To Conform to Proofs, continued: The courts, as is above noted, are liberal in this respect, but occasionally there is a decision which seems to disregard Section 84, and to reverse a judgment for an error which affects the substantial rights of the parties not at all. A lease offered by plaintiff in evidence is declared to be a variance, and, although he had proved a good lease (and ultimately had a judgment) the opinion says the court very properly refused to let him amend to conform to his proofs because it had, by his inducement, during the trial, held the amendment unnecessary. It would seems that this was a typical case for the allowance of an

amendment to conform to the proof. A technical mistake by counsel, in which he was supported by the court itself, is treated as a controlling point in the case, regardless of the substantial rights of the parties. There were other reasons, however, which justified the reversal. 

But, on the other hand, it is intimated that leave to amend should be granted when the evidence shows a variance and without amendment the evidence which creates the variance will be excluded. 8

$ 252. Immaterial Amendments: The allowance or denial of leave to amend will not justify a reversal unless it affects the substantial rights of the parties. And it was held proper for the court to strike out an illegal alternative promise and let the case stand on the valid alternative.2 On the same principle an amendment to plead something not in the case or which would be of no avail, e.g., the statute of frauds, will not be permitted, nor to plead something, e.g., want of consideration, the contrary of which, i.e., consideration has been proved without dispute, and denial of leave to plead the statute of limitation by amendment was sustained because the plea tendered was insufficient. 

And so again an amendment which does not aid previous defects is rightly refused; but when it is denied because unnecessary, if necessary, the Supreme Court should treat it as made.® 

If an immaterial amendment is denied it is not an error even though a material one, if asked, should have been allowed."

$267. Answer in General: We have touched the subject o the answer in the chapter on the Method of Code Pleading. 

If the defendant does not demur or if his demurrer is overruled he must either traverse,¹ i.e., deny, some material allega. tion of the complaint, or confess and avoid, i.e., allege some new fact which avoids the conclusion which would follow from the allegations of the complaint." The pleading by which he does this is called the answer. He has an absolute right to file it.¹

The code tells us what the answer must contain :5 "First: A general or specific denial of each material allegation in the complaint intended to be controverted by the defendant." "Second: A statement of any new matter constituting a defense or counterclaim, in ordinary concise language without unnecessary repetition." 

It follows that an answer that neither denies nor avoids is of no force, and it is so held,' and it is held that a good defens undenied entitles the defendant to a non-suits; while the insuf ficiency of the complaint is ground for demurrer or motion in arrest," and each defense in the answer must be complete in itself, except by proper references.10

§ 269. Inconsistent Defenses: It seems to be well settled that inconsistent defenses, that is, defenses which cannot both be true, are permitted by the code. But plaintiff may not in one count affirm and in another disaffirm a contract, yet when defeated on the validity of a trustee's deed he may claim the lien of the trust deed. Answering a complaint for wages, after a wrongful discharge, a denial of the discharge and a denial that plaintiff's work was satisfactory were permitted.“ 

The court may not strike out a defense because inconsistent with another defense, since there is no way to tell which is true and that question of fact must be tried."

§ 271. Verification: The verification, under the code, has no resemblance to the verification in common law pleading. It is an affidavit of the truth of the pleading to which it is appended. The complaint may or may not be so verified, but if it is, all other pleadings, except demurrers, must be. The affidavit must be made by the party except when he is absent or unable and when an agent or attorney has knowledge of the facts, and must state that the pleading is true of his own knowledge except as to the matters therein stated on information and belief and as to those matters be believes it to be true.¹ 

When the verification is by an attorney or agent,¹ it must state why the principal does not make it. When on behalf of a corportion it need only state that the facts stated are true to deponent's best knowledge, information and belief. If the complaint is on a written instrument, which is set out in hæc verba the answer must be verified even if the complaint is not,² or the genuineness of the instrument is admitted, and it need not be introduced in evidence.³ Where the verification is required an answer without it is a nullity.*

§ 272. Abatement: A plea in abatement, at common law, consisted of the allegation of facts which defcated the action but not the cause of action, that is, the right on which the action was based. Examples were the pleas to the jurisdiction. of the court and the plea to the capacity of plaintiff to sue.¹ 

A plea in bar, on the contrary, showed facts which defeated the cause of action. Examples of the latter were the pleas of release and of son assault demesne. Either of these defenses, if maintained at the trial, determined that the plaintiffs had no right of action. One consequence was that he could not maintain another suit for the same cause, but the plea to the jurisdiction merely showed that the plaintiffs could not maintain the suit then present, because the court into which he had caused the defendant to be summoned had no power to consider the matter. The same is true under the code. The decision for the defendant on such a plea, obviously cannot prevent another action for the same cause because the court has no power to give judgment, either for or against the plaintiff's

THE ANSWER 

261 claim but can only dismiss the case; likewise if plaintiff has no capacity to sue, there is no case to decide. 

At common law pleas in abatement were preliminary and were waived if not made before a plea in bar.²

The plea to the jurisdiction was not always classed with pleas in abatement but was regarded as sui generis, 1 Chit. 440, yet no other example serves us here quite so well. So under the code, Davis v. 

Davis, 70 C. 37, 38-9, 197 P. 241. 

21 Chit. 440. In Kephart v. Peo., 28 C. 73, 75, 62 P. 946, we find the term "plea in bar" used on mandamus to denote an answer (or pleading) diverted against the capacity of the relator to sue. 

§ 273. Abatement, continued: Abatement under the code, however, is not a preliminary plea, as at common law, but is to be pleaded with all other defenses. If not so pleaded the point is lost. The code as compared with the older practice simplifies matters in abatement and, in effect, treats the first five grounds of demurrer in Section 60 (want of jurisdiction, of capacity to sue, another suit pending, defect of parties, misjoinder of causes), if they do not appear in the complaint, as matters in abatement. § 274. Abatement, continued: That the right of action is not mature is regarded as matter in abatement,¹ but this seems contrary to reason. Until maturity there can be no breach, if no breach, then no cause of action, if no cause of action then judgment for defendant. This appears to be an abatement of the suit because after maturity another action may be brought, but the appearance is misleading. The added fact of the breach makes a different cause, or rather, more accurately, there was no cause until maturity. This is made clear if we compare the plea on this account with that on account of incapacity to sue

where the plaintiff may have a perfect cause of action, but, by reason of a defect in himself (outlaw, alien enemy) he is not allowed in court; likewise of misjoinder of causes, defect of parties, another suit pending where the cause of action may be perfect but the action faulty. Whereas prematurity is a fault in the right of action; nothing is wrong with the action itself. 

11 Chit. 453; U. S. Co. v. Newton, 50 C. 379, 388-9, 115 P. 897. This case says it must be presented "by special plea." Whether this means confession and avoidance or abatement cannot be gathered from the opinion. 

§ 275. Abatement, continued: This may be made clearer also by consideration of the grounds of demurrer in Section 56. 

We can hardly say that a demurrer would not lie to a complaint which showed no breach of the contract in suit; but if it shows that the contract is not mature there is no breach; then no cause of action is stated and a demurrer for want of facts must be sustained; and here note that the code provides no other ground of demurrer that would fit the case. 

The following seems the logical way to treat the question of immaturity: 1. If the complaint shows the right of action to be immature, defendant should demur for want of facts; 2. If it falsely shows maturity he should deny the contract, generally or specifically; he never made that contract'; 3. If the complaint merely fails to state any time of maturity," the defendant should allege that the contract was to pay or was extended to pay on such a day, not reached at the commencement of the action (or according to the fact) and not otherwise. The only precedents to the contrary of these propositions are the dicta in U. S. Co. v. Newton, 50 C. 379, 388, 389, 115 P. 897, which cites nothing in its support, and in Olson v. Harvey, 68 C. 181, 185, 188 P. 751, and Watson v. Lemen, 9 C. 200, 202, 11 P. 88.

§ 277. Misnomer, What Constitutes: This was a subject of abatement at common law and may be so under the code but is usually treated more summarily. The Denver and Rio Grande 

Railway Company is not a misnomer for The Denver and Rio Grande Railroad Company because the companies of those names are distinct existing companies,¹ but where the defendant named in the record had ceased to exist its successor by consolidation was held liable, its president having been served.²

So if he intends to sue the Railroad Company and serves it, but by mistake names it the Railway Company, of what consequence is it, upon the question of amendment, whether or not there is a Railway Company. § 280. In General: The replication is the plaintiff's response to the defendant's answer.¹ As we have explained, if the plaintiff does not demure he must either deny some material allegation in the answer or allege some additional fact, "new matter," which will destroy the conclusion which the defendant by his answer has sought to draw.2

The plaintiff may, as we have seen, move to strike any part of the answer upon any grounds which would justify striking part of the complaint, such as that it is evidential, a conclusion of law, or irrelevant, redundant or immaterial. After these motions, if there are any, have been decided against him, he may demur, and if he does not do that, he may reply," whereby he must deny or confess and avoid. A denial of “all new matter" in the answer was held good against a demurrer, but said to be subject to a motion to make specific.

The replication may in like manner be attacked by motion or demurrer, and for like reasons, yet only the sixth and seventh grounds of demurrer mentioned in the code are appropriate to the replication. Every material allegation in the replication is taken as denied, consequently whenever the replication is in confession and avoidance this automatic denial raises issues of fact which go to the jury with all such issues. It has been claimed that the inhibition of pleadings after the replication works an injustice but was held not to do so in the particular case because the court had admitted all the evidence which further pleadings would have justified."

§ 283. Cases on Replication: Replications, like other plead ings, are often criticized in that they are "inartificially drawn, yet sufficient in substance.¹ We are not helped by such remarks because they never tell us what the defects are. 

¹Scott v. Stutheit, 58 C. 540, 542, 146 P. 766; Musgrove v. Brown, 93 C. 559, 27 P.(2d) 590.

§ 284. Departure: Departure has been variously defined.¹ 

Chitty says "that the replication must not depart from the allegations in the declaration in any material matter ***” departure in pleading is said to be the desertion by a party of the ground of the case or defense which he has previously made, and recourse to another; perhaps "change of the ground of claim or defense" would be a good definition. It occurs when the replication or later pleading contains matter "not pursuant to the declaration or plea, etc., and which does not support and fortify it."

There are here two categories, each clearly defined: 

1. A new cause of action or defense; and, 2. A material allegation inconsistent with some material allegation in the previous pleadings of the same party.

The first will generally include the second, because the material facts which constitute one cause of action are not often consistent with those which constitute another. It is also true that matter "not pursuant to the declaration or plea" must be either immaterial, in which case it will not be a departure, or inconsistent with it; but an example of the second category may occur without the first. 2 The second kind of departure is illustrated in a case in which the replication denied "all the allegations" of the answer, one of which was that the complaint's allegation of plaintiff's

incorporation was true; thus the plaintiff had denied what he must prove to win. The first category is illustrated in a case in our court of appeals. Other examples of these two categories appear later in this chapter. ¹A statement of a new cause of action by amendment has been called departure. Bearman v. Bronfin, 94 C. 88, 28 P. (2d) 805. 

21 Chit. Pl. 644. 

Hill B. & T. Co. v. Gibson, 43 C. 104, 106, 95 P. 293. The opinion says "the replication is inconsistent with the complaint, a defect which under the common law was called a departure." 

4Moyle v. Bullene, 7 C. A. 308, 312, 44 P. 69. Same as Common Law. § 285. Departure, continued: This defect might occur at common law in the replication or any later pleading but since code pleading stops with the replication, and the defect cannot occur earlier, it can be found there only. 

Departure cannot be tolerated, because, if it were, no issue could be reached and endless prolixity would be sanctioned.¹

§ 293. Departure, How Objected To: The objection to departure may be made by demurrer or motion to strike the objectionable allegation. It seems reasonable that when the replication amounts to a new cause of action a demurrer should be the proper mode, but if it contains but one objectionable allegation, a motion to strike. Since, however, the demurrer searches the record and so attacks not only the replication but the complaint, it is of advantage to use it. 2 Departures frequently go unnoticed by both the courts and counsel. The appellate courts, it need not be said, do not search for errors, nor do they mention all that they see.

§ 294. Departure, Illustrations: In an action for damages on the statutory liability for the breaking of a reservoir the defendant pleaded that the damage was caused by an act of God, the plaintiff replied that negligence of defendant contributed to the injury, and the court held there was no departure, saying the plaintiff "can shift from one kind of legal action to another kind of legal action so long as the cause of action itself is not changed.""

This clause seems to contradict itself. How can a different kind of action be the same cause of action or based on the same cause of action? Perhaps by kind of action is meant form of action, as at common law, but such a distinction could mean nothing under the code.

But even though they produce the same result, is the statutory liability which is placed upon him who maintains a reservoir the same cause of action as his negligence? Either can be the basis of an action without the other, then each must be a cause by itself.

It seems pretty clear that the replication was an argumentative denial.2 An act of God cannot be partly an act of man; the contributory negligence, therefore, would be evidence to show there was no act of God, and would be competent evidence to support a traverse of the defense, therefore such a traverse was all that was necessary, and should have been pleaded. 

There was clearly no departure, but the above quoted proposition is difficult to maintain. 

¹Ryan Gulch Co. v. Swartz, 83 C. 225, 233, 263 P. 728. The citations in support of that dictum (31 Cyc. pp. 360, 361, 362, 365, 381, 382) all concern amendments, not replications; and most courts permit a change of cause of action by amendment, and in such case the reasons against such change by replication are wanting, so these pages are not persuasive in favor of the decision. 

2See the dissenting opinion, p. 233. 

31 C. J. 1174. All the cases agree in excluding human agency, Michaels v. N. Y. C. R. Co., 30 N. Y. 584.

Grand Val. Co. v. Fruita Co., 37 C. 483, 493, 506, 86 P. 324. The case is confusing unless carefully read. The opinion states (p. 493) that, since the complaint stated that the plaintiff stockholder had received notice of a certain assessment, an allegation in the replication that no such notice had been published as the by-laws required was a departure; and this would seem to be right; because, although it could not come within the second category, since both the allegation in the complaint and that in the replication might be true, it is, if material at all, at least an attempt to add a new ground for the relief demanded in the complaint, and therefore belongs to what we have called the first class of departures.

Then again on rehearing, pp. 506-7, the opinion, after conceding that the complaint did not state the receipt of notice, says that plaintiff could not "change position and rely upon failure to publish notice of the assessment, after silence upon that point in the complaint"; and then refers to the matter as a departure.

It is clear from this case and from some others that the allegation of any new ground for the relief sought by the complaint is a departure. § 296. Last Clear Chance: In an action for injury by negligence, although plaintiff may be guilty of contributory negligence, yet if defendant might still by due care have avoided the injury he is liable. This refutation of the defense of contributory negligence is usually and properly a matter of replication, but it has been held that if both contributory negligence and subsequent negligence (Last Clear Chance) both appear in the complaint, it is not subject to general demurrer.2

§ 297. Definition: The term "admission" has many meanings but here it is used in its strict technical sense, viz: A concession of the truth of a material allegation in the opponent's pleading. It is closley related to aider, q. v. 

The purpose of pleading is to find the points in dispute and the most important thing to that end is to eliminate the points not in dispute. The admission does this and every material allegation undenied is thereby admitted whether elsewhere expressly admitted or not.¹ The term, however, is used by the courts to denote other acknowledgments.2 

¹Employers, etc., Co. v. Morris, 14 C. A. 355, 356, 60 P. 21; Briggs v. 

Peo., 21 C. A. 85, 91, 121 P. 127; Teller v. Hartman, 16 C. 447, 448, 27 

P. 947; Houck v. Williams, 34 C. 188, 141, 81 P. 800. So an answer which denies duress but fails to deny want of consideration admits the latter. McClelland v. Bullis, 34 C. 69, 81 P. 771. 

2For example: A concession made at the trial outside the pleadings. 

Coe v. Coryell, 27 C. A. 61, 146 P. 791. Plaintiff's allegation that a third party owns one-half is an admission the plaintiff owns but one-half. 2 3 

§ 298. Effect: The admission establishes the truth of the material allegation admitted and no proof of that allegation is necessary. A party cannot claim the negative of his admission, even though the jury say otherwise, and may not contest his own allegations. It is said that one may not disprove what he has failed to deny nor prove what he has failed to allege, and in eminent domain, the respondent can get no more for his land than he has alleged it is worth, and admissions and averments bind the parties throughout the case,' and he must take all the consequences. But, manifestly, this can only refer to material allegation, ultimate facts, otherwise the minutest evidential fact would have to be alleged and denied. 

¹Moorehead v. Erie Co., 43 C. 408, 96 P. 253; Curtis v. McCarthy, 53 

C. 284, 286, 125 P. 109; Schildt v. Com'rs, 52 С. 509, 511, 122 P. 910; the rule holds in mandamus, Jones v. Bank, 74 C. 140, 219 P. 780. Nor is it proper, Denver Co. v. Howe, 49 C. 256, 267-8, 112 P. 779. If the admission does not dispense with proof of what use is it?

Yet some-

times the admitted fact is proved to enable the jury better to understand the evidence in respect to the disputed allegations, i.e., the issues. 

2Denver v. Bowen, 67 C. 315, 321, 184 P. 357; Greenlees v. Chezik, 68 C. 521, 190 P. 667; Agnew v. Agnew, 67 C. 81, 185 P. 259; Brown v. Barth, 67 C. 214, 216, 184 P. 300; New England Co. v. Shook, 27 

C. A. 30, 38, 145 P. 1002. The admission was that a certain note was the note of a certain corporation. 

3Harvey v. D. & R. G. Co., 56 C. 570, 139 P. 1098.

Withdrawal: It is the general rule that an admission cannot be withdrawn,' but withdrawal has several times been permitted. No rule, however, has been established by which we can determine what will justify permission. It is said that permission is in the discretion of the court, but only on a substantial showing made at once on discovery of the error.2

§ 304. Matters of Law: It ought not to be necessary to say that a matter of law cannot be admitted. An exception, however, seems to be made in case of the claim that a statute has not been passed with the formalities prescribed by the Constitution, upon which it is held that the lack in the procedure must be pleaded and proved.¹ 

¹Adams v. Clark, 36 C. 65, 91-2, 85 P. 642; Peckham v. Peo., 32 C. 140, 75 P. 422, Anderson v. Grand Valley Irr. Dist., 35 C. 525, 85 P. 313; 

Marean v. Stanley, 21 C. 43, 39 P. 1086. These cases all take the paradoxical position that the "facts" which show that a statute has not been constitutionally passed must be pleaded, although its unconstitutionality cannot be admitted, yet its constitutionality is admitted by failure to allege that which shows its unconstitutionality. We have, then, pleadings determining the law.

It seems clear that on the same principle a party should be required to allege the facts by which he expects to maintain any other proposition of law, e.g., the decisions by which a rule of common law has been established, or the "fact" that the statute has never been passed at all. 

The question is: Is the statute constitutional or not? That is a question of law. These decisions make it a question of fact.

§ 305. What It Is: The doctrine of aider is so manifestly fair and just that we expect it to appear and it does appear in pleading under the code. It is a corollary of the principle that at every stage of the pleadings if nothing further is done, one side or the other is entitled to judgment on the record as it stands. An answer which supplies a fact wanting in the complaint avoids the defect,¹ so the replication may aid the answer.2

It follows that the error, if any, in overruling a demurrer to a complaint is harmless if the defendant answers and avoids the defect. 8

The word "aided" is used with reference to an attempt to support a demurrer by facts dehors the pleadings.*

§ 312. In General: The importance of ultimate fact, con clusion of law and evidential fact in pleading requires treatment in separate chapters, yet their relations are such that the discussion of one is also a discussion of the others.

It is said that ultimate fact is a conclusion by reasoning on evidentiary facts, and that evidentiary fact is acquired by the senses, i.c., sight, hearing, taste, etc., but that proposition does not help us much to determine whether any particular allegation is ultimate or not. 

The courts very often use the term "ultimate fact" and other terms of pleading inaccurately. This, in the pressure of work, cannot always be avoided. "Ultimate fact" seems to

be used in a wrong sense and "tender issue" is certainly so used in several cases.2 

¹Bjelka v. M. & Z. Co., 88 L. J. 925. 

2Nichols v. C. B. & Q. Co., 44 C. 501, 518, 98 P. 808. See Ch. 28 on "Issue." 

§ 313. Comparison of Legal Conclusion and Ultimate and 

Evidential Fact, Definitions: All allegations are included in these three categories, and, since that is so, the definition of each is essential to the understanding of any, and yet no satisfactory definition of any of the three has ever been given. 

It has been said by the Supreme Court that the principal and perhaps the only way to tell what is ultimate fact is by precedent, and that would seem to be correct, because if we try to define the term logically, we find that there is no middle ground between conclusion of law and evidential fact. 

It would seem that the only logical definition of conclusion of law is: Any proposition the affirmation of which requires the decision of a question of law. As soon, however, as we try to apply this rule we find more exceptions than affirmances. 

Our court of appeals has said that ultimate fact is a conclusion from evidential fact (which agrees with Chitty), but adds that it to some extent involves conclusion of law. In the same case the same court has said that in an action for malicious prosecution "without probable cause" is a conclusion of law and also an ultimate fact. Logically the statement is right, if in order to use the term "probable cause, we must decide a legal question, viz., do the known facts constitute probable cause, but legally the statement in such case would be wrong, because, for purposes of pleading, conclusion of law and ultimate fact are mutually exclusive terms. There is no case better than this to illustrate the proposition that precedent is the only key to the definition of ultimate fact. 

The ordinary way, acknowledged everywhere to be right, to allege the making of a promissory note is to say that the defendant made and delivered to the plaintiff his certain promissory note, etc. Well! What is a promissory note? Only the law tells us. We have, then, determined a question of law when we said "promissory note." So, of the words "made" and "delivered." What constitutes making and delivery is determined by reference to the law and in no other way; therefore, to say "made" or "delivered" we must first answer a question of law. This is illustrated in Peo. v. Finch, 19 C. A. 

512, 520-23, 76 P. 1120. The allegation was "levied," and it is said that levy is an ultimate fact and implies taking possession because possession is necessary to a lawful levy; thus

ULTIMATE FACT 

285 determining a question of law. A similar situation arose in 

Hanna v. Barker, 6 C. 303, 312-13, where it was argued that "delivered" was a conclusion of law, but the argument was rejected.

Examples of this sort might be multiplied without number. 

¹Denver v. Bowen, 67 C. 315, 337, 184 P. 357; in Bjelka v. M. & Z.

Inconsistency in the Decisions: It is clear, from these cases, that, legally, one may sometimes allege in pleading something which requires the previous determination of a question of law, and the conclusion seems unavoidable that any fact, the allegation of which does not require such determination, will be a matter of evidence. 

Consider a complaint for assault and battery. The ultimate fact is "that defendant assaulted and beat the plaintiff."

Before the pleader can allege this, he must decide a question of law, viz: "What is an assault and battery?" and must reach a conclusion thereon. The evidence will be, with many details, let us say, that defendant slapped plaintiff's face. 

Is there any way to allege the transaction that will not amount to one or the other of these statements? Evidently not. 

But the first states what is universally regarded as ultimate fact and the second, whatever we may call it, is directly evidential.

There is then, logically, no such thing as a proposition (fact) which is not either evidential or a conclusion of law. 

Of course, the example of assault and battery is but one. 

The like, however, may be multiplied indefinitely.

Here again we reach the conclusion that the only way, at least the only practicable way, to know ultimate fact is by precedent. Use the approved forms. 

§ 324. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: The decisions of a court of last resort are supposed to be consistent with each other, and, of course, ought to be so. If they are not some of them are wrong; but no such court ever reached perfection in this respect and the Supreme Court of Colorado is no exception to the rule. We will note a few instances of real and apparent variations in its opinions and decisions with reference to pleading ultimate fact. 

In Lynch v. Smyth, 25 C. 103, 109, 54 P. 634, it was held that the ultimate fact was the execution by the defendant of the bond in suit, and that evidence of ratification was competent to establish that fact. To the same effect is Hoosac M. & M. Co. v. Donat, 10 C. 529, 533, 16 P. 157; Denver v. Bowen, 67 C. 315,.

The court does not notice the situation,¹ and the point seems not to have been raised by counsel, but, on page 477, the court seems to be of the opinion that the allegation of ratification was necessary. In Hale v. 

Goodell, 49 C. 95, 102, 111 P. 708, all the details of the making of a contract by agents are alleged but with neither an allegation that the principal made it nor any equivalent. The complaint is held insufficient on the ground that the ultimate fact of ratification is not sufficiently alleged. It would seem that the real defect was the omission of the allegation that the defendant made the contract.

The opinion was by Elliot, J., whose ideas on this subject we have noticed elsewhere. In Lothrop v. Union Bank, 16 C. 257, 27 P. 696, after an answer denying the execution of the note in suit the replication alleges that it was executed by defendant's authorized agent.

§ 325. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: In modern business where almost all sales as well as other contracts are made through agents, it would be a serious burden if the complaint must always allege the agency or a ratification. No attorney for a wholesale house, bringing an action for goods sold and delivered against a Colorado retail house, would consider such a manner of pleading.¹

Another case which seems inconsistent with the standard rule in Colorado as to a complaint in an action to quiet title, is 

Brothers v. Brothers, 29 C. 69, 70, 66 P. 901. The details of a parole transfer of land in consideration of services, followed by delivery of possession and improvements for years, are alleged, and are called ultimate facts. But the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that in an action to quiet title the only necessary allegations, (i.e., the only material allegations, code, Section 78) are that the plaintiff is the owner and in possession, and that defendant claims some adverse interest but has none. These are said to be the ultimate facts (by the same judge who wrote the opinion in Brothers v. Brothers), in 

Schlageter v. Gude, 30 C. 310, 312-13, 70 P. 428. The cases directly and indirectly supporting this last proposition are too numerous to cite here.

It seems probable, however, that in Brothers v. Brothers, the detailed allegations were in the replication, to show equity against the claim of the defendants or some of them.

§ 326. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: More over it sometimes happens that a defendant, proper to be joined in a suit to quiet title, (e.g., an escrow holder) though he claims no interest whatsoever, yet some act by him (e.g.. delivery of the escrow) is necessary or expedient for complete relief. In such case it would seem proper in order to do full equity to state the facts that justify such relief, even though not necessary to a mere decree quieting the plaintiff's title. 

And it sometimes happens that an inducement, necessary or convenient to explain the case or justify some form of relief, amounts to or reveals a separate cause of action. An example of such a case is Harkinson v. Harkison, 101 Fed. 71, where sufficient facts for an action in assumpsit were stated as inducement to explain an action for deceit.¹

Still another and remarkable instance of inconsistency with the general rule as to pleading ultimate fact and not evidence appears.2 This was an action for specific performance of a contract signed by agents of the seller. A demurrer to the complaint was sustained. The complaint set out the contract and the evidence relating to its execution in great detail and then alleged a ratification. The opinion says that even if the allegation of ratification is sufficient, if taken alone, it is nullified by other allegations, which, the opinion says, show that the principal did not know the terms of the contract at the time of the alleged ratification. These allegations were almost entirely evidential, which the opinion does not notice, but proceeds on the unquestionable proposition that a complaint must be consistent with itself and so affirms the judgment.

§ 330. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: It may be noted that, in Downing v. Ag. Ditch Co., 20 C. 546, 551, 39 P. 

336, the opinion, after saying that it is unnecessary for plaintiff to state how or of whom he acquired his superior right to water, goes on to hold that if he attempts to do so, he must not do so in uncertain terms. It seems, however, that, if the mere state-

297 ment that he has a superior right is enough, that "superior right" must be an ultimate fact, and, if that be so, the statement as to how it was acquired must be evidence of that right, as in case of an allegation of ownership of land and proof of title by deed. It would follow that the allegations of how or of whom the water right was acquired were nullities,² or, if not absolute nullities, yet that they could not supply the place. of the ultimate facts. 

Carroll v. Vance, 39 C. 216, 220, 88 P. 1069, however, holds that the mere statement of a superior right to water is a conclusion of law and that the method of its acquisition is ultimate fact. The only safe way, then, to allege ownership of a priority to water is to allege it in general terms followed by a statement of the method by which it was acquired, with what detail has not been held. § 331. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: In Mar tinez v. Martinez, 57 C. 292, 297, 141 P. 469, is a curious inconsistency. The trial court had stricken much evidential matter and the opinion says that the error, if any, was harmless because the allegations stricken, though eliminated in the pleadings, could have been proved notwithstanding, and yet says that the court "might well have overruled the motion to strike." But if the allegations stricken could have been proved anyhow there must have been other sufficient ultimate facts, "material allegations" under the code, to constitute a cause of action, and it follows that under Chapter XII of the code and Sections 66 and 78, the stricken portion was immaterial and so was properly stricken and the court might not "well have overruled the motion." The result of the opinion, however, seems right. 

In Soden v. Murphy, 42 C. 352, 355, 94 P. 353, it is held that proof that defendant received plaintiff's money from Powell is a fatal variance from an allegation that he received it from 

Miller who paid it to Powell for plaintiff. This case probably will not be followed for the variance was on a matter of mere evidence. The action was substantially for money had and received. The ultimate fact was that it was received for plaintiff's use and the source of its reception was immaterial.¹

¹Enright v. Midland Co., 33 C. 341, 343, 80 P. 1041, holding that change of evidential facts is not an amendment, and Oligarchy v. 

Farmers Co., 40 C. 291, 296, 88 P. 443, holding that the method by which stock was acquired is immaterial. Immaterial here means in pleading, not in evidence. 

§ 332. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: It has been held in N. Y. Life Ins. Co. v. Holck, 59 C. 416-18, 151 P. 

916, that the statements of facts from which the ultimate fact may be fairly inferred is good against a general demurrer. This cannot be law. It cannot stand with the many decisions to the contrary. It is almost a contradiction in terms and is a sanction of typical argumentative pleading and of the allegation of evidential facts to any extent; facts which have been many times held to be of no force, and upon which no issue could be formed. 

The point in this case was that the complaint did not allege the death but merely that the insured had been absent for more than seven years. The argument of the opinion is that such an allegation was proper because plaintiff could not allege the actual death. The minor premise is wrong. The plaintiff could allege the actual death and could prove it by evidence of the facts he had alleged.

The case is one more of the many that afford us a precedent on pleading ultimate fact, yet can hardly be followed. 

Somewhat similar is School Dist. v. High School Dist., 25 

C. A. 510, 517, 139 P. 1039. The high school district sued the school district for tuition of pupils sent from defendant district for high school instruction, under the statute, (S. L. 1909, p. 

488, sec. 1) which requires in such case the payment of "necessary tuition fees.”

The claim was that the complaint did not state a cause of action. The opinion says it should have stated the charge, which was $2.50, the maximum under the law, was necessary, or "the facts from which said conclusion might be drawn" but that the omission was of form only. 

This seems twice wrong. "Necessary" was an ultimate fact, because it is a conclusion from other facts and requires the decision of no question of law. It was not a conclusion of law by any definition of that term; neither was it evidence of anything. It was a material fact, i.e., one without which the complaint was insufficient (Code, sec. 78), because, by the statute, there could be no liability without it, therefore the complaint was subject to demurrer; and, since it was an ultimate fact, the "facts from which said conclusion might be drawn" were evidential. 

This reasoning may be tested concretely. What would be "the facts from which, etc."? That the cost of the high school,

ULTIMATE FACT 

299 per pupil, was $2.50 or over? Suppose that allegation is denied and the court leaves that to the jury as an issue, their answer could not determine the case. If they found that the cost was less than $2.50 that would not compel the conclusion that the charge of that sum was not necessary, but would merely tend to prove it; and even if they should find that the cost was over $2.50 the conclusion that the charge was necessary would not be inevitable. The real issue was "necessary vel non," and the pleadings should have been so framed as to express it. 

They did not express it and so failed in their main purpose and function. 

To put the case briefly: If "necessary" was the ultimate fact, the facts which show necessity could not be, and so ought not to be alleged. § 333. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: Again, in 

Mutual Life Ins. Co. v. Reid, 21 C. A. 143, 153, 121 P. 132, it was held that an allegation that the insured executed and delivered to Buckley, who was then and there the agent of the plaintiff, his note for $213.92 for the full annual premium upon said policy, was a sufficient allegation of payment of the premium. There is no question, however, that payment to an authorized agent is payment to the principal and it seems obvious that payment to the principal is the ultimate fact, evidenced by proof of payment to another and proof that such payee was an authorized agent.¹

It is true, however, that an issue, agent vel non, might be reached which would decide the case, so, perhaps, the case here is not so certainly wrong as N. Y. Life v. Holck or School 

District v. High School District, which we have noticed above. 

In divorce cases the rule against pleading evidence seems to be disregarded,' at least when alleging cruelty, but we find no practical statement of what details of acts of cruelty must be stated and the only rule seems to be the discretion or opinion of the judge, which, of course, is no rule at all. 

1See Contracts Made Through Agents, Ch. 45. 

2Geisseman v. Geisseman, 34 C. 461, 83 P. 635, citing Sylvis v. Sylvis, 11 C. 319, 323, 17 P. 912, and Rosenfeld v. Rosenfeld, 21 C. 16, 40 P. 49. 

§ 334. Inconsistency in the Decisions, continued: In Thomas v. Ray, 48 C. 423, 426, 110 P. 77, "entitled to possession" is said to be the issue in replevin, which cannot stand with the decisions of Baker v. Cordwell, 6 C. 199; Hanna v. Barker, 6 

C. 303; Roller v. Smith, 76 C. 371, 231 P. 656; Bank v. Trinidad

C. 362, 96 P. 177; Elliot v. First N. B., 30 C. 279, 70 P. 421; or

Street v. Sederburg, 41 C. 128, 132, 92 P. 29. In Baker v. 

Cordwell, the opinion expressly says that "entitled to possession" is a conclusion of law which flows from the allegation of ownership, which is obvious, and it is also obvious that if "entitled to possession" is a "material allegation," no other allegation in replevin is necessary, because it is an allegation of the final conclusion of law which will be expressed in the judgment. It is as if, in an action for goods sold and delivered, the complaint should merely say "the defendant owes the plaintiff one hundred dollars.".

It should be noticed that in ejectment the code expressly provides for the allegation "entitled to possession." Why?

301 The court says that the ultimate facts of a defense "must be determined from the entire defense and not from one or more paragraphs thereof," but it is not easy to see what this means. Ultimate facts should be alleged, not determined from other facts.

In another case, which was to enjoin a trustee's sale because the note secured thereby had been paid, though the only ultimate facts were the execution of the note and deed of trust, the threat to sell and the payment, and the only issue the payment, yet a vast amount of evidence was set out but ignored by the court.* 

The term "conclusion" is sometimes used instead of the term "conclusion of law" or "legal conclusion," as if a "conclusion" were forbidden. A conclusion of fact, however, is usually an ultimate fact, everywhere permitted to be alleged, and an ultimate fact is almost always a conclusion of fact, so a claim that an allegation is a mere conclusion is inconsequential.

It is hardly within reason that deductions, reasonable or not, should take the place of material allegations. Issues could not be formed under such pleadings. How could à deduction be denied? § 341. Further Decisions, continued: In Kenney v. Daugh erty, 67 C. 56, 185 P. 471, the complaint, which is under the forcible entry and detainer act, is set out in full. It is based on a dispossession of plaintiff by actual force, under C. L. 

Sec. 6366. The defendants denied entry by force and claimed that to be the only material fact. The opinion, page 59, says that many, if not all, of the other allegations are allegations of material facts and were properly pleaded in accord with said section, e.g., beating and striking plaintiff, so that the answer which merely denied taking possession by force did not satisfy 

C. L. Sec. 6378, which requires the answer to "either specifically admit or deny all of the material facts set forth in the complaint."

The ground of this decision is the forcible entry and detainer act, and is stated so to be, on page 60, where it is said not to be governed by the code. The clause in Section 6366 which the court regarded as controlling was: "shall set forth the substantial facts upon which the plaintiff relies," but there is no explanation of the conclusion that the details of the force, after the allegations of forcible dispossession, are "the substantial facts upon which the plaintiff relies," or why, after a denial of force, a denial of the methods or kinds of force adds anything, or, while force is the principal material fact and unquestionably an ultimate fact, a denial of it should not be a complete defense. The decision seems wrong, but, at all events, it has

no application to pleading under the code. It seems pretty certain that this case was originally brought before a justice of the peace. If not the court ignored C. L. '21, Section 6386. § 342. 2 § 347. In General: We have noticed, in the chapter on the 

Complaint, the rule that matters of mere evidence should not be alleged, and the reason, that such a course confuses the issues and sometimes conceals them. It violates a recognized rule of pleading. The Colorado reports are full of cases which reveal allegations of evidential matter. Some of these cases. contain decisions concerning such allegations, some dicta, some comment or suggestion, and some merely ignore the point; many condemn such pleading in general terms. It is to be regretted, however, that in so few instances has the court stated definitely what the allegations were which they were condemning. While there is no express approval of evidential allegations in general there are several opinions in which allegations which seem purely evidential are apparently approved or given weight in the arguments by which the court reaches its conclusion. It is held that by stipulation the pleadings may be used as evidence."

§ 348. Purpose: The pleading of evidential fact is usually the result of carelessness or mental indolence, but sometimes it is deliberate. The attorney, for example, of one injured by the alleged negligence of some corporation hopes to gain something with the jury by some prejudicial allegations, perhaps violent objurgations to the prejudice of the defendant, which he hopes to read to the jury or get to their attention in some way other than by proper evidence. It is evident, however, both from history and from the code that the pleadings are not for the jury, and it is so held in Colorado.¹ The issues are to be stated and explained to the jury by the court.¹ 

¹Cook v. Merritt, 15 C. 212, 214, 25 P. 176.

§ 351. Evidential and Material Mixed: Sometimes allega tions of matters immaterial even as evidence are mixed with evidential facts.¹ Often an answer denies and then alleges evidence to support the denial, equivalent, in substance, to the special traverse of the common law system, one of the things the code was made to get rid of. Occasionally a thoughtless reason is given, e.g., a complaint is held good because "it is simply a narration of the facts as given by the plaintiff in his testimony," an apparent sanction of evidential allegations, but doubtless not so intended. Evidential matter is usually found in company with the fault of verbosity. Sometimes the allegations so confuse the issues that the real issue is lost and a new trial becomes necessary." 5 3

§ 353. Treated as Material: Evidential allegations are often treated as if they were material,¹ for example, such an allegation has been held to be admitted by failure to deny it,2 not, however, when it is recognized as evidential. In such a case, failure to deny is held not to be an admission. Nor does a demurrer admit an evidential allegation. It often happens that a pleading states sufficient ultimate facts and adds evidence. Of course, such a pleading may be good against a general demurrer, as some of the cases in the note hold. Occasionally an allegation which appears evidential is taken to aid another whose sufficiency is questioned. And many mix evidential matter with conclusions of law. One complaint states ownership and adds evidential facts which defeat it. In Hale v. Goodell, discussed in the chapter on Complaint, evidential allegations to show authority of an agent, having been held insufficient, it is further held that, being insufficient, they nullify the words "thereunto duly authorized." Evidential matter is referred to as explaining other parts of the complaint,10 and in an action to recover money obtained by fraud an answer of evidential matter was held to show the parties were in pari delicto.

§ 355. Evidential Matter in the Answer: Argumentative denials have been treated briefly under the title Answer. They are very common, and sometimes are added to a general denial or to a proper specific denial. They are always evidential and

always both the cause and consequence of confused thinking. 

We note here a few of the cases where the court ignored the fault. After denial of the execution of a bond the answer alleges that it was signed in blank. Instead of a denial the answer alleges a different contract, or facts tending to show that intervening "savings depositors" were not such. In an action to quiet title, the allegation of title in defendant is a sufficient denial of plaintiff. A separate defense which consisted of argumentative denials was stricken out, but the reason is not stated. Facts inconsistent with defendant's employment are held to amount to a denial thereof."

Comments: The greater number of the foregoing cases which we have cited on this question of pleading evidential facts, indeed almost all of them, are cases in which no decision upon the question is rendered. By no means all of such instances have been cited, but we have collated here a majority of the Colorado cases on the question in the hope that they may be of use to anyone who may find it necessary to study or use illustrations of the common ways of pleaders in the State. Practically none is an authority in respect to this method of allegation.¹

The following part of this chapter, however, is an attempt to give the student and practitioner a fair showing of the law in Colorado with reference to the allegation of evidential matter. 

The leading case is Cuenin v. Halbouer, 32 C. 51, 53-4, 74 P. 

885, in which Mr. Justice Campbell, who is still on our supreme bench, discusses the question with illuminating clearness, showing the fallacy of such allegations as they are illustrated by

the argumentative denial. A denial of such an allegation states no defense,¹ it need not be denied, and a demurrer does not admit it. The rule against pleading evidence extends to an affidavit which charges contempt. In actions for negligence the fault is common and the pleadings are sometimes set out in full in the reports."

§ 357. Evidential Allegations Held Sufficient: Although in no case has the court sustained evidential allegations as such, yet in some cases it treats them with apparent approval and in some bases the decision thereon. In one case the complaint seems to have stated with some ultimate facts all the evidence there was, which is set out by the court in detail and a demurrer to this complaint is overruled.¹ In another the details of the authority of the boss of a boy killed by negligence are said to be admitted by the demurrer; which is equivalent to a decision that they were material allegations. In another opinion by Eliott, J., the pleadings are stated with great detail and the particulars of the way plaintiff acquired title are held to be admitted by demurrer. In but one case are evidential allegations distinctly approved with argument to maintain the approval, but even there they are not regarded as evidential.*

§ 360. Allegations Held Evidential¹: Evidential facts which support ultimate facts should be omitted. It is not necessary to set up the several steps by which a title is acquired. "A simple averment that the title is vested in the plaintiff" is sufficient; nor the facts which make up a trust,3 "they belong to the domain of evidence."3 Matter admissible in support of a denial is evidence. Evidential allegations do not change the cause of action. Averments of a series of facts by which defendant acquired title to land are mere evidence. If defendant in ejectment sets up his own title it leaves the issue still the same, title in plaintiff vel non." The addition by amendment of evidential facts does not help a complaint. One cannot, by pleading evidence obtain a ruling of the court to determine its effect as evidence, and such pleading does not require a reply. An allegation that one delivered a statement of account to another who made no objection is not an allegation that an account was stated between them.10 "Pleading is

,"11 a statement of facts, not of the evidence of facts. "That plaintiff was, under and by virtue of a certain conveyance, entitled to the immediate possession * is not a sufficient statement of the right of plaintiff in replevin.12

§ 362. Allegations Held Evidential, continued: In man damus to compel an irrigation district to deliver warrants the court criticizes the pleadings severely for pleading evidence.¹ 

Evidence and ultimate fact in pleading the statute of limitations are distinguished and explained.2 Allegation of proposition and acceptance does not allege a contract and a denial of it does not raise an issue. So in divorce based on a common law marriage, the allegation in the answer that the parties lived together on a provision of future marriage and the allegation in the replication that plaintiff had requested defendant to marry him ceremonially, are evidential, not material facts. and, not withstanding, the issue was simply marriage vel non.* 

Facts by which title was acquired are mere evidence. The ownership should be directly alleged, and an allegation that land is the property of the defendant is mere evidence to support the denial that it is a highway.5 Sometimes evidential destroy the force of an ultimate allegation, e.g., ownership, by qualifying it, creating an affirmative pregnant.

A statement that the assessment was made on such and such a date is a statement of evidence.

1Sigel-Campion Co. v. Ardohain, 71 C. 410, 411, 207 P. 82. the proper way to allege the contract. Denver v. Bowen, 67 C. 315, 184 P. 357.

§ 376. Surplusage: Evidential allegations are often treated as surplusage. They always are such when sufficient ultimate facts are stated.¹ In one case, however, it is said that although it is unnecessary for plaintiff to allege how or of whom he acquired his superior title (to water right), yet, if he attempts to do so, he must states details, a proposition which a little consideration shows to be a paradox. Where there are enough material allegations, all evidential allegations should be ignored if not stricken.

§ 378. In General: Something has been said of legal con clusions in the chapter on the complaint. Without unnecessarily repeating what was there said we add some comments and cases of more or less interest on that subject. 

The distinction between pleading law and conclusions of law should be noticed. It is never proper to state what the law is except in case of foreign laws and private statutes.¹ We find examples of such allegations,2 but no decision supports them. 

Municipal charters usually provide that they shall be regarded as public statutes. Municipal ordinances must be alleged. It is sufficient to allege that the ordinance was adopted duly, regularly and legally. 

Denver v. Colo. Spgs., 67 C. 288, 184 P. 373. The facts showing passage are not necessary, Id. It is enough to state the section number and title and date of passage, Miller v. Colo. Spgs., 3 C. A. 309, 33 P. 

74. In Wilson v. Barney, 90 C. 461, 9 P.(2d) 1058, a municipal ordinance is set out in substance and a copy attached. In D. O. & C. 

Co. v. Mills, 21 C. A. 582, 122 P. 798, plaintiff plead a speed ordinance. 

2In Bovee v. Boyle, 25 C. A. 165, 139 P. 1039, and in Denver v. 

Bossie, 83 C. 329, 266 P. 214, a statute is pleaded in hæc verba. In 

Rio G. Co. v. Orchard Dist., 64 C. 334, 337, 171 P. 367, the substance of a statute is set out. See Ch. 10 on Material Allegations. § 379. Treatment: Legal conclusions, however, are very common, always deprecated, when recognized as such, but more often ignored or unnoticed. 3 Like evidential allegations they are not traversable,2 are not admitted by failure to deny, and at best are surplusage and should be stricken out. They are not authorized by the code," nor admitted by demurrer. A legal conclusion is bad even in a garnishee's answer, and in findings of the Industrial Com-

mission. Being surplusage, a pleading with sufficient material allegations is good against a general demurrer although it contains them."

He who alleges or admits a legal conclusion is not bound by it, e.g., that defendant's act was larceny,¹º and a denial of it raises no issue.¹¹

§ 381. Allegations Impliedly Held Not Conclusions of Law: 

It seems that an allegation that a tax deed is "void on its face" is not a conclusion of law. The Court of Appeals held that the allegation of indebtedness was a sufficient allegation of failure to pay. It logically follows that "indebted" is an ultimate fact and a material allegation and not a conclusion. of law; but, if so, the only necessary allegation would be "that defendant is indebted to plaintiff in the sum of $. and a denial that defendant is "indebted" would be sufficient to let in any defense; as on the plea of nil debet at common law the opposite, however, seems to be implicit in Mutual Aid

§ 387. Legal Effect: The statement of the legal effect of a contract is called a "legal conclusion" but it has always been the law that one might allege a contract either in hæc verba or according to its legal effect. This was true not only in 

Assumpsit but in Covenant and Debt. The real trouble, as we have tried to show in the chapter on the Complaint, is that, by any logical definition, the allegation of the legal effect does actually involve the determination of a question of law, hence the necessity of reliance on precedent. 

¹Patrick v. Colo. Smelting Co., 20 C. 268, 275, 38 P. 236. The decision is that the statement of a written contract in hæc verba controls the allegation, in the same pleading, of its legal effect.

Peculiar Cases: In an action against a school district by a high school district to recover for tuition, under a statute which permitted the charge of an amount "necessary" to pay for such tuition, it was said that the complaint should allege that the amount claimed "was a necessary charge, or the facts from which said conclusion might be drawn.' The court did not notice that both alternatives could not be right. 991 

A complaint, in attacking a tax deed, alleged that certain things, enumerating them, required by statute, were not done "as required by law." The court held the allegation sufficient because it would have been so if the quoted words had been omitted, a reason that seems clearly unsound. To say that one did not do a certain thing is not the same as to say that he did not do it as required by law, and the latter proposition is a conclusion of law by its own terms. "Having alleged the facts, it was not necessary to allege the legal conclusion.''3

§ 394. In General: The original code, sec. 57, read thus: 

"The answer of the defendant shall contain a specific denial to each allegation intended to be controverted by the defendant and may contain a statement of any matter in avoidance or a counter-claim constituting a defense. * *››

The present section, 62, was enacted in 1887, in an act amending and enacting substantially the whole code. Section 62 is awkwardly expressed but it is clear enough that the only real change it makes is in permitting the general denial. This was done through the influence of some old common law lawyers who regretted the disappearance of the general issue of the common law system. Like the general issue it conceals the real issue and so frustrates the main purpose of pleading which the word "specific" in the original code was intended to accomplish.

It did not, however, accompilsh it. The reason for the failure was that the courts never, so far as denials were concerned, enforced the provisions that defenses must be separately stated, nor that only "material allegations" should be denied'; so it became a habit for pleaders to deny the allegations of the opponent, material and immaterial, seriatim, in one long sentence, thus giving, in effect, a general denial. This looked and was foolish and the general denial was permitted. 

The result is that unless all the allegations are material the real issues are not disclosed and not evident even when the allegations are all material. 

¹Code of 1877, § 60; Code of 1887, § 59; Courtright's Mills Anno. 

Code, § 65; Code 1921, § 65. 

2Code of 1877, §§ 61, 72, 73 and 153; Courtright's Mills Anno.

Code, 

§§ 62, 66, 78 and 189; Code 1921, §§ 62, 66, 78 and 190. 

§ 395. In the Original Code: If the original code had been obeyed and nothing but material allegations allowed to remain in a pleading, everything else stricken out, and each remaining material allegation intended to be controverted had been separately denied, expressly as a separate defense, the issues would have been clear cut and definite, much time saved, the courts more efficient and justice advanced.

The general denial, in substance, is that the defendant denies each and every allegation in the complaint, and that is sufficient. 3 2 

The answer must of course be responsive to the complaint," and a denial of matter not alleged is a nullity. All material allegations not denied are admitted. A petition to determine heirship needs no answer. The question is: "Who are the heirs?''4

§ 396. Information and Belief: The code permits, where the facts are not presumptively within the knowledge of the defendant, what is sometimes called the "denial on information and belief." It is really a denial for lack of knowledge, information and belief. The form of such denial, required by the code, is that (defendant) has not and cannot obtain sufficient knowledge or information on which to base a belief. An
