§ 398. Form of Denial: The customary form of denial of a single allegation is: "The (defendant) denies that-" (the plaintiff delivered the horse). This is an imitation of the chancery practice and, with the admissions there required, was well adapted to the purpose of that system, to produce a full disclosure of evidentiary matters, but is not so fit for the purpose of finding the issues as is the categorical denial in the specific traverse at common law.¹ Any form of denial, however, that is definite, is sufficient. "Has no right, title or interest" is a good denial of title. A denial, however, in the replication of "all allegations contrary to the amended complaint" is no denial.³ 

¹See above, this chapter. In Boone's Forms the word "not" is used. 

Estees gives both methods. Estees Pl., § 3195-3197. 

2Leach v. Torbert, 71 C. 85, 89, 204 P. 334. 

3 Fitzwater v. Norcross, 95 C. 527, 530, 37 P.(2d) 522. Indeed it is logically a denial of denials, and therefore futile. 

§ 399. Specific Denial: The specific denial is a denial (i.e., any direct negative) of one material allegation. A material allegation is one which if omitted from a pleading would leave it insufficient.2 Such denial is the exact equivalent of the common or specific traverse of the common law. It need not be said that a negative of an essential to any syllogism will destroy the conclusion, and the application of this rule to the legal syllogisms of pleadings needs no explanation.³ 

4 It follows, of course, that a denial of an immaterial allegation will be a nullity, and so is a denial of a mere conclusion of law. It is common to deny damage and damages, though it was not done at common law."

The denial of a negative averment should, of course, be in the affirmative, and the burden of proof then sometimes shifts."

§ 401. General Denial: The general denial is now more commonly used than any other. It is sometimes called the general issue. Its usual form is: "The (defendant) denies each and every allegation in said (complaint)." This form is variously modified, e.g., by adding the words "not herein admitted, "" or some such qualification³; or, instead of "complaint" by using the term "paragraph (four) of said (complaint).' Such methods of using the general denial are sanctioned and common. 

A denial of "each and every material allegation" has been questioned, and has been passed unnoticed," and so of a denial in a replication of all new matter in the answer, and this is held subject to a motion to make specific.? 6' It is held that a general denial in an answer in ejectment admits defendant's possession, that under such a denial defendant may prove that a trustee's deed in plaintiff's title is fraudulent, and that almost any defense is covered by it.º

§ 404. Argumentative Denial: An argumentative denial is a statement of fact inconsistent with some material allegation of the opponent instead of a direct negative of that allegation. i.e., a fact which could be proved under the general denial.¹ 

It is condemned2 in both the common law and code systems, because it always confuses and sometimes prevents the issue. 

Prof. Pomeroy is very severe in his objection. 3 

For example: The complaint alleges that defendant has converted the automobile of the plaintiff to his own use. The answer says that the automobile in the complaint mentioned is the automobile of one XY. The replication denies that the said automobile is the automobile of XY. The issue formed is "of XY vel non. If the jury find not, the case is not determined because the chattel still may or may not be the property of the plaintiff. If, on the other hand, the answer says that the automobile is not the automobile of the plaintiff, proof that it is the property of XY or anybody else will be relevant to support the denial. So it is held proper to strike out the allegation of any fact which might be proved under a denial.5 and an answer with nothing but an argumentative denial needs no reply, or denial,' and does not put the allegation in issue.

Of course, actual argument in pleading is out of place." It should be in the brief.

³Cuenin v. Halbouer, 32 C. 51, 54, 74 P. 885. Argumentative denial referred to as "by way of confession and avoidance if it may be so termed." Empire Co. v. Chapin, 22 C. A. 538, 541, 126 P. 1107. 

§ 412. Special Traverse: At common law what was really an argumentative traverse was tolerated in that peculiar pleading called the special traverse, which consisted of a statement of a fact or facts inconsistent with some material allegation of the declaration, followed by the "absque hoc," which was a backhanded denial of the fact which had already been denied argumentatively. The rule against argumentativeness in pleadings under the code is constantly violated by pleading which is in substance a special traverse, one of the common law technicalities which the code was intended to abolish. 1 For example2: The plaintiff in ejectment alleges that he is the owner of Lot X. The special traverse is in substance "the defendant is the owner of said lot, without this; that the plaintiff is the owner thereof." The inexperienced code. pleader (and sometimes others), answering, will say "denies that the plaintiff is the owner of said lot but alleges that the defendant is the owner thereof"; the exact equivalent of the special traverse. "This mode of pleading is faulty in the extreme. 994

The real issue here, is, of course, plaintiff's ownership vel non; but when the replication denies defendant's ownership a false issue is formed; false, because it will not determine the case. If the jury should find that defendant was not the owner that would not determine that plaintiff was; yet he must recover on the strength of his own title, and must prove it.5 Proof of defendant's title is evidence in support of the denial of that of plaintiff."

There are many examples of this kind of pleading.'

460. Examples, continued. § 425. In General¹: Facts which are consistent with the material allegations of the complaint but inconsistent with the right of the plaintiff to a judgment in his favor, may be alleged to avoid plaintiff's claim to that right. Such a fact alters the minor premise of the legal syllogism so that the conclusion no longer follows. It is called "confession" because it tacitly³ admits the material allegations of the complaint, and "avoidance" because it makes void the conclusion that plaintiff should have a judgment. All "new matter" must be in avoidance.' 

¹See Denial, Ch. 26. 

2Hallack v. Blake, 4 C. A. 486, 488, 36 P. 554; Denver v. Solomon, 2 C. A. 534, 542, 31 P. 507.

Pedotto v. Yantorno, 72 C. 1, 209 P. 279. Seemingly contra, First 

Nat. Bank v. Shank, 53 C. 446, 128 P. 56. 

4"It does not disprove a single averment of fact in the complaint but merely prevents or destroys the legal conclusion" which would result from their truth. Wyman v. McCarthy, 93 C. 340, 342, 26 P.(2d) 245.

If it is inconsistent with any material fact in the complaint it amounts to an argumentative denial and is properly stricken, Id. See Pom. Rem., 2d Ed., § 630.

§ 427. 

When Necessary: As appears in the chapter on denial, there is some confusion in the decisions as to what facts are admissible in evidence under a denial and what must be pleaded in confession and avoidance. The abstract rule is not questioned, i.e., that no fact inconsistent with any material allegation of the complaint need be alleged in the answer,¹ but facts consistent with them must be, yet in the concrete application of this rule the cases have not been uniform. 

¹Indeed, should not. 1 Chit. 515 N. Z.; Walker v. Inv. Co., 79 C. 170, 173, 244 P. 465; McDonald v. Peo., 29 C. 503, 508-9, 69 P. 703; Mott v. Baxter, 29 C. 418, 68 P. 220; Wyman v. McCarthy, 93 C. 340, 341-2-3, 26 P.(2d) 245. 

2Adams v. Tucker, 6 C. A. 393, 396, 398, 40 P. 788.

Claim of title by defendant, under chattel mortgage, in replevin (or trespass de bonis) is said to be confession and avoidance, in Gomer v. Stockdale, 5 C. A. 489, 492-3, 39 P. 355. This is contrary to Payne v.

Williams, 62 C. 86, 160 P. 196, and to the many cases which cite and follow it and others; Buchanan v. Scandia Co., 6 C. A. 34, 39 P. 899; Morris v. Wilson, 39 C. 464, 466, 90 P. 845; Penn. Mut. v. Ornauer, 39 C. 498, 90 P. 846; Cuenin v. Halbouer, 32 C. 51, 54, 74 P. 885; Mott v. Baxter, 29 C. 418, 68 P. 220; Hallack v. Blake, 4 C. A. 486, 488, 36 P. 554; 

McAlpine v. McAlpine, 86 C. 135, 278 P. 614; David v. Gilbert, 85 C. 

184, 192, 274 P. 821; Walker v. Inv. Co., 79 C. 170, 178, 244 P. 465; 

Gromer v. Papke, 71 C. 440, 441, 207 P. 862; Gaffner v. Nelson, 66 C. 

586, 185 P. 338; but consistent with Mason Sales Co. v. Tier Co., 78 

C. 42, 45, 213 P. 117, which holds that any special property in defendant

in replevin must be in confession and avoidance, otherwise of general property. The reason for this distinction is not evident. 

The principle is inconsistent with Bailey v. Sullivan, 75 C. 346, 225 P. 

880, a case in replevin which holds that a replication which alleges a right under a chattel mortgage, is not a departure from a complaint which alleges ownership. If so, defendant's allegation of his chattel mortgage is an argumentative denial of plaintiff's ownership, and not confession and avoidance. See Departure. Wyman v. McCarthy, 93 C. 

340, 26 P.(2d) 245, however, settles the matter correctly and probably forever. 

§ 428. "New Matter': The code, unfortunately, used the term "new matter” instead of "matter in avoidance" in referring to confession and avoidance, and that has produced a seemingly irresisitble tendency in many pleaders to allege in the answer every fact that it is desired to prove,¹ and the courts have not been wholly consistent in treating this kind of mistake. New matter has been variously defined but seldom is it in term recognized as in confession and avoidance though often tacitly so.³ 

¹An example of this is Novelty Co. v. Whitcomb, 47 C. 110, 112, 106 

P. 1012, where in addition to general denial and contributory negligence, the defendant alleged facts which tended to negative negligence and proximate cause and and to prove contributory negligence. Judges are misled in the same way. Wyman v. McCarthy, 93 C. 340, 26 P.(2d) 245.

The concurring opinion, pages 344-5. The argument requires the premise that every "material substantive fact which, if true, constituted a complete defense" should be alleged as new matter, which is not true. 

The majority opinion makes this clear. See Payne v. Williams, 62 C. 

86, 160 P. 196, and the cases which cite it. Baisch v. Mueller, 53 C. 

474-5, 128 P. 466, is contrary. See Assumpsit, Quantum Meruit. 

2Matters in "avoidance" are referred to as "new matter" under the code. Koll v. Bush, 6 C. A. 294, 297, 40 P. 579. But also as in avoidance, § 77. 

There are three quoted definitions in David v. Gilbert, 85 C. 184, 192, 274 P. 821. 

§ 429. Analysis: The distinction between the two categories of matters in confession and avoidance, i.e., 1. justification or excuse and 2. discharge, has not been noticed in the decisions under the Colorado Code. Matters in discharge, however, are uniformly recognized as in confession and avoidance, e.g., release and accord and satisfaction.¹

It is said that "anything impeaching the validity of a contract" should be pleaded as a defense. Of course a defense in confession and avoidance not pleaded will not be considered.*

Consideration: There is much confusion in the Colorado decisions as to the pleading of want and of failure of consideration. In reason it seems clear that want of consideration, wherever it is a defense at all, is a traverse. If consideration be omitted where required it leaves the complaint insufficient. It is therefore a "material allegation" and denial of it, then, is a sufficient defense.2 Failure of consideration, however, since there was once a valid contract, would seem to be a matter of confession and avoidance. If we keep this distinction in mind we ought to be able to discover some consistency in our cases, but it seems impossible.

§ 433. Consideration, continued: Want of consideration is available as a defense only where the want is total.¹ 

¹Vreeland v. Murray, 62 C. 322, 162 P. 148, and partial failure cannot be proved under a plea of it. § 434. Consideration, continued: Space will not permit a complete discussion here, but the proposition that want of consideration is a traverse, with full and careful discussion, is held

in Alden v. Carpenter, 7 C. 87, 1 P. 904, and that case has never been expressly overruled.

Courts often fail to distinguish cases of failure of consideration from those of want. The final decision in cases of failure is usually right, but as a matter of pleading they furnish no analogy to cases of want of consideration.¹

§ 436. Consideration, continued: It is true that such a decision is contrary to Alden v. Carpenter; but it is believed there is no decision in Colorado which holds that a direct traverse of the consideration alleged in the complaint has been held insufficient. 'Indeed, how else could "the facts which show that there was no consideration" be alleged.¹

The cases which hold that the plea of no consideration is a confession and avoidance, mostly, if not all, show a mere statement that "there was no consideration for said (note)," or something substantially equivalent; and, holding that to be insufficient, they then jump to the conclusion that it must be "specially pleaded," which, in legal parlance, means "pleaded in confession and avoidance," a conclusion which is not justified. 2 

¹For example: The complaint alleges that the plaintiff sold to defendant an automobile and in consideration thereof defendant promised to pay him one thousand dollars. The defendant answers "that the plaintiff did not sell to him an automobile" or "denies that the plaintiff sold him an automobile." How could it be said that such an answer was not a perfect defense? How that it was not a traverse?

How that it does not state "the facts which show that there was no consideration"? 

2Sometimes that it is a conclusion of law; Dowdey v. Maxwell, 73

§ 437. Consideration, continued: Alden v. Carpenter was an action on a promissory note and it was held that a statement that there was no consideration was a traverse of the implication of a consideration in the note. Under the cases just noticed the defendant would be required to "confess," i.e., tacitly admit, that there was a consideration and then allege facts to show there was not, in avoidance. To allege facts which show that any material allegation is not true is an argumentative denial, and inconsistent with Payne v. Williams, 62 

C. 86, 160 P. 196, and the many cases which hold that such facts may be proved in support of a denial. 

Again: If there was an apparent consideration, e.g., a pretended sale of something that did not exist, it would be possible to allege "the facts which show that there was no consideration"; but if the note was purely nudum pactum, simply without any consideration apparent or otherwise, what else could defendant answer but that there was no consideration?

If a specific consideration were alleged, as the supposed sale in the preceding note,' he may of course say that plaintiff did not sell, but that will be a traverse, and any series of facts he may allege to that end will merely show that the allegation

of the specific consideration is untrue and consequently must be an argumentative traverse.

In conclusion, on this point, we can say with confidence that where a specific consideration is alleged any direct negative or denial thereof will be sufficient to show want of consideration; that where there was a consideration, but it has failed, the facts which show that failure should be alleged in confession and avoidance, and that where the allegation of consideration is in general terms or where it is presumed and there never was any consideration whatever, we have no sufficient guide in the conflicting Colorado decisions.¹

Payment, continued: The question of payment as confession and avoidance is discussed in Alden v. Carpenter, 7 C. 87, 91, 1 P. 904, and it is there shown that it is, in essence, a traverse. That position seems to be logically unassailable in

all actions on contracts for the payment of money. The breach of a contract in suit is essential to a cause of action on the contract. The only possible breach of a contract to pay is non-payment. Non-payment, then, is a material allegation,¹ and its denial will form an issue." Since, then, a general denial denies every material allegation, it denies non-payment, and proof of payment should be competent under it. This has been directly declared, citing Alden v. Carpenter.

None of the later cases has expressly overruled either Alden v. Carpenter or Watson v. Lemen, but all have ignored them. 

Unreasonable though it be, safety forbids us to treat payment as a denial of the breach of a contract to pay.

§ 454. Bona Fide Purchase: In actions on a negotiable instrument the presumption is that it is held bona fide.¹ actions respecting rights in real estate, under the statutes respecting record of deeds, the cases are contradictory. Some hold that a complaint by the holder of an unrecorded instrument must allege notice to a subsequent purchaser, while others hold that the subsequent purchaser, defendant, must plead his bona fides and lack of notice in confession and avoidance. Everett v. Todd holds the point but does not assert it. 

Schneider v. Cross says it "follows" Everett v. Todd, but decides the case on other grounds, i.e., even giving Schneider the benefit of Everett v. Todd, he could not win, because the issue, "notice or not," had been tried. The opinion is not clearly expressed. As in Schneider v. Cross, the defendant in 

Myers v. Hayden, 82 C. 98, 102-3, 257 P. 351, alleged lack of notice which was denied and the issue tried. The court held that was enough.

It is held that a defendant whose claims do not appear of record and who attacks the title of the plaintiff, who is a subsequent purchaser, on the ground that he (the plaintiff) took with notice of defendant's rights must not only allege that plaintiff took with notice but must show that all intervening purchases did also.*

Outside the strict subject of pleading, it is held that an overdue trust deed of record is notice of an unrecorded trustee's deed."

Effect of the Issue. 

§ 461. In General: We have shown in Chapter 1 that the basic purpose of pleading is to reach an issue¹ a proposition of law or fact affirmed in the pleadings on one side and denied in those on the other. That that is the purpose of code pleading is shown by Chapter XII of the code and other sections and decisions.2

We have shown, too, that the question involved in the issue must be one the determination of which will determine the case, and a true issue must have the alternative "or not" (vel non).* If there is no issue there is nothing to try, and a good answer in confession and avoidance undenied, leaves the defendant entitled to a judgment."

§ 462. 

Inaccurate Use of Term: The term "issue" has been so inaccurately used by our courts¹ that it requires some care to extract from the opinions clear rules on the subject, but if the code itself and the exact meaning of the term are kept in mind the task is not hard. 

The courts have been inexact in their statements, unavoidably so. Evidential allegations denied are often called "'issues. 12

It is said that the only issue was-then stating several. The term "issues thus joined" is used to denote questions which had arisen on a protest against a change of point of diversion.* 

It is correctly used in Chetelat v. Kelter, 7 C. A. 68, 42 P. 495; Koll v. Bush, 6 C. A. 294, 296, 40 P. 579, where the issues were: Was the plaintiff discharged or not? And were his services satisfactory or not? 

Ehrenbrook v. Ehrenbrook, 90 C. 437, 438, 9 P.(2d) 610, is a good case for study. The opinion states issues briefly, including controverted evidential allegations. There were really two cases, one to enforce a resulting trust in plaintiff's favor as to one-half of a ranch, and the other to enforce a right given by a will to purchase the other half (or the whole if the trust claim failed). As to the first case, so far as the opinion shows, there was one issue, trust vel non, and its determination would determine plaintiff's right. All other disputes were evidential. 

As to the second case there were two issues: A. Compliance with the will by plaintiff vel non, and, B. Ownership in testator vel non; complete, typical issues, because if either were the sole issue it would determine the case. It would have been enough, in the first case, to allege that defendant held title to the ranch as trustee (Logan v. Clough, 2 C. 323, 326-8), for testator and plaintiff and that she refused to convey plaintiff's share to him.

In the second case the plaintiff should have merely alleged that the testator was the equitable owner (Rice v. Bush, 16 C. 484, 485, 494, 27 

P. 720; Brooks v. Black, 22 C. A. 49, 50, 123 P. 131; Phillippi v. Leet, 19 C. 246, 35 P. 540; Gwillim v. Asher, 71 C. 143, 146-7, 204 P. 609); or even merely owner (Foster v. Coffey, 71 C. 171, 173, 204 P. 900); that he died leaving the will, stating the substance of its provisions, which gave plaintiff the right to purchase, and that plaintiff was ready and willing, had tendered, etc., and the answer should have merely denied these allegations. All else in the answer was evidential, e.g., that the testator was defendant's agent went to show that he was not the owner, and that defendant was not trustee, but it could not be an issue, because, whether he was agent or not he might or might not be an owner, and defendant might or might not be a trustee. 

2Horn v. Reitler, 15 C. 316, 317, 25 P. 501, is a good example. The real issue was ownership in plaintiff vel non. The "issues," as stated by the court were questions upon evidence, which need not, and so should not, have been alleged in the pleadings, but should have been proved under the real issue. See Baker v. Cordwell, 6 C. 199; Hanna v. 

Barker, 6 C. 303; Payne v. Williams, 62 C. 86, 160 P. 196, and the

THE ISSUE 

377 cases which cite it. 

The common case of trespass on land illustrates this point very well. The complaint says that the defendant with force and arms entered the close of the plaintiff and (set his haystack on fire); the answer denies that defendant entered, etc. The evidence tends to show that tracks to and from the stack are the defendant's. 

If this is the only evidence hasty thought will conclude that the issue is "tracks of the defendant vel non," and the error is natural enough, because, as the evidence has turned out, the decision of that question will probably decide the case; but when we remember that the issue is the outcome of the pleadings we see that it is an error which, in some other case would lead to an absurdity. Suppose, for example, evidence is offered that defendant entered to drive away the real trespasser. If the issue were "tracks of the defendant vel non" such evidence would concede the affirmative of the issue, yet, if true, would be a complete defense to the action.

Other cases in which the term "issue" is used to denote disputes in the evidence are: Coffin v. Johnson, 20 C. A. 567, 573, 86 P. 354; 

Millett v. Barth, 18 C. 112, 113, 31 P. 769; Tadlock v. Lloyd, 65 C. 40, 41-2, 173 P. 200; Paulson v. Bergman, 62 C. 93, 94, 160 P. 189; Kendall v. Metroz, 65 C. 387, 176 P. 473; Clark v. Knox, 32 C. 342, 344-5, 348, 352, 355, 76 P. 372; Crawford v. Birkins, 16 C. A. 532, 534, 66 P. 687.

But in this case the court doubtless means that the issue is "ownership in Crawford vel non." Many cases cited below in this chapter are examples of this use of the word.

§ 465. Issues, How Formed: The code, in Chapter XII, provides for issues of law and issues of fact. An issue, whether of law or fact, must be a question the decision of which will decide the case.¹ An issue of law is raised by demurrer,2 and not otherwise." 

It is said that issues either of law or fact may be raised in a proceeding in mandamus, but the one of law is properly and usually raised by motion to quash. This matter is further treated in the chapter on the demurrer. An issue of fact is raised only by the denial of a material allegation, that is, an allegation of a fact essential to the case of him who alleges it. It is a necessary consequence of this rule that it is not raised by a denial of anything else, conclusion

§ 475. Particular Issues: The ubiquitous, ever recurring issue is owner vel non.¹ More often than not a law suit will be found to arise out of a dispute about the ownership of land, goods, evidences of debt, or money. Examples constantly before us are in Replevin, Ejectment, Conversion and Trespass on land, sometimes in actions on contracts and often in equity cases, e.g., Quiet Title. 

In an action for conversion the sole issue was "ownership by plaintiff or not'; so in replevin, and ejectment*; and in an action to quiet title. A plaintiff brought an action to compel an administrator to inventory a note signed by him payable to the intestate, and alleged that it belonged to the estate which the administrator denied. § 476. Further Examples: In various sorts or kinds of action the issues have been declared by our higher courts. We mention some of them in the note.¹

On 

1¹Assumpsit: Money advanced-allegation of promise to repay. general denial, defendant was allowed to prove advances were a gift. 

Payne v. Williams, 62 C. 86, 160 P. 196. This is the leading case on the point that anything inconsistent with the affirmative of the issue may be proved under the general denial. In Bank v. Esser, 75 C. 110, 112-13, 224 P. 227, the issue, promise vel non, is considered and stated. 

Also in Belisimo v. Ceresa, 80 C. 325, 327, 328, 251 P. 531. In Mason v. Walker, 67 C. 530, 186 P. 544, the issue was on the answer, payment vel non.

Negligence: The issue was negligence in starting the car vel non. 

Denver Tram. Co. v. Cowan, 51 C. 64, 70, 77, 116 P. 136. In an action against a railroad company for negligent treatment of cattle in transit, the number of cattle killed is spoken of as matter for issue, Atchison, etc., Co. v. Baldwin, 53 C. 426, 429, 128 P. 453, but it could not determine the case. The proper way to meet the situation is to plead the less number of cattle as a partial defense, e.g., "as to all of said cattle alleged to have died-etc., except (100 head), defendant denies that they died."

Conversion: In an action for the conversion of diamonds, the real issue is discussed, but a dispute in the evidence is stated as the issue. 

Silberfield v. Solomon, 70 C. 413, 416, 202 P. 113. Upon a counterclaim the issue was property in defendant vel non, and property in plaintiff should not be alleged but proved under a denial, general or specific. 

First Nat. Bank v. Booth, 77 C. 122, 124, 235 P. 570. 

Intervention: The denial of intervenor's right makes an issue. Stokes v. Dollard, 94 C. 206, 208, 29 P.(2d) 706. In Mitchell v. Reed, 16 C. 

109, 112, 26 P. 342, though a justice of the peace case, the evidence is carefully reviewed, and the ultimate question (issue) stated, ownership by Reed vel non.

Ejectment: A denial that plaintiff is entitled to possession raises no issue, Roller v. Smith, 76 C. 371, 373, 231 P. 656. On the issue of

Statute of Limitations, alleged by defendant and denied generally a tax deed is evidence of color of title, Gibson v. Huff, 26 C. A. 144, 141 

P. 510.

Libel: Notwithstanding the jury are judges of both law and fact, issues must be made up and tried as in other cases. Meeker v. Post 

Co., 55 C. 355, 360, 135 P. 457.

Quiet Title: In Empire Co. v. Webster, 52 C. 207, 213, 121 P. 171, plaintiff's title seems to be regarded as the issue, but this is inconsistent with the rule that the answer must assert a title to constitute a defense.

777 

See Action to Quiet Title. In Scott v. Watkins, 61 C. 244, 245-6, 157 P. 3, the answer alleged a tax deed and advertisement for four weeks. The advertisement was denied and it was held that there was an issue, and plaintiff should have been allowed to show the defects. Reversing 25 

C. A. 340, 138 P. 432. So upon general denial with claim of title the defendant may in his evidence prove the invalidity of plaintiff's tax deed, Jones v. Empire Co., 25 C. A. 382, 138 P. 62.

A denial of plaintiff's title and an allegation of title in defendant raises an issue of fact. McMillen v. Hayman, 74 C. 300, 221 P. 893, and the burden is on the plaintiff. See also Phares v. Don Carlos, 74 

C. 356, 221 P. 883.

Adverse Suit: This action is anomalous. The issue is said to be whether either party is entitled to a patent from the United States. 

Manning v. Strehlow, 11 C. 451, 18 P. 625. It is really two issues, plaintiff entitled to patent vel non, and defendant entitled to a patent vel non; each against the other, and both against the United States. 

See also Thomas v. Chisholm, 13 C. 105, 107-8, 21 P. 1019, and cases there cited.

Mandamus: In Mandamus to compel the State Treasurer to pay a warrant of a certain class, whether the warrants already registered exhausted the funds of that class was held to be an issue. Stuart v. 

Nance, 28 C. 194, 199, 63 P. 323.

Attachment: A traverse in attachment must make an issue. A denial of the affidavit in the present tense is not sufficient. Mitchell Co. v. 

Lumber Co., 89 C. 215, 218, 1 P.(2d) 97.

Damages: It is said that the court cannot submit the question of damages unless an issue was made on it. Mountz v. De Bar, 61 C. 363, 365, 157 P. 1163, but the meaning of the case is that damage, as distinguished from the ad damnum or the prayer for judgment, must be alleged. Damages, i.e., the amount of damages, is not issuable. Tucker v. Parks, 7 C. 62, 68, 1 P. 427.

§ 478. In General: It is an unquestioned rule, expressed in various ways that the allegations and the proofs must agree,¹ otherwise the pleadings would be of no use. 

The difficulty which we meet when trying to enforce this rule, is the ever recurring one of the distinction between conclusion of law, ultimate fact and evidential fact, which many cases show a failure to recognize.2 This is made clear when evidence of ratification is allowed as one method of proving the execution of a contract.3

§ 481. In General: The subject of the allegation of owner ship deserves special treatment, although it is mentioned elsewhere.¹ Here, perhaps, more than elsewhere, the fault of the allegation of evidential facts is manifested, yet there is no proposition of remedial law better established than that the allegation "than-plaintiff is the owner" is an allegation of an ultimate fact which requires the support of no more particular allegation,2 and the fact that the source of title is added does not restrict the proof to that source.³

§ 488. 

In General: We have shown that the distinction between actions ex delicto and ex contractu must be and is maintained in the code practice and pleading. We will now consider more particularly the view of the Colorado courts on actions ex delicto. 1 An action ex delicto is upon a tort, that is, a violation of a primary duty, given by law, without a contract, to every one in a like situation. The simplest case is assault, the violation of defendant's duty to respect the person of another and of the corresponding right that it be respected. 

Motive or bad faith is no part of a conversion, yet the Supreme Court once said that where administrators converted for the estate stock which belonged to a third party, there was "no element of tort," because they acted in good faith.2 

It often happens that he who converts a chattel believes it to be his own, but he is liable none the less. Motive, however, is sometimes relevant as evidence tending to show that defendant did what he is accused of or that his defense is untrue.³

§ 495. In General: Trespass at common law was an action for forcible injury to the person or property or relative rights of another.

For an injury to the person or mere damage to property, it was called simply trespass; for entry on land or building, trespass quare clausum fregit; for taking goods, trespass de bonis asportatis or trespass de bonis; all, however, were one form of action. All these terms are still much in use,¹ 1 and wherever trespass would lie at common law an action under the code may be maintained. In trespass de bonis the proper allegations are plaintiff's ownership, the taking and conversion. The complaint may be in the words of the common law declaration. Indeed there is no better form for it. The injury to property must be to a possessory right. The allegation in trespass de bonis is that defendant "took and carried away" (the automobile) "of the plaintiff," and "took" is the gist of the action," and constitutes a conversion." 2 4 It was a rule of the common law and it still prevails that any abuse of lawful authority may render one a trespasser ab initio, as unnecessary violence in arrest, or unlawful acts after a lawful entry." § 501. Trespass De Bonis: This sort of action is not uncom mon in code practice,¹ but, since it need not be so denominated, it is usually thought of merely as conversion,2 and we notice it in that category. and is good against a general demurrer. So at common law Trover would lie wherever trespass de bonis was proper. "Williams v. Stringfield, 76 C. 343, 231 P. 658.

§ 503. Trespass to the Person: This cause of action is illustrated most simply by assault and battery, but any injury to the person which is caused by force will justify it. In practice, however, in perhaps all instances of this sort, where the injury is not wilful, the theory of trespass is forgotten, and, by analogy to case, negligence is made the basis of the action for damage to the person, usually called "personal injuries."" 

It was true at common law and probably is still true that where negligence and force were combined, as in collision of vehicles, the plaintiff may choose which theory of his case he will adopt.2 In some cases the theories are hopelessly mixed."

In General: The term "trover" is much used,¹ though the form of action has been abolished, and, practically both trover and trespass de bonis have become merged in an action for conversion. Indeed, at common law they were largely concurrent remedies, i.e., trover would lie wherever trespass de bonis would. So trover was a remedy against the sheriff for him whose goods had been taken on attachment against another."

As in trespass the plaintiff must have possession or a right to immediate possession at the time of the conversion. Any property, general or special, in the goods which gives such right is enough." A chattel mortgagee may maintain the action against his mortgagor who has sold the mortgaged goods."

In General, continued: Conversion has been defined as "Any distinct, unauthorized act of dominion or ownership, exercised by one person over personal property belonging to another. 991 The definition is ponderous. A better one, expressing all that is in it, is "Any act of adverse dominion over the chattel of another." The definition is sometimes ignored. A sale by a pledgee to himself is not a conversion. A carrier's misdelivery is conversion. This case does not notice the point but it is unquestionable.5 

con- At common law conversion was alleged in two forms of action, trespass de bonis and trover. In the former the allegation was that the defendant "took" the goods and " verted them to his own use," in the latter that plaintiff "lost" them, defendant "found" them and "converted them to his own use. The method of conversion was not alleged. The allegations in trespass are sufficient today, and, indeed, so are those in trover, but it is not now necessary to allege the loss and finding, and at common law they were not traversable. 

The Supreme Court has called an action which alleged taking and conversion trover."

What Should be Alleged: The ultimate facts in an action for conversion are ownership of the plaintiff and conversion by defendant.¹ These, then, are the "material allegations" required by the code, and it follows that nothing else should be alleged except what the rules of certainty demand, i.e., time, place, value, names, etc., which are not traversable.2

§ 510. Ownership, How Alleged: In alleging ownership, 

"of the plaintiff" is enough.' That "plaintiff is the owner is also sufficient, but the former has the advantage that under it plaintiff may prove anything that shows in him the right to immediate possession, for example: A chattel mortgage.2 To controvert the plaintiff's title, defendant should deny "that the (watch) in the complaint mentioned was at the time of the alleged conversion the watch of the plaintiff,' or deny "that plaintiff was at the time of the alleged conversion the owner of the (watch) in the complaint mentioned," or say "that said (watch) at the time, etc., was not the watch of the plaintiff." The issue will then be: Plaintiff the owner vel non, and defendant may prove ownership in himself or anyone else, to sustain his traverse.³

§ 511. How Conversion Alleged: Since "conversion" is an ultimate fact it should be so alleged,¹ and the facts constituting conversion are therefore evidential and should be stricken out.2 

Pleading such facts is the same fault as argumentative denial, which Professor Pomeroy condemns so vigorously, i.e., alleging facts from which the ultimate fact may be inferred, yet it is a common fault and sometimes is even added to a proper allegation of the ultimate fact. The complaint, then, should allege simply that "the defendant converted the (watch) of plaintiff to his own use,' "' and the answer should deny that the defendant converted the (watch), whereupon evidence for and against the fact of conversion will be relevant," and the addition of argumentative matter adds nothing. This accords with the familiar rule that the plaintiff must rely on the strength of his own title and not on the weakness of defendant's."

§ 516. In General: The action for compensation for damages caused by negligence was a familiar one at common law and is more so in code practice. The form of action under the old system or trespass on the case, that form of action sired by the Act of Westminster II and brought forth by the clerks of chancery, which was finally developed into a form of action which included all sorts of causes ex delicto not embraced within the definitions of other forms. The action now is, of course, based on the same material, ultimate facts as formerly, and there is no occasion for any difference in the statement of them, yet the tendency of the nisi prius courts has been to tolerate, and, indeed, sometimes to compel the allegation of evidence and even details of evidence in this more than in any other sort of action¹; we have, however, no decision of our Supreme Court which expressly upholds such a manner of pleading, but, as is shown elsewhere, many which condemn it.2

The typical case of this sort is the so-called personal injury case, of which the most common are automobile collisions, injuries by electricity and railroad accidents. Others are for negligence of physicians, surgeons, attorneys, elevator operators, etc., including damage to property. The list is never complete.³ 

¹A notable case of an intolerable amount of evidential matter is 

Boltz v. Bonner, 95 C. 850, 35 P. (2d) 1015. The faulty complaint led, almost forced, the defendant to commit the same fault with the result that the issues were lost, thus the evidential matter, sometimes said to be necessary to inform the opponent, confused his information. 

2Damage caused by neglect of ditches is an example. But that caused by the breaking of a reservoir is actionable by statute without negli-

There is no gence. Garnet v. Sampson, 48 C. 285, 286, 110 P. 79. excuse but Act of God or the public enemy. Id., 304-5.

In most cases the plaintiff cannot know the exact nature of the negligence. 1 § 517. At Common Law: In the case of a collision, either trespass or case would lie at common law; trespass, because the damage was caused by direct force, and case, because want of due care was its origin. The code pleaders have forgotten trespass and invariably pursue the mental conception of case; rightly, because the defendant's real fault, the basic cause, is defendant's want of due care, and the force is but an incident. 

1Claflin v. Wilcox, 18 Vt. 605. This illustrates the indefiniteness of the categories of legal liability called forms of action.

390, 402-3, 115 P. 901; so in Elkton Co. v. Sullivan, 41 C. 241, 250, 92 P. 679, no general allegation of negligence appears. Inconsistently, incompetence of foreman cannot be shown under a general allegation of negligence, Greeley v. Foster, 32 C. 292, 75 P. 351, and, inconsistently with itself, this case seems to hold that a denial of negligence is a complete defense.

The defendant negligently and carelessly stayed on the left side of the road until it was impossible for him to turn out soon enough to give plaintiff his right of way, is a good statement of negligence. 

Martin v. Carruthers, 69 C. 464, 195 P. 105.

Negligence of a carrier by automobile in using a bus in bad repair was stated with great and apparently unnecessary elaboration, in Seeing 

Denver Co. v. Morgan, 66 C. 565, 185 P. 339. They were held sufficient against a motion to make more specific and certain.

That defendant negligently permitted seepage to escape without reasonable or proper effort to prevent it is a sufficient allegation of negligence, North Sterling District v. Dickman, 66 C. 8, 10, 178 P. 559.

An allegation of negligence in general terms is sufficient against a general demurrer and a demurrer for ambiguity and uncertainty, Fox v. 

D. C. Tr. Co., 57 C. 511, 143 P. 278. Consistently, D. Tram. Co. v. 

Cowan, 51 C. 64, 70, 77, 116 P. 136, declares that the issue there was negligence or not. Yet Stratton's Ind. v. Starett, 51 C. 17, 25, 117 

P. 351, seems to say the contrary. 

Under an allegation of failure to sound the warning gong, plaintiff may prove an ordinance which requires it without alleging the ordinance. 

D. C. Tr. Co. v. Martin, 44 C. 324, 330, 98 P. 836. 

In Tunnel Mfg. Co. v. Cooper, 50 C. 390, 402-3, 115 P. 901, appears a complaint with no general charge of negligence. In Elliot v. Field, 21 C. 378, 41 P. 504, a motion to make more specific and certain was overruled, and the opinion proceeds on the idea that there remained a complaint good against a general demurrer.

Under an allegation of failure to examine gas pipes for obstructions, plaintiff was allowed to show failure to examine for leaks. United Oil 

Co. v. Roseberry, 30 C. 177, 69 P. 588.

Where an injury was caused by the explosion of a car of dynamite it was not necessary to allege what caused the explosion, Wilson v. 

C. & S. R. Co., 57 C. 303, 318, 142 P. 174. (Because the contents of the car was a nuisance?)

It is enough to specify many acts of negligence and to allege that the injury was caused by some one or more of them. Williams v. Delta 

Pool, 89 C. 586, 590, 5 P.(2d) 583. Does not the court here in reality ignore the specifications? 

A passenger for hire need only prove that his car overturned, he need prove the particulars of the negligence even though he has alleged

them. Rio G. W'n Co. v. Rubenstein, 5 C. A. 121, 123, 38 P. 76. It must follow that he need allege no more.

An action for damages for insults by a conductor was regarded as ex contractu. Bleecker v. Colo. & S. Co., 50 C. 140, 114 P. 481.

These propositions appear with more or less clearness in other cases. 

The following summary is ventured: 

1. Any negligence may be proved under a general allegation of negligence. 

2. Without a general allegation only the specified negligence may proved. 

3. If both general and special are alleged either or both may be proved. § 519. Further Cases: It is held that in an action against a railroad company for killing stock, the complaint must allege the defendant's negligence though the death is primary proof thereof.¹

§ 522. Electricity: Negligence of those who furnish electric current has become a rather frequent cause of action. The electric companies are held to very strict accountability, it would seem almost to a liability under a constant rule of res ipsa loquitur.¹ So an allegation that defendant permitted its wire to touch the branch of a tree and so fall and remain on the ground. So of unnecessarily leaving a wire too low³; in which case the necessity of leaving it too low is a matter of confession and avoidance.

The substance of a complaint for using uninsulated wires is stated and held sufficient.* In an action for negligent installation, the complaint is set out in full and held sufficient against the company which installed the lights. Proof of negligence in location of electric wires is held not competent under an allegation of negligence in installation." 

¹Denver Elec. Co. v. Lawrence, 81 C. 301, 308-9-10, 73 P. 39. This case holds, in effect, that an allegation that one in the ordinary use of an electric light receives a shock which causes a serious damage is sufficient to constitute a cause of action against the light company,

i.e., it is negligence to furnish a current strong enough to do the harm. 

Compare, Denver Tramway Co. v. Reed, 4 C. A. 500, 36 P. 557. Contributory negligence by the choice of the unsafe way has appeared in several cases in Colorado, but no where has the method of pleading it been determined.

§ 529. Assumption of Risk: This is a defense in an action by a servant for the master's negligence. The servant is said to assume the risk of a danger incident to the work and known by him. Logically it seems to be equivalent to contributory negligence or a species thereof. This defense usually appears in actions for injuries by reason of an unsafe place to work. 

It is logically in confession and avoidance, and it is often so pleaded, but it has been held that, though not pleaded, if the assumption is shown by plaintiff's evidence he cannot recover.³

It is also held that if the complaint shows that plaintiff assumed the risk he must lose.*

The servant incurs the danger. If he knows it he is negligent, if not, he does not assume the risk. Pleading assumption of risk, then, ought to follow the rules in respect to contributory negligence, and be in confession and avoidance. See Confession and Avoidance and the opinion in D. & F. N. R. Co. v. Smock, 23 C. 456, 459, 48 P. 681, in re pleading plaintiff's knowledge of defect.

§ 530. At Common Law: The old action for false represen tations was case, or, waiving the tort, assumpsit, on the theory that the representation was a promise. Under the code, however, the mental conception of the action is case, that the deceit is a tort and the action ex delicto; yet there can be no sound reason why assumpsit may not still be used, and it might be advisable in Colorado in some cases, e.g., when evidence of defendant's knowledge of falsity is wanting or doubtful.2 3 

But the tort must be distinguished from breach of contract and an action for breach of covenant of title is not an action for deceit. In at least one case, a count for deceit is joined with one on contract. The plaintiff may rescind or sue for damages or both,5 and in some cases he may choose to recover for money had and received.Ⓡ Whether

Essentials: A form for a complaint in this sort of action is Estees Pl. & Pr., 4th Ed., Section 2772. It is for procuring property by fraud, but the frame is appropriate in any case of obtaining anything by deceit. The substance of such a complaint is: 1. That the defendant for the purpose of inducing plaintiff to sell him goods represented to plaintiff that he was solvent, etc. 2. That plaintiff was thereby induced to sell, etc. 3. That said representations were false (negative each categorically) which defendant then and there knew. 

4. That defendant has not paid for said goods.

It is hard to see that this does not state a cause of action, but we shall see that under the Colorado decisions the question of its sufficiency cannot be answered inconsiderately. We shall find it convenient at first to ignore the allegations of certainty, time, place, etc., because, in considering substance, they are usually immaterial and so confuse thought. 

§ 532. Essentials, continued: We venture the proposition that under the Colorado decisions the complaint for deceit may be analyzed thus¹: 

1. The defendant-for the purpose of inducing-(plaintiff to do something). 

2. Represented to plaintiff (something material to his purpose). 

3. Plaintiff believes and relied upon said representation. 

4. And was thereby induced (to do and did what defendant desired). ༦༤ 5. The representations were false (negative them categorically). 6. 

Defendant knew they were false when made.2 

7. That plaintiff has thereby suffered damages (facts according to legal measure of damages). 

8. Demand of judgment.¹

We will take up these allegations separately in the above order.

§ 546. Defenses: The only practical defense to this action. 

is denial. A general denial will permit almost any evidence that can support a defense, except pleas of discharge, like release and accord and satisfaction. 

It is no defense that plaintiff did not inquire. He is not bound to inquire.¹ If defendant relies upon the fact that he had reasonable ground to believe and did believe his representations were true, he must plead it, and deceit as a defense must be pleaded."

Fraud and wilful deceit are grounds for execution against the body. The action must, of course, be in tort."

§ 547. Form: Whatever form of complaint is proper or sufficient elsewhere, it seems clear from the foregoing that an intelligent use of the analysis above in this chapter will enable any one here to draw an unassailable complaint for deceit. The rules of certainty should of course be followed, time, place, value, etc., but all else is unnecessary, and, on motion, will be stricken out. § 548. Nature of the Action: As the name given by the code declares, the action commonly called ejectment, is an action for the possession of real property. An action in which the complaint alleges right of possession in plaintiff with entry and ouster by defendant and a prayer for possession and damages is ejectment.¹

The action is used to oust defendants who have taken possession by flooding plaintiff's land for a reservoir.2 One out of possession may have an equitable trust declared in his favor.3 

Where the action from the record seemed "to be one in ejectment" amendment was ordered on reversal to frame the pleadings accordingly.¹

One with a legal title who is not in possession must bring ejectment and not a suit to quiet title but one may join an equity suit to cancel deeds for fraud with an action to recover possession of the property they purport to convey,5 yet ejectment and partition cannot be joined. Ejectment is suggested as a substitute for an action to quiet title for a tax-title holder." 

An action is called an action "in the nature of" ejectment.

561. Practice. § 558. Origin and Nature: Formerly, in England it was lawful for one lawfully entitled to the possession of land to take possession by force. The only risk he ran was that his title might be held bad by the courts.¹

This led to frequent breach of the peace and even bloodshed." 

Several statutes were enacted by parliament to remedy this evil which have been imitated in the United States with more or less variation in the various states. The original acts were criminal and provided punishment for forcible entry. The later ones provide (sometimes additionally) a summary civil remedy, under certain conditions, for the person rightfully entitled to possession against one who unlawfully detains the land in question, and this has almost entirely done away with the cases which involve force. This remedy is known as forcible entry and detainer or unlawful detainer. 

126 C. J. 802 (§ 4). 

2See The Paston Letters (London about 1912). The Duke (or Earl) 

of Norfolk claimed title to a manor of Sir John Paston and attacked the castle with artillery and three thousand men, some of whom were killed by the defenders. Sir John was indicted for murder and only escaped by favor of the king (Edw. IV) who was his personal friend. 

This attack was in spite of the statutes of 5 and 15, Rich. II, but before that of Henry VI. There were several such incidents in the history of the Pastons. About 1449, Margaret Paston writes from 

Norwich to her husband in London to bring cross-bows and quarrels (points for cross-bow bolts) because their rooms are so low that they cannot shoot through their windows with their long bows.

This was to defend against forcible entry. 

3Rudolph v. Thompson, 66 C. 98, 179 P. 151, and cases there cited.

Some states have both the civil and criminal remedies.

Miscellaneous Cases. 

1 § 562. In Code Practice: There is no such thing under the code as replevin as it was understood at comman law. That system had two forms of action to recover possession of personal property, detinue and replevin, the basic difference between which was that in detinue the plaintiff awaited judgment in his favor before taking possession of the chattels in question while in replevin he took possession upon the commencement of the action and returned it if defeated. The code abolished these forms of action with all others, but, of course left substantive right in every one to the possession of his own and a civil action to obtain it, which action amounts to detinue. The necessity, however, of immediate possession by plaintiff to prevent, at times, great injustice, caused the inclusion in the code of the Chapter V, which provides a remedy, auxiliary to an action for possession, by which, upon giving a bond and showing certain facts, the plaintiff at any time. before judgment may obtain immediate possession of the property in dispute, being bound by his bond to return it or its value if defeated. This turns the action into the substance of the old replevin and although the code calls this auxiliary proceeding "claim and delivery," the compilers of the code and lawyers and courts call it and the action which it aids "replevin."" Sometimes, too, they call them claim and

§ 563. Complaint: The action for possession lies wherever the plaintiff at its commencement¹ is entitled to possession on whatsoever ground. The distinctions of the common law between detinue and replevin have been abolished and the complaint alleges the ultimate facts, whatever they may be, usually ownership, which entitle him to possession, and those that entitle him to such judgment against the defendant, usually detention and refusal to deliver. Sometimes taking is alleged. Then or at any time before judgment he may proceed under the chapter on claim and delivery2 which turns into the equivalent of replevin what was the equivalent of detinue. 

The sufficient ultimate facts are that defendant has possession of (an automobile) of the plaintiff and has refused and refuses to deliver it to the plaintiff. It is said that the usual form of complaint in replevin is "ownership and right of possession in plaintiff and taking and detention by defendant"; but taking is unnecessary. It is said that ownership, right of possession and unjust detention after demand are enough. If, however, there was a taking by defendant at a time when plaintiff was entitled to possession no demand upon the defendant is necessary to create a cause of action."

§ 569. Answer: The defenses comprehend everything which nullifies plaintiff's right of possession. § 572. Complaint: We know of no case in the higher courts of Colorado which touch upon pleading in an action for slander alone,' but there are several cases of libel in the reports. The substance of a declaration for libel is the publication in writing or printing of a false defamatory statement with inducement and innuendo, and with special damage unless the statement is libelous per se, e.g., a charge of a felony, of a loathsome disease, or in relation to plaintiff's occupation or business,² or which will subject him to odium.³

§ 579. Defenses, continued: The traverse of the publication rarely appears because that allegation is almost invariably true and easily proved. The common defenses are privilege and mitigation of damages, less often the truth of the charge.¹ 

That the charge was common report is a good plea in mitigation of damages, but not a complete defense. So of the plea of lack of malice and ignorance of the falsity, but that facts which mitigate must be pleaded. A mere denial of malice is no defense when the charge is libelous per se,5 and it does not constitute a good plea in mitigation of damages. 3 

¹In Republican Co. v. Conroy, 5 C. A. 262, 38 P. 423, the defendant pleaded truth, privilege and, in mitigation, good faith. Such pleas are proper, Meeker v. Post Co., 55 C. 355, 358, 135 P. 457. Code, § 75.

§ 580. Defense of Privilege: What constitutes privilege must be learned from the law of torts. Privilege is absolute or qualified.¹ Absolute privilege is immunity from liability for defamation, and none but public officers acting in discharge of their duty are protected by it. Qualified privilege is any privilege that is not absolute. In respect to pleading it is enough to say that the communication must be a privileged one, on a privileged occasion, by a privileged person, to one within the privilege.2

Qualified privilege is a defense in confession and avoidance, but if the facts to establish it appear in the complaint a demurrer will lie, and actual malice will destroy the privilege.* 

136 C. J. 1289, 1240. 

236 C. J. 1289. "Morley v. Post, 84 C. 41, 48, 268 P. 540; Radovich v. Douglas, 84 C. 

149, 268 P. 575. The qualified privilege here evidently was report to an employer concerning the character of his employee. By her statutory denial of the employment of plaintiff defendant was held to have destroyed her claim of privilege, since to maintain it she must have intended in good faith to give an employer information.

§ 581. Nature of the Action: These actions, nominally ejectment, are anomalous. The peculiarity is that plaintiff and defendant are both, in effect, plaintiffs, because either, to entitle himself to a judgment, must allege and prove a right of possession good as against the United States, so defendant cannot rely on the weakness of plaintiff's title, as in ordinary ejectment, and it is possible that neither will be entitled to a judgment.¹ A mere denial of plaintiff's allegations will give defendant no standing.2

It is held that it is unnecessary in a complaint in support of an adverse claim, to allege that the adverse claim was filed within the sixty days of publication prescribed by statute nor that action was begun within thirty days thereafter.3

§ 584. Fraud: There are actions, although they are comparatively rare, other than for deceit, which are based on fraud.

Deceit is a fraud whereby the plaintiff is deceived and so led to act to his harm, but he may be harmed by other frauds not involving deception. Of this class are actions for conspiracy to defraud.¹ Direct allegations of conspiracy are not necessary if the complaint shows the facts which constitute it.² 

There is no limit to the variety and complexity of such cases. 

They are usually in equity.

§ 590. In General: It will be convenient to treat of actions on specialties and on simple contracts under the heads "covenant" and "assumpsit" as at common law, but first we will speak generally of actions on contracts. 

The material allegations in a complaint on a contract are: 

1, the contract; 2, the breach; 3, the effect of the breach.¹

To allege the contract it is, of course, necessary to show a valid contract, one that the law will enforce, so, for example, it must appear that there was a seal, or else a consideration.2 

The breach must be shown to be a violation of some duty imposed by the contract, and that violation must appear to be such as to injure the plaintiff. 3 Let us take, then, the simplest possible case. The defendant 

B has ordered a watch of A, a jeweler, at the agreed price of $100.00 and the watch has been delivered. The following complaint would stand against a general demurrer : "The plaintiff alleges that he sold and delivered to defendant a watch and in consideration thereof defendant promised to pay the plaintiff $100.00 but has not paid the same nor any part thereof." 

¹In Peo. v. Parker, 54 C. 604, 132 P. 56, the substance of a complaint on an administrator's bond is set out, but it seems far from concise. 

2Schwalbe v. Postle, 73 C. 181, 214 P. 388. 

3 Standard Ins. Co. v. Friedenthal, 1 C. A. 5, 10, 27 P. 88. 

§ 591. Contract, How Alleged: As at common law the contract must be set out in hæc verba or according to its legal effect. The latter method is usually the better and is always so when the contract is long and but a small part relevant, but where the construction of a written contract is doubtful it is well to set it out in full and so get an adjudged construction on demurrer rather than on motion for nonsuit for variance. The term "legal effect" is sometimes used inaccurately.2

3 A complaint which states facts which constitute a contract and further facts which destroy it is insufficient. A statement of a contract in hæc verba controls an inconsistent statement of its legal effect.* An inducement is often necessary. It is an allegation of facts leading up to and explanatory of the principal statements, e.g., that plaintiff or defendant is a corporation, organized, etc., or that defendants are partners under the firm name and style, etc., or that "the plaintiff and defendant were engaged" in some joint enterprise. Then should follow the ultimate facts which show the contract, i.e., the plaintiff's primary right. 

The complaint should allege that for a consideration (stating it) the defendant promised, or that under his seal he agreed."

The statement of a contract is sometimes a proper inducement to an action for fraud,' and sometimes such inducement is sufficient to state a cause of action by itself. So occasionally we have facts which constitute a cause of action in tort as inducement (or surplusage) in a complaint on a contract. An inducement merely explanatory is not traversable.10

§ 593. Performance: Following the facts which constitute the contract should come the averments of performance by plaintiff of whatever the contract requires him to perform,¹ and the fulfillment of whatever conditions are contained in it.² So a complaint on an express promise to pay for services must allege the performance of the services.³

The allegation of performance at common law was a somewhat technical matter, but under the code it may be stated in general terms. On an allegation of performance plaintiff may not prove an excuse for non-performance," or that defendant prevented full performance. In case defendant has prevented full performance plaintiff may sue for damages or on quantum meruit for what he has done."

Section 72 seems not to refer to conditions not under the control of the plaintiff, e.g., when the defendant has surplus funds. The safe way is to aver the fulfillment of such a condition specifically. The defendant in alleging an unfulfilled condition need not negative an execption thereto; that is a matter for the plaintiff to allege in his reply.

§ 599. At Common Law: The common law form of action for damages on a sealed instrument was covenant and the form of the declaration was exceedingly simple and well established,¹ and there is no reason why it would not stand as a complaint, yet more often than not a complaint on a sealed instrument is drawn in analogy to assumpsit. The custom, however, of using seals upon various instruments such as attachment, replevin or injunction bonds has largely been abandoned and they are often drawn without a seal. This perhaps accounts in part for the disuse of the older form of statement. 2 This form of complaint is appropriate, as at common law, to enforce liabilities on all sealed instruments including those of sureties on bonds of officials and of all fiduciaries.³ It is held that a previous judgment against the principal is not necessary and that he is not a necessary party.¹ 

Covenant is the right action on all covenants of title and against incumbrances."

In an action on an injunction bond, items of damage were alleged to be "on account of the existence" of the injunction which was held to be enough to show that they were caused by it. On such a bond the principal and surety may be joined as defendants. Indemnity bonds of various kinds are subjects of actions.8

§ 600. Covenant Compared With Assumpsit: Since by our present laws a contract of any sort may be made either with or without a seal the only difference between the two is that with a seal the complaint should allege that the defendant, by his deed, sealed with his seal, covenanted and agreed, etc., while without a seal it should allege that the defendant in consideration of........ .......etc., promised, or undertook and promised.¹

As in assumpsit it is necessary to allege only those covenants contained in the deed which are relevant to the cause in hand.² 

In an action for royalties on a lease for quarrying clay it was held that though the lease was sealed by but one defendant the complaint was good because the objection was not made in time, but it was also said that the action was not on the covenant. ¹See any common law form book. Estees and Boone are satisfied with merely using the term "covenanted" or "deed." See their form books, especially 1 Estees, §§ 986, 1265. 

2Sanford v. Halsey, 2 Denio, 235, e.g., in an action for breach of the ordinary covenants of title by failure of title, only the covenant of seizin need be alleged. Of course, the breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment and of the warranty may also be added if relevant, which they generally are. 

3Schaffer v. Loveland, 67 C. 454, 186 P. 532. 

§ 601. Analysis: The action may be analyzed thus: 

1. Inducement. Usually unnecessary. 

2. That defendant by deed sealed with his seal covenanted and agreed to...... 

3. Averment of performance. 

4. Breach. 

5. Damages. 

§ 602. Defenses: The defenses in covenant do not differ from those in assumpsit except the defense "not the seal of defendant," equivalent, perhaps, to "non est factum" of the common law. There are, however, some differences from the common law practice; for example, where the breach of a covenant of seizin was assigned as "not well seized" and the defense was a general denial it was held that the burden was held to be on the plaintiff to show that the defendant was not well seized.2 

1This would, in all ordinary cases be covered by the general denial, in other cases by a denial of the execution of the instrument in suit. 

2Landt v. Major, 2 C. A. 551, 31 P. 524. This seems to put the burden on the negative and is contrary to the common law, but the opinion is well reasoned and follows the supreme court of Michigan.

§ 603. In General: General and specific technical terms are so necessary that they cannot be disused, and so the terms "assumpsit," "general assumpsit" and "special assumpsit, although the form of action, assumpsit, has been abolished, are still much in use, because there are no short paraphrases that will supply their denotations. The terms denote, in substance, just what they did at common law. Assumpsit is an action upon promise, express or implied, made upon a sufficient consideration. Special assumpsit, (not, at common law, a distinct form of action) is an action upon an express promises or a promise to do something other than to pay money, general assumpsit is on the implied promise to pay for an executed consideration. The same facts, even expressed in the same words as in common law pleading will, under the code, produce the same results.5 A great plurality of actions is assumpsit and a great majority of them is general assumpsit.

A plaintiff often has his choice of assumpsit or an action for conversion. This occurs whenever the evidential facts will prove both. If a trustee converts trust funds to his own use it is a tort, but he may be sued on his implied (or express) contract faithfully to administer."

Special and general assumpsit are often joined and the plaintiff is sometimes required to elect on which he will rely.?

§ 607. Special Assumpsit, Answer: What has been said of the answer is for consideration here.¹ The denial of any of the six requisites of the complaint will be a good defense.2 This is held in the case of the damage, but in the case of performance where the code permits a general allegation in the complaint the cases are in conflict. It is held that a denial of the allegation required by Section 72 of the code is insufficient,5 yet it is hard to see how anything the defendant might say could be anything more than an argumentative denial of performance. It could not be confession and avoidance because it lacks confession. On the contrary it is alleged to controvert the allegation of performance. The clause "if such allegations be controverted" evidently refers to denial and the requirement that "the party pleading shall establish on the trial the facts showing such performance" looks to the issue performance vel non. It is plain that David v. Gilbert is logically right.

§ 610. General Assumpsit: The varieties of this species of assumpsit are many. Wherever there is an executed consideration which has been requested or accepted by the defendant the action is appropriate, e.g., for goods sold and delivered, goods bargained and sold, work and labor, professional services, money lent, money had and received, money laid out and expended, rent, etc., etc.,

The action for the reasonable value of goods sold, where no price was agreed on, was called quantum valebant and for work and labor or other sources quantum meruit.¹ These actions are the usual ones by plaintiff merchants against delinquent customers, by workmen for wages, and by physicians, lawyers and other professional men to recover their fees, etc., etc. Under the code the same facts alleged in the same words as at common law produce the same judgment. It is held that the value of the services must be alleged. It is of course true that if there is a subsisting express contract there can be no quantum meruit and there can be no recovery on quantum meruit where an express contract is pleaded and proved,* nor on a count for an agreed amount." An attorney cannot recover fees even on an express contract unless they are reasonable. 

A judgment for defendant on an express contract is not res adjudicata on a later quantum meruit."

§ 612. General Assumpsit, Money Had and Received: The action for money had and received at common law, covered a wide diversity of cases, in some of the states any case where one had money which in equity and good conscience belonged to another. The decisions under the code recognize this.¹ The typical case is money received by plaintiff's agent. The extreme case is where the taker (even a thief) sells the stolen property and receives money therefore. The owner may waive the trespass, sue in assumpsit for the money and the law will imply a promise by defendant to pay it to him. The implication is a matter of substantive law and the code does not vary it, but in view of Wilcox v. Jamieson, 20 C. 158, 36 P. 902, and the like cases it becomes a question, what are the "ultimate facts," the "material allegations" in such a case. Doubtless the allegations in the common law form for money had and

received would be sufficient.³ The real issue in such case is usually title in plaintiff vel non. Is the money the plaintiff's or not.

It is held that indebitatus assumpsit will lie for money paid on duress of goods, and that it is for money had and received.* 

A complaint which amounted to this sort of action alleged that a bank which had collected certain items had not paid over the money. The proof was that it had put the items in the hands of another who had embezzled the collections. It was held that the proof was of a cause ex contractu. Another was an action to recover money paid for a license under a void ordinance."

§ 615. General Assumpsit, Money Lent: The indebitatus form is sufficient here, or of course, the fact of lending at defendant's request alleged in any manner. An allegation, with time and place, that plaintiff lent defendant at his request

73 1 ($100) and that defendant has not paid it, states a cause of action and the allegation of the implied promise is unnecessary. It is not necessary, in such a case to allege the maturity since the law implies that the loan is payable on demand,¹ nor to allege that it is payable on demand because that is the implication of law.¹

§ 626. How Alleged: In case of an action against a defend ant upon a contract made through his agent there is some apparent confusion with reference to what the complaint should say about the agency, but if the cases are carefully read the confusion mostly disappears. 

The proper way to declare upon such a contract is to allege that the defendant made or entered into it, and, upon trial prove the agency and the contract by the agent. That the defendant made the contract, e.g., bought the goods, is the ultimate fact and the agency is part of the evidence to prove it.³ 

It was held that it was sufficient to allege that the goods were sold and delivered to the principal, which was clearly right; but the opinion goes on to say that the better way is to allege all the facts, which cannot be true if Lynch v. Smith is. Of course, the ultimate fact only should be alleged, anything more should be struck out. This becomes clear if we assume that, in the watch case stated above, the plaintiff's salesman sold the watch to the defendant and a messenger delivered it to his housemaid. The allegation would be that the plaintiff sold and delivered to defendant. No one would for a moment think otherwise.5 Ratification, on the above principles, is evidential and not ultimate fact. It is apparently held that on a plea of infancy by defendant, plaintiff may reply ratification."

§ 630. In General: It will be helpful to say something of some specific causes on contract and their treatment by the Colorado Courts, although they are nearly all controlled by the rules in respect to special and general assumpsit and covenant. These refer to actions at law. Equitable actions based on contracts are treated in another chapter. 

§ 631. Bonds: The pleadings with reference to the various bonds upon conditions are not substantially different from one another. The material obligations are the obligation with the substance of the condition and the breach and such facts as show the relation of the plaintiff to the transaction.¹ Upon a bond payable to the people the action is properly in the name of the people, and on a constable's bond must be so. Some cases show the substance of complaints on bonds with more or less detail. The ordinary action at common law was debt, but it was regulated by several statutes. Covenant was a concurrent remedy and for unliquidated damages the sole one.

The question is occasionally raised whether a surety can be joined with his principal in an action for a breach of the condition. The answer depends on the construction of the condition and upon the statutes with reference to the matter."

§ 632. Bonds, Redelivery: In an action on a redelivery bond in attachment the complaint must allege a demand for delivery from the attachment defendant'; an allegation of a demand upon the sureties is not enough.¹ The complaint must also allege that plaintiff had judgment and that the attachment was not dissolved, or some equivalent statement."

In an action on a replevin bond the complaint must allege not only that the plaintiff has not delivered the goods but also that he has not paid their value.
