§ 634. Bonds, Fidelity: The following allegations were held sufficient in an action on a fidelity bond.

The execution and delivery of the bond by the surety to the beneficiary, the payment of the premium to the surety, the pecuniary loss to the beneficiary by the wrongful acts of the employee, the amount of the loss, the facts constituting the waiver of notice of loss and proof of loss and performance by plaintiff.¹ 

¹American Surety Co. v. Morris, 78 C. 504, 506, 242 P. 983. 

It is, of course, understood that the relevant terms of the bond, or the instrument in full should be set out. 

§ 635. Insurance Policies, Necessary Allegations: The gen eral rules with respect to actions on insurance policies do not differ from those concerning actions on other contracts. If the policy is under seal what we have said as to covenants is relevant here, and if unsealed, what is said about assumpsit will be pertinent. It is true, however, that some situations and questions arise in these actions which deserve especial attention.

In one case the complaint upon a fire insurance policy is set out in full,¹ and with proper adaptations to meet variations of fact would doubtless serve for a form of complaint on any fire loss or, indeed, upon any contract of insurance. In another case the substance of a complaint and answer on a life policy is stated, which, with the above form, is a good guide to a complaint on such a policy.2

It is said that the substance of a complaint is the contract of insurance, the fulfillment of the condition of liability and the amount of the indemnity to which plaintiff is entitled,³ and in an action on an assessment policy it is not necessary to allege the number of members, but only the terms of the policy and performance by the insured.*

1German Ins. Co. v. Hayden, 21 C. 127, 40 P. 453. The allegation that "said sum is now due" should be omitted. The answer is also set out in full and is a sound one but needlessly verbose. A complaint is discussed in Clarke v. Assurance Soc., 96 C. 134, 39 P.(2d) 785. 

2Knights of Security v. 'Considine, 61 C. 474, 158 P. 282. In this and in German Ins. Co. v. Hayden, the real defenses are based on warranties. 

United Workmen v. Taylor, 44 C. 373, 375, 99 P. 570. Properly understood this is correct and clear but it must always be considered that in alleging the contract of insurance, all the requisites of assumpsit or covenant must be recognized. 

4 Mutual Aid Ass'n v. Colmar, 7 C. A. 275, 282, 43 P. 159. 

§ 636. Insurance Policies, Necessary Allegations, continued: 

It not seldom happens that a proof of full performance is impossible and that there is some excuse, for example, waiver, for failure to perform the remainder, and the plaintiff then alleges performance with the exception and the excuse.¹ 

Waiver cannot be proved under an allegation of performance.2 

Where both the insured and pledgee of the policy were dead and the widow of the insured brought suit alleging that the debt had been paid, it was held that the complaint need not state that it was paid before the death of the insured, or that the proofs of death were furnished by plaintiff rather than by the pledgee. Often we have case of an attempt to show a reinstatement of a forfeited policy. In one case one insurance company sued another on the promise to reinsure $2,000.00 of a $5,000.00 policy. A demurrer to the complaint was sustained for non-compliance with C. L. Sec. 2535.5 

¹Helvetia Ins. Co. v. Allis Co., 11 C. A. 264, 267, 53 P. 242. The complaint alleged performance except proof of loss and that the insurance company had waived that. The complaint stated the "facts of waiver" but we do not know what they were except from the evidence as it appears in the opinion. They consisted of the conduct of the company's general agent in negotiating with the owner concerning the loss. 

2Barclay v. London Co., 46 C. 558, 568, 105 P. 865. 

3Order of Pyramids v. Dixon, 45 C. 95, 99, 100 P. 427. The allegation that the debt had been paid seems to anticipate the defense that the policy had been pledged. 

An example is Brun v. Sup. Council, 15 C. A. 538, 63 P. 796. The facts to justify the reinstatement were held insufficient. 

5United Am. Ins. Co. v. Union Fire Ins. Co., 82 C. 72, 257 P. 246. 

§ 637. Insurance Policies, Defenses: A common defense is false warranty or false statements in the application.¹ An answer stating that the insured had warranted that Lou Lampken, the beneficiary and plaintiff, was his wife, that she was not, that one Carrie Lampkin was and that he was living with the plaintiff in adultery, that he knew said statement was false when he made it, that these facts were material to

3 the defendant, and that defendant would not have issued the policy if it had known the truth. This answer is held good both as a plea upon a warranty and upon a false representation. In another case the plea was one of misrepresentation as to health, that the insured had paretic dementia and knew it. The court held that the only question under the pleadings was whether he knew it.

The method of pleading misrepresentation in the application is not governed by the lex loci contractu but by lex fori and so the law of Iowa that to permit such a plea, the application must be attached to the policy, has no force here.¹

§ 648. Broker's Commissions: Actions by brokers for services in various transactions, especially in making sales of real estate, have been common in Colorado. Like other transactions in contract the typical case is simple and easily understood; the broker is employed and does what he is employed to do. Usually the employment is to procure a purchaser.¹

The broker usually tells his attorney that the owner "listed the property" with him for sale, or "gave it" to him for sale, or "put it" in his hands for sale or some such indefinite expression of his contract with his employer. The attorney must interpret this into an employment to procure a purchaser "ready and willing and able" to buy at the employer's price and terms. If the broker has done that he has earned a commission.

The common law form of action was general assumpsit for work, labor and services.2 The same is doubtless sufficient under the code." 

¹Sometimes the employment is by a purchaser, Ziegler v. Corbin, 65 

C. 138, 173 P. 945. The complaint is set out clearly in full and the substance of the answer and the replication stated. 

22 Chit. Pl., 37, 78. Any other form of assumpsit might be used but no costs for excess in length could be recovered. Rule Trin. T. 1 W. 4; 

1 Arch. N. P. 135-6.

Yet it has been held at nisi prius that the name of the purchaser must be alleged. 

§ 649. Broker's Commissions, continued: Sometimes the contract is more definite, e.g., the amount of the commission is fixed, in which case, of course, a quantum meruit cannot be adjudged¹; and occasionally, indeed often, the sale is made on terms arranged by the parties and not on those originally stated to the brokers by the seller, in which case the broker who has procured the purchaser is still entitled to his commission. After payment under the contract of sale is due, "ready, willing and able" to purchase is irrelevant. In such case the complaint must allege payment or tender according to the contract. A count on an express contract and one for a quantum were joined. The allegation that the broker's customer bought is equivalent to an allegation that he was ready, willing and able.* 3 3 

¹Hallack v. Hinckley, 19 C. 38, 34 P. 479, states the pleading, in substance, in this sort of action, and in Okey v. Jones, 70 C. 152, 197 

P. 752. The substance of the complaint is set out. The employment is alleged to be "to procure a purchaser" and the alleged performance is that plaintiff "procured and produced" one L., who was ready, willing and able to purchase on "terms agreeable to" the defendant and that a contract of purchase was executed. 

2Okey v. Jones seems to be a case of this kind.

³Stelson v. Haigler, 63 C. 200, 203, 165 P. 265. If the contract of sale was an option this seems right, but if it was a binding enforceable contract of purchase and sale it seems wrong. 

4Fist v. Currie, 49 C. 284, 288, 112 P. 689. This is inconsistent with the proposition in Henry v. Montezuma Co., 55 C. 182, 185-6, 133 P. 747, that the fact of sale is evidential, which seems clearly right, because, if the plaintiff has procured a purchaser he is entitled to a commission even though there be no sale, and, if there be a sale he is not so entitled unless he has procured a purchaser, so a traverse of the sale would form no issue, since the decision of it would not determine the case. 

The same reasoning will control the question of readiness, etc. If the one procured be ready, the commission is due whether there be a sale or not, and if he is not ready, then commission is not earned, but if a sale, he was ready. The sale, then, is evidence of readiness. § 650. Broker's Commissions, continued: It is clear from what we have said that the complaint, if for quantum meruit, need state only the ordinary indebitatus count with the name of the purchaser, and if on an express contract must state the contract, whatever it is. It may be to procure a sale, or to procure a purchaser, but the difference is of little consequence, because if there was a sale there was a purchaser, and if there was a purchaser, procured by plaintiff, ready, willing and able, whether there was a sale is immaterial, so it is enough to say that plaintiff procured a purchaser (naming him) ready, etc., even though there was a sale; the sale then being a matter of evidence. So even if the employment was to sell or procure a sale the complaint may allege a sale or that the plaintiff procured a purchaser ready, etc., and that the defendant refused to sell to him. 1 'Henry v. Montezuma Co., 55 C. 182, 185-6, 133 P. 747. This should be taken into consideration in reading those cases, e.g., Wagner v.

If the employment was to procure a sale of course the complaint must allege that plaintiff procured the sale or allege general performance under code § 72; and so of any special employment, e.g., to obtain a loan. § 651. Warranty, Nature: It has been noted in the sections on the action for deceit that the plaintiff may waive the tort and sue on the promise. Both actions were called false warranty in ordinary parlance at common law. There is, however, another transaction which has actually no element of tort, that is where there is an agreement, apart from any assertion, that something is true. Examples are the ordinary covenant in a warranty deed that the premises are free from encumbrance, and the typical case of warranty of the soundness of a horse: "I guarantee (warrant or agree) he is sound."

These actions at common law were covenant and assumpsit but under the code they are classed together.

669. Subjects of Equity. 

§ 658. In General: We have noticed elsewhere that actions which would formerly have been in chancery and in which, therefore, the pleadings would have been according to the chancery practice, are, in code practice, governed by the same rules of pleading as are actions at law and that those rules are according to the theory and purpose of the common law system of pleading, to reach an issue, and not according to the chancery system, to disclose the evidential matter which controls the rights of the parties. It is not so easy, however, in a complicated equity case, always to determine exactly what is ultimate fact, because the old system, based on a different plan, is no guide in that respect. 

What we have said on the subject of code pleading in general is all relevant to equity actions, as well as those at law, but it may be of some use to mention some of the views of the Colorado courts on actions for equitable relief.

Equity, since the code as before it, will grant what relief is proper upon the facts, regardless of the prayer,¹ and, indeed, equitable rules and principles are the same now as then.' So one who seeks equity must do equity³ and to enjoin a tax deed one must pay or tender a just tax.¹

§ 659. Jurisdiction: There is no definition of an action called "equitable" (or in equity) under the code except to say that it is for equitable relief, and that means such relief as was given by chancery before the code. It was given only

where the law could not furnish a remedy or an adequate remedy for the plaintiff's trouble. So, in code practice, if one can have adequate justice by any action equivalent to any of the old common law forms of action he cannot obtain what is called "equitable" relief. It follows that the complaint in equity must allege facts which constitute a wrong that law will not remedy, but both chancery and the code have enlarged and modified these restrictions. This can be best made clear by illustration. The code² says that in all cases equitable relief may be granted and that is held by the Supreme Court, but the decisions are that the equitable facts must be alleged and proved. Consistently with this equitable relief is often sought in law suits, in addition to damages. It is said that a complaint which alleges ground for injunction but asks only damages is a bill in equity."

277 P. 781; Mosco v. Jeannot, 86 C. 441, 445, 282 P. 874. Compare

Carpenters, etc., 24 C. A. 438, 134 P. 1007. But why cannot plaintiff have such relief as the facts alleged and proved will justify? Pope v.

Relief: We have mentioned above that one may not have equitable relief where there is an adequate legal remedy. 

That proposition is unquestioned and clear, but some confusion of thought appears in the application of it. 

Difficulty arises in the determination of the consequences of a mistake of the pleader in this respect. 

1. A complaint alleges matters which justify damages but not the intent or purpose of the action or the prayer which are all for equitable relief; or 2. 

It seeks one equity while the allegations justify only another; or 

3. It seeks damages, replevin or ejectments when the allegations require equity.

§ 666. Tendering Equity: When a plaintiff asks equity of defendant, he must do equity and must tender it in his bill. 

The familiar example is rescission of a contract or cancellation of a deed obtained by fraud. The plaintiff alleges the fraud, usually false representations, with facts which show that the deed was thereby procured and then tenders or offers to pay into court for the defendant the consideration which he, the plaintiff, has received or whatever is necessary to put defendant in status quo¹; so a bill to cancel stock issued in payment of a debt of the corporation must offer to do equity with the holders of the debt.2 But a failure to allege a continuation of the tender of the status quo in an action for rescission will not warrant disturbing a judgment which orders the return of the status quo.3

§ 669. Subjects of Equity: Upon what subjects equity will act is rather a part of equity jurisprudence than pleading but we notice some of them briefly. The ordinary ones are relief from fraud, or mistake, administration of trusts, injunctions, accountings, mortgage and lien foreclosures, determination and enforcement of trusts, bills of interpleader, liquidation

of partnerships, creditors' bills and bills to quiet title. These classifications are descriptive, not definite. The classes are not mutually exclusive and there are auxiliary proceedings, such as the temporary injunctions and receivers.

§ 670. Necessary Allegations: The remedy for fraud and mistake is often equitable, and the allegations, if such relief is sought, must, of course, show equity. Mistake is usually treated with fraud because their consequences and remedies are similar. The plaintiff finds himself in the same difficulty whether he was led into it by the fraud of the defendant or by their mutual mistake. In either case the remedy in equity is the same,¹ usually restoration of the status quo. The mistake must be shown to be mutual and that it was the "mistake of both parties" is sufficient for that purpose.2 The substance of a complaint to reform a settlement because of an inadvertent credit of $1000.00, given by plaintiff on his account with defendant, is stated.s *It is never sufficient to allege fraud in general terms, and it cannot be proved unless properly alleged. A complaint which alleged a conspiracy between the president and attorney for a corporation to secure its business for themselves was held good, and the facts in an action to cancel a deed for fraud are set out fully and held sufficient."

682. Mechanics' Lien. 

§ 680. Nature of the Proceeding: Mortgage and lien foreclosure is a common proceeding and it is regarded as in equity because various kinds of relief other than judgment for possession or damages are necessary, and, historically, it is in equity, but a general demurrer will not stand to a complaint which shows a right to a judgment on a mortgage note even though no right of foreclosure is shown.¹

It is said that in the foreclosure of a mechanic's lien it is not enough to allege, as we ordinarily do, that certain defendants "have or claim some right," etc. but plaintiff must allege the particulars which give him his superior lien.2 The mortgage in Colorado is a mere lien, to be enforced only by foreclosure and sale.³

The allegations for foreclosure of a mortgage are the indebtedness, usually a promissory note, the mortgage, with its relevant conditions and terms, and a description of the property, the breach, usually failure to pay the note. The prayer is that the property be sold to pay the debt. It is seldom indeed, however, that the complaint is so simple; there is commonly failure to pay taxes and insurance, often charges of waste and other matters of great variety. 4. 

The parties defendant must include all who have or claim any interest in the property in question inferior to the mortgagee, and a receiver of the rents will often be appointed in case of waste or failure to pay taxes or insurance, if the security is narrow and the mortgagor insolvent, and the plaintiff may have an injunction against waste, or even before foreclosure may maintain an action for damages for waste." 

The holder of a tax title, however, is not a proper party to a suit to foreclose because his title is paramount but this objection is waived by answer. 'Murray v. Ready, 85 C. 544, 277 P. 298; C. M. A. C. § 297, C. L. '21,

§ 681. Enforcement of Liens: The substance of a complaint to enforce a lien is not different from the foreclosure of a mortgage. The duty, usually a debt, which the lien secures, must be shown, the facts which constitute the lien, and the breach of the duty. These facts are the skeleton of every complaint to enforce a lien, but contracts and statutes which create the lien are usually somewhat involved and the necessary allegations in a particular case cannot be determined by general rules.

It is said that a complaint to enforce an attorney's lien must state every fact "essential to the existence of the lien."" The substance of a complaint upon an agistor's lien is set out and held sufficient. It is held that one who claims a right of possession by reason of a pledge must plead it.³ 2 

¹Gooding v. Lyons, 63 C. 328, 332, 166 P. 564. Doubtless this means no more than the general rule with respect to all complaints. 

2Auld v. Travis, 5 C. A. 535, 540, 39 P. 357. The material allegations seem to be set out on page 540. 

3Benish v. Jones, 68 C. 484, 486, 190 P. 538. This seems inconsistent with the proposition that under an allegation of ownership, one may show an equitable right. See Complaint, Ch. 12 and Ultimate Fact, Ch. 23. 

§ 682. Mechanics' Lien: The complaint on a mechanic's lien must show that the labor performed was for one or more of the purposes specified in the statute,' and full compliance with the statute concerning mechanic's liens.2 Every fact necessary to the creation of the lien must be alleged, and it seems to be held that it is not sufficient to allege as we almost invariably do in the foreclosure of mortgages that some defendant "has or claims some interest, etc." but has none.

A mere count for work and labor "along the line of and upon said canal" is not enough. A complaint, however, that alleges that the material and labor were used on the land in question is sufficient although it does not say that the land was necessary for the convenient use and occupation of the building." It is held that a complaint on foreclosure of a mechanic's lien states a cause of action if it shows any kind of a lien whether on separate properties or a blanket lien on several.

Limitations and Laches. Aider. § 683. History: Historically, this action has been a function of equity, when there was no legal remedy, for the sake of peace, because it is well for all parties to know how their title stands, to protect the possession against overhanging claims injurious to free dealing with the property, and sometimes to avoid a multiplicity of suits.

The code¹ as interpreted by the courts makes this action and the pleadings in it simpler than any other. Any one in possession may maintain it against anyone who claims an interest adverse to him. The complaint need allege only that plaintiff is owner (or whatever he claims) and in possession, that defendant claims some interest adverse to him but has none.2 The prayer is that plaintiff be adjudged to be the owner (or whatever he claims), and the defendant to have no interest. We collate in the note some cases showing peculiar conditions. 8

§ 684. The Nature of the Action: The action is a call by one in possession upon a supposed claimant to come into court and set forth his claim, and show it to be good if he can. The cases are consistent with this theory and based upon it. The proposition is: One without an interest cannot question the title of one in possession, so defendant must allege an interest in himself before his denial of plaintiff's title can be considered.¹ 

¹Schlageter v. Gude, 30 C. 310, 70 P. 428; McLaughlin v. Niles Co., 88 C. 202, 205, 294 P. 954. It logically and inevitably follows that defendant must prove his right or interest before he may give evidence against that of plaintiff and some of the cases are consistent with that proposition and inconsistent with the contrary. Empire Co. v. Bender, 49 C. 522, 525, 113 P. 494; Muntzing v. Harwood, 25 C. A. 292, 295, 137 P. 71; Relander v. Riggs, 20 C. A. 423, 428-9, 79 P. 328, holds that if a defendant seeks to quiet his own title, and is defeated he cannot object to plaintiff's lack of proofs; McLaughlin v. Niles Co., states the essentials of the complaint most clearly. * * The defendant is the real plaintiff and his rights should be settled and decreed. It is not enough that he go hence without day. Green v. 

Halsted, 77 C. 578, 238 P. 40. The very purpose of the action is to determine the adverse estate of the defendant, Harrison v. Hodges, 49 C. 105, 107, 111 P. 706. "The defendant is called upon to plead any title or interest he may have and sustain the same by proper proof at the trial in order to defeat plaintiff's title." Eliason v. 

White, 23 C. A. 213, 214, 128 P. 887. A defendant must prove some interest or he cannot complain that plaintiff has not proved possession. 

Church v. Nielson, 23 C. A. 211, 128 P. 880. It would seem from 

Lambert v. Shumway, 36 C. 350, 85 P. 89, that a defendant must prove his title in order to attack that of plaintiff, but the opinion may refer merely to pleading. However, in Empire Co. v. Bender, 49 C. 522, 525, 113 P. 494, it is held that "the moment defendant's alleged adverse title failed" of proof "it had no further interest in the cause and could raise no other issue." So in Muntzing v. Harwood, 25 C. A. 292, 295, 137 P. 

71, citing Empire Co. v. Bender. Young v. Rohan, 77 C. 70, 234 P. 694, is inconsistent with this.

§ 685. The Nature of the Action, continued: Some cases, however, are inconsistent with the proposition that one without an interest may not question the title of the possessor. 

Chief among these cases are those which hold that if plaintiff's title is denied, he must prove it before the defendant is called upon to prove his own.¹ This seems to be the law in 

Colorado. Notwithstanding all this, however, the real and only issue is "title or interest in defendant vel non, because that is the only issue that will determine the case. If the defendant has title or interest, the plaintiff, to the extent of defendant's interest, has not, and the case is determined; so if plaintiff has title the defendant has not, and the case is determined, but if plaintiff has not title the defendant's rights are undetermined and if plaintiff has less than a fee defendant's rights are undetermined. Such cases miss the point that the plaintiff, being in possession, is presumptively entitled against the world, and therefore the burden of proving title is logically on the defendant.³ 

¹House v. Grable, 25 C. A. 405, 406-7, 138 P. 1012. 

This case definitely holds that the action is not in effect an action by defendant, and even though defendant must allege a title in himself, before he may deny plaintiff's, yet when plaintiff's title is so denied, he must prove it or fail. Buckland v. Fielder, 48 C. 153, 109 P. 262; and so is not only inconsistent with all the cases which hold that he may not deny plaintiff's title unless he alleges his own, but is inconsistent with itself. That is: One out of possession, by merely alleging title can compel one in possession to prove his title or lose it, even though the outsider has proved no right; that though defendant must allege his title in order to deny that of plaintiff, he need not prove it unless plaintiff proves his. 

2Wall v. Magnes, 17 C. 476, 30 P. 56; Clark v. Huff, 49 C. 197, 112 

P. 542; Empire R. & C. Co. v. Webster, 52 C. 207, 121 P. 171; Reynolds v. Campling, 23 C. 105, 46 P. 639; Walters v. Webster, 52 C. 549, 123

P. 952; this seems right in the case of vacant land where plaintiff's possession is constructive only, and based on his title. Lambert v. 

Murray, 52 C. 156, 160, 120 P. 415, says the relative merits of the two titles are involved which is not strictly true if plaintiff has actual possession. Wannamaker v. Pendleton, 21 C. A. 174, 184-5, 121 P. 108, holds that it is incumbent on both plaintiff and defendant to show title, a proposition which seems inconsistent with itself. 

Empire Co. v Bender, 49 C. 522, 526, 113 P. 494. This is tacitly recognized in Mulqueen v. Lanning, 53 C. 146, 148-9, 124 P. 577. So in Lougee v. Wilson, 24 C. A. 70, 72, 131 P. 777, it is held that it is the defendant and not the plaintiff that must stand or fall by his own title, and see Pom. Rem., 4th Ed., § 266. The plaintiff need prove only possession or, in case of vacant land, title sufficient to show constructive possession. Lougee v. Wilson, 24 C. A. 70, 73-4, 131 P. 777. 

§ 686. Proper Allegations: Notwithstanding the many cases cited in the foregoing sections and others like them some pleaders persist in alleging elaborate evidential matter.¹ That plaintiff is the owner and in possession of the premises in

question, and that defendant claims an interest or estate therein adverse to plaintiff which is without right, are the ultimate facts and are a sufficient statement of a cause of action to quiet title. The complaint need not, indeed should not, set out the character of the defendant's adverse claim; that is his duty.

§ 690. Removal of Cloud: The action to quiet title is some times distinguished from an action to remove a cloud from a title, but under the Colorado code they may be joined, at least an action to enjoin the execution of instruments which would cloud a title was held proper, and a deed obtained by fraud may be cancelled in this sort of action. The action to remove a cloud, like that to quiet title, requires the allegation of title in the plaintiff. An equitable interest in one not in possession will support an action to remove a cloud.* 3 2 

Allegations that the deed attached was "fraudulent, forged and without plaintiff's consent" are sufficient without saying that he did not acknowledge it. It is intimated that an action to enjoin a cloud will not lie when an action to remove it would afford an ample remedy."

699. Form of Action. 

§ 697. Nature of the Action: At common law, when two merchants came to a misunderstanding over their mutual accounts, their legal remedy was the common law action of account.¹ It was used between partners and others¹ where equity was also early employed, because of the expense, delay and technicalities which encumbered the common law form of action, until, in some jurisdictions, equity, even before the codes, superseded the older method, and in Colorado, since the code, the law action is forgotten and an action for an accounting is regarded as an equitable action." 2 

An accounting often follows as a matter of course in an action for some other equitable remedy. This is within the principle that when equity once takes hold it will do complete justice.

It was often, even at common law, a concurrent remedy with assumpist for money had and received, and is so now." 

Guardians, executors, administrators, stewards, conservators and all classes of trustees are subject to the action at all times to account for their trust funds. The substance of a complaint to compel a guardian to account and for a ne exeat is set out." 

An action by a chattel mortgagor against the mortgagee for selling the chattels at less than a reasonable price was called an action for an accounting.7 'Tidd's Practice, 1-2; 1 C. J. 602. The action was also used against partners, bailiffs and co-tenants in common. Id. and 1 Chit. 39, 488.

all the parties are treated as if each were a plaintiff and the others defendants,¹ and a judgment is rendered in favor of him entitled thereto even though he is a defendant and has filed no counter-claim. A counter-claim, in an action for damages for breach of contract, may justify an accounting but not unless it asserts an equitable claim which will destroy plaintiff's case. ¹Craig v. Chandler, 6 C. 543. 

2Crandall Co. v. Tanquary, 23 C. A. 564, 567-8, 130 P. 1084. 

Harris v. Thompson, 61 C. 87, 93, 156 P. 149. § 699. Form of Action: There seems to be no decision in 

Colorado which definitely states the necessary allegations of a complaint for an accounting, and, indeed, the facts which justify that remedy are so various that it would not be easy to give a general statement of them. Harris v. Thompson, supra, makes it clear that to justify an accounting on a contract the action must be to enforce rights under the contract, not for damages for its breach, and, if we carry out that principle, the action must be to enforce some primary right, either an equitable right to a mere accounting or some other right¹ to which an accounting is incident. In the latter sort the allegations must, of course, show a right to the principal relief, whatever that may be; in the former the allegations must put the defendant into one of the many positions in which he is bound in equity to account.2

It is, of course, impossible to state a general form of complaint for an accounting that will answer the purposes of every case, but below is an example of one in an action against an agent. The facts are purposely made very simple. In most cases there would be many complications, but the ultimate facts would not vary greatly. It is, of course, unnecessary to show anything due from defendant. Plaintiff has a right to an accounting, though the balance be against him.

Trusts. 701. 702.

Resulting Trusts, continued. $ 700. In General: The adjudication, enforcement and administration of trusts is one of the peculiar branches of equity jurisdiction.¹ It adjudicates, i.e., determines, that there is a trust, enforces, i.e., compels its fulfillment, and, if necessary, directs and controls its administration. 2 To obtain an adjudication that property is held in trust for a judgment debtor it is enough to allege that it is held in trust for him without the facts that make up the trust, and it is not necessary to allege that an express trust was in writing.3 

Equity will not only decree a trust but will, in a proper case declare it null and void. 

¹Stuart v. Chaney, 71 C. 279, 206 P. 386, a complaint and crosscomplaint were held to show equitable cognizance because to enforce a trust. 

2Kilham v. Bank, 30 C. 365, 371, 70 P. 409; Logan v. Clough, 2 C. 323. 

3Doll v. Gifford, 13 C. A. 67, 70, 56 P. 676. The pleadings are discussed and the complaint held good either for an express or resulting trust. 

4E.g., when made in fraud of creditors or the widow's allowance, Grover v. Clover, 69 C. 72, 73, 75, 169 P. 578. 

§ 701. Resulting Trusts: While the statute of frauds for bids the establishment of a trust except by writing there are circumstances in which the courts of equity will adjudge that a trust exists without writing by reason of the conduct of the parties. Different names are given to such a trust, e.g., constructive trust, resulting trust, trust ex maleficio, etc., but these names are descriptive, not definitive. The basic principle is akin to estoppel. The typical case is where money is given by one to another to purchase property for the giver and the other takes the property in his own name.' Equity will declare him to be a trustee and compel him to account, and, if necessary, convey the land. So where a mother conveyed property to her son on his promise to declare a trust in one-third of it to her the trust was held enforceable, partly because of the confidential relation." 

1Cree v. Lewis, 49 C. 186, 190, 112 P. 326. 

2Bohm v. Bohm, 9 C. 100, 10 P. 790. The substance of the crosscomplaint which alleges the trust is set out very fully. This case goes

very far. Perhaps none farther. The allegations should be studied carefully by one who draws a complaint to declare and enforce a resulting trust. It will be seen that there is much evidential matter but the material allegations can be gathered from the opinion, viz, the conveyance, on the promise of the grantee to declare the trust, with no other consideration, the confidential relation and the refusal to declare the trust, reconvey or account. § 702. Resulting Trusts, continued: In another case in which the cross-complaint alleges a resulting trust, the court offered no criticism.¹ A claim and intervenor under a resulting trust alleged that he furnished the money which bought the property which the attachment debtor took in his own name and his interest was held superior to that of an attacking creditor without notice of his rights.² 

1Fagan v. Troutman, 25 C. A. 251, 138 P. 442. The allegations were that one Davenport, the husband of plaintiff's mother, since deceased, had bought the property in question with her money, taking it in his own name. 

2Campbell v. Bank, 22 C. 177, 181, 43 P. 1007.

§ 706. Necessary Allegations, continued: Several of the cases already cited state and discuss the substance of a sufficient creditor's bill. No exact form can be prevised, but it is clear from those decisions that allegations that plaintiff has a judgment against the defendant debtor, upon an indebtedness incurred before the fraudulent transfer, that he has attached, levied execution or filed a transcript, that the debtor has conveyed or transferred property to defendant and without (or with inadequate) consideration to defraud his creditors including the plaintiff, will suffice. 

It is also clear that an allegation of insolvency, non-residence, or any impracticability of a judgment will suffice in its place. That the conveyance was voluntary and without consideration and rendered the grantor insolvent and without means to pay his debts held sufficient.2 

These allegations are often very prolix, but may and should be made concise, as the code requires. It is easily done. 

The court states the substance of a complaint, and, criticizing it as inept and prolix, yet holds that it states a cause of action

§ 707. Defenses: The defenses are the obvious ones in all equity suits; principally denial of the material allegations of the complaint. The code provisions, of course, as to these denials, are in force,' and the old equity rule which required an admission or denial of every allegation is no more.

The effect of a mere denial of the charge of want of consideration for the fraudulent transfer has not been determined, but it is customary to allege in the answer that there was a consideration and what it was. The burden of proving this is on the defendants.2 The defense of innocent purchaser is common.³

CHAPTER 54. 

Deed as a Mortgage. $708. In General: 

An absolute deed is often given as security for a debt or some other obligation. The rule against variation of writing by parol is, in such case, stretched or avoided to allow proof of the actual nature of the transaction, that the intent was security and not an actual and final conveyance. 1 The action to declare such a deed to be a mortgage is usually brought by the grantor (mortgagor), but it may be maintained by the mortgagee. If by the mortgagor it is in the nature of a bill to redeem,2 if by the mortgagee it may include a prayer for foreclosure." 

¹Borcherdt v. Favor, 16 C. A. 406, 66 P. 251; Thomas v. Wisner, 66 C. 243, 180 P. 744. 

2See Redemption. 

3 Borcherdt v. Favor, 16 C. A. 406, 66 P. 251. 

§ 709. The Complaint: The complaint should allege the debt, or other obligation, the deed, and the fact that it was given to secure the debt, that plaintiff is ready and willing, and offers to pay and redeem, that defendant refuses to accept redemption and claims the deed is absolute.¹ Any sort of transaction by which one acquires title to the property of another as security will be declared in equity to be a mortgage and will be foreclosed as such and redemption allowed.2 If the mortgagee has sold to an innocent purchaser the mortgagor may recover the difference between the price and the mortgage debt.8

§ 710. Principles: To draw proper pleadings in such a case it is well to know the principles on which it rests, but the decisions by no means agree on that point. Fraud or mistake has been said to be the basis of the right to vary the terms of the deed and perhaps that was originally so in the cases now in question, but California repudiated that theory as "unsound in priciple and unsupported by authority, " and asserted the true principle to be the same as that by which equity destroyed the forfeiture under the common law mortgage, that is: Not to vary the deed "but to establish an equity superior to its terms."

As it ignored the terms of that mortgage,² so now it ignores any terms that undertake to establish a forfeiture, and views with suspicion anything that looks like an attempt to create one.³ In Colorado, however, the whole matter is controlled by the code¹ and a mortgage is but a lien.5

It seems certain that if we follow the code and the principles laid down in Ver Straten v. Worth, and in Pierce v. Robinson that the allegation stated above for the complaint are all that ought to be stated, that they constitute the "material allegations" and that more detail is evidential. So Rietze v. Humphreys, 53 C. 178, 182, 125 P. 518, quotes from Borcherdt v. Favor, 16 C. A. 406, 66 P. 251. "If a transaction resolved itself into a security, whatever may be its form and whatever name the parties may choose to give it, it is in effect a mortgage." If this is true the allegation of a debt and the deed to secure it which is claimed to be absolute stated a cause of action, and more is evidence, p. 184. The offer to redeem is an offer to do equity, not necessary where the only object of the suit is a construction of the contract to determine the relation of the parties, pp. 184-5. Usually the only defense is to deny that the deed was given for security and the real contest is in the evidence. § 711. Redemption: The bill to redeem is an actin in equity to obtain the right to redeem from a mortgage or other lien where that right has been denied by the mortgagee. It is a feature of most actions to declare an absolute deed to be a mortgage. The lien is not controverted by the plaintiff, but the equities, whatever they may be, which are claimed to justify the redemption, are stated. The action has not been frequently before our higher courts. It is the only remedy for a chattel mortgagor after default. It was, indeed, the original proceeding by which the "equity of redemption" from the terms of absolute forfeiture in mortgages was established. 

¹Leopald v. McCartney, 14 C. A. 442, 446, 449, 60 P. 640.

§ 712. Nature of Action of Interpleader: The bill of inter pleader was a well recognized sort of suit in chancery but is not expressly authorized by the code. The nearest approach is in Sections 17 and 21. It is an action to compel two defendants who make inconsistent claims against the plaintiff to litigate their conflicting claims. A not uncommon example is the case of a tenant, rent from whom is claimed by two, each of whom claims title to the rented premises. The tenant may bring a suit called interpleader to force them to litigate their rights and so determine to whom he shall attorn. 

A defendant moved to substitute as defendant another who claimed the sum in dispute. The grant of this motion was said to "constitute an effective interpleader of the two claimants." 

The term is sometimes confused with "intervention," even by the courts. Burr v. Clement, 9 C. 1, 9 P. 633. It is correctly used in 

Mosquito Co. v. London-Butte Co., 96 C. 536, 537, 45 P.(2d) 175. 

2Mosquito Co. v. London-Butte Co., 96 C. 536, 537, 45 P.(2d) 175. 

§ 713. Interpleader In General: An early case was essentially a bill of interpleader by a taxpayer to learn to which of two counties he should pay taxes on his cattle,' but it was not named as such. A similar suit with respect to real estate was brought against Park and Chaffee Counties, but there it was recognized as interpleader. The Great Western 

Sugar Company brought an action of interpleader to determine to which of two claimants it should pay the proceeds of certain beets. And it is held that wherever plaintiff is likely to have to pay twice, equity will protect him whether you call it interpleader or not.

§ 715. Intervention, Nature: Intervention under the code is of two classes: Intervention in an action and intervention in an attachment proceeding. It is of the former that we treat here. The common law knew nothing of this practice; it is borrowed from equity and so we treat it as in equity. Though the code permits it in a lawsuit, yet even there it is treated as if it were a proceeding in equity.¹

The intervention is by petition. The intervenor claims some interest in the subject or object of the action and asks to come in and protect it.²

A copy of the petition must be served on the adverse parties.³ 

The requisites of the petition are the same as those of a complaint on the same facts. The right of the plaintiff must appear, also a violation of it and some resulting right, e.g., possession of the property in dispute. 

¹Code, §§ 16, 17, 22, 23 and 24. 

2Stone v. D. & S. L. R. Co., 78 C. 323, 241 P. 532. The intervenor claims something himself, the plaintiff in interpleader disclaims and asks that claims of others be determined.

Code, §§ 17, 23. 

Skinner v. Harker, 23 C. 333, 341, 48 P. 648. 

§ 716. When Intervention Lies: Any claim with one of the parties or against all or any. The note collates some of the cases.¹

§ 718. Nature: Injunctions may be considered as of two classes, temporary and permanent. The permanent injunction is the ultimate purpose of the suit. The temporary is an auxiliary proceeding to aid, usually by holding the status quo, an action for another purpose, sometimes to aid an action to secure a permanent injunction. Sometimes a permanent injunction is additional to other equitable relief. 

Under the former system, if an injunction was necessary to aid an action at law, it was secured in chancery, or on the chancery side of the court, but under the code in the same action.¹

On dissolution of a temporary injunction, the plaintiff still has a right to a trial of the main case on the merits, even in an action for a permanent injunction.2 

¹Boglino v. Giorgetta, 20 C. A. 338, 342-3, 78 P. 612. The complaint stated ground for injunction but asked only damages and it was held that it was a bill in equity. 

2Vallero v. Camilla, 53 C. 312, 125 P. 497. The action was to enjoin a sale of plaintiff's real estate under execution. On dissolution of the temporary injunction the court dismissed the bill and the judgment was reversed. 2 

§ 719. When Action Lies: Injunctions are regarded as in equity and equity must be made to appear, so the court will not enjoin a mere trespass; there must be facts to show danger of irreparable injury,¹ e.g., threat of repetition, which may be implied in the allegations of repetition.2 A complaint to enjoin collection of certain taxes was held bad because it did not allege a threat or intention to enforce collection, and a complaint to enjoin enforcement of taxes and an execution was held to show no equity. A complaint to enjoin an assessment for a storm sewer was held good. To enjoin a tax deed, plaintiff must pay or tender the just tax." 

¹Smith v. Schlink, 15 C. A. 325, 335, 62 P. 1044; Morris v. Cheney, 81 C. 893, 255 P. 987. 

2Boglino v. Giorgetta, 20 C. A. 338, 342, 78 P. 612. An action to enjoin the flooding of plaintiff's land.

It seems that after the judgment is vacated the defendant can answer only such defenses as he has alleged in his motion to vacate and his affidavit of merits. If the motion is on the ground that the judgment was without jurisdiction of the person of defendant an affidavit of merits may be required but is not traversable. § 725. Specific Performance: When there is no remedy at law or when legal remedies are inadequate equitable relief is proper. This basic rule of equity is enforced in certain cases where damages for breach of contract will be an inadequate remedy, by compelling the defendant to do what he agreed to do. The typical case is the refusal to convey land which defendant has contracted to convey.2 In such case, the purchaser may have a decree that the defendant convey or that the decree shall constitute a conveyance.

The plaintiff may recover damages if he chooses even though he might have had specific performance and also when specific performance has become impossible; and he may have damages even in an action for specific performance when it turns out that the latter relief is impossible." 

¹O'Donnell v. Chamberlin, 36 C. 395, 404, 91 P. 39, e.g., if nonperformance will embarrass the plaintiff in his business, or if damages cannot be accurately ascertained, Senter v. Davis, 38 Cal. 450.

He sells and conveys to B by deed, which describes Y, and B takes possession. Why may not B have both deeds corrected? All equities seem with him and only technicalities against him.

§ 737. In General: Although a discussion of pleading in general includes much concerning litigation in respect to water rights, as well as to other kinds of property, it is desirable to take special notice of that subject. 

The Constitution of Colorado and the statutes determined that the right to the use of the water of the natural streams of the State depend upon prior appropriation for a beneficial use. What appropriations were prior to others was a vital question, and the legislature, therefore, by the well-known statutes,¹ provided for the adjudication of these rights by general decrees in actions to which all carrier claimants in each water district were made parties. It is held that such a proceeding is not a civil action under the code, that it is sui generis and that ordinary rules are not always applicable to it. Such decrees were rendered in every water district and water is distributed to the several ditches accordingly.

§ 753. Will Contest, Pleadings: The will is presented together with a petition that it be admitted to probate. Any one who is interested and wishes to contest the probate of it may file a "caveat or objections" which state objections to the probate of the will or to the validity of some provision thereof or both and is subject to demurrer for insufficiency, motion to make more specific, amendment and answer as in pleading as in civil cases under the code.¹ The caveat, then is a sort of complaint, yet the practise is to require the proponent to first make formal proof of the execution of the will, and the issue is said to be devisavit vel non which would put the burden on the proponent, but it is held that when the proponent has made a prima facie case the burden of showing undue influence or unsound mind is on the contestant. All said elsewhere is then relevant here.

The heirs frequently consent to the probate but they may withdraw this consent at any time before probate is ordered.5

It would seem, then that the real issue is devisavit vel non, that the proponent must make a prima facie case, then contestant must show his claim, e.g. want of capacity, but that the final burden to show capacity by a preponderance of the evidence is on the proponent.

§ 756. Quo Warranto, In General: The code has dodged this name and calls the proceeding "Action for the Usurpation of an Office or Franchise," such a ponderous and awkward term that it is never used, but the old name Quo Warranto still stands.2 The purpose of the two proceedings, if they may be called two, is the same, i.e., to try the title to an office or franchise, and their methods do not greatly differ. We do not attempt to go elaborately into questions of practice or procedure in quo warranto, but only so far as to make the matter of pleading clear. We are concerned now with the code's method of laying the facts before the court, which is, in this quo warranto, by complaint, answer and replication, as in an ordinary civil action, and, otherwise than of old, the complaint may show the rights of the claimant, plaintiff, as well as the defects in the title of the incumbent. The action

is ordinarily brought by the district attorney, but when he consents or refuses to act a private party may bring the action." 

2The modern action is really a modification of the action or information in the nature of quo warranto, long ago substituted for the ancient quo warranto. They are now one and the same, People v. Keeling, 4 C. 129. By the old action the court said: "Show why you are in or get out"; by the new action it says: "Let us see who has the better right." Lockhard v. Peo., 65 C. 558, 178 P. 565.

Quo Warranto and not Mandamus is the proper remedy to oust a city councilman and install his opponent. City Council v. Peo., 19 C. A. 

399, 75 P. 603. See Mandamus. It was used to test the validity of an election for directors of an irrigation district, Peo. v. Milan, 89 C. 556, 558, 5 P.(2d) 249. It is the proper method to test the validity of proceedings to incorporate a town. Velasquez v. Zimmerman, 30 C. 355, 70 P. 419. This proceeding is not to redress a private wrong where a public right is not involved, but it may redress a private wrong when a public right is involved. Weisbrod v. Lockhard, 26 C. A. 439, 440, 143 P. 273, and if the matter is public the relator cannot stipulate for a dismissal, Lockhard v. Peo., 65 C. 558, 178 P. 565.

§ 757. Quo Warranto, The Complaint: The complaint must show the office or franchise in question, that the defendant is occupying it or exercising its functions and allege facts which show he has no right to it, and, if it is intended to install the person rightly entitled, the facts which show his right must, of course, be alleged. The rules which govern the allegations are as in ordinary actions. The substance of a complaint is set forth in Weisbrod v. Lockhard, 26 C. A. 439, 143 P. 273. It may be in general terms, and the defendant must then show his right. The ultimate fact is that defendant is exercising a franchise without right thereto.3 3 2 The pleading in an action to prevent an election to incorporate a town were construed as quo warranto.*

Mandamus, When Proper: In general the court will not control the discretion of the respondent,¹ but will compel him to act, and, if the duty is clear and unquestionable will compel him to do it. So where he has exercised his discretion and decided a matter the court will compel him to complete it. If the rights of third parties are involved, mandamus is not the remedy, but if such rights are invalid it is proper, conflicting claims cannot be considered.*

Mandamus is the only remedy on municipal bonds issued under the Territorial Act of 1868,5 or on coupons from County 

Refunding Bonds or warrants of an irrigation district." 

Mandamus by the real party in interest lies to enforce a private right,s to compel a county treasurer to issue a second tax deed to correct a defective one," to compel the delivery of water under a contract as well as under a statute,10 and to compel the Public Utilities Commission to obey the Civil Service Law. It will not lie to oust a councilman and install his opponent.12

§ 762. Mandamus, The Procedure: A petition and affidavit are filed whereupon an alternative writ is issued which commands the respondent to do what plaintiff desires or show cause why not, but if notice of the petition is given, the alternative writ is unnecessary. The alternative writ takes the place of the complaints and states the facts which constitute the plaintiff's right and is treated somewhat like a complaint. The petition, if notice is given, is treated like a complaint. In Colorado mandamus is not a prerogative writ; the facts are to be pleaded as in an ordinary action at law,º and it is a civil action. The answer to the alternative writ is called, since the writ is addressed to the respondent, the "return." In Colorado the return may aid an insufficient writ, and it seems there may be a replication to the return.º 

A reply does not admit the legal sufficiency of the return.10 

The successor of a respondent whose official term has expired must be substituted.11

§ 764. Mandamus, The Allegations: In an action to compel a county board to levy a tax to pay a judgment against the county, the allegations were the recovery of the judgment, a demand on the board of a levy to pay it, that it had not been paid, and an order of the board refusing the demand. A judgment upon a demurrer sustained was reversed.¹ The requisite allegations are discussed in Board of Public Works v. Hayden, 13 C. A. 36, 56 P. 201, their substance set forth and the complaint held good."

It was said that to compel a county board to levy a tax to pay a judgment the power of the board to levy the tax must appear from the complaint. 

1 Peo. v. Rio Grande Co., 11 C. A. 124, 52 P. 748. Was not the order evidential? Should not the allegation have been "refused to levy" in support of which the order would have been evidence? 

2Board Pub. Works v. Hayden, 13 C. A. 36, 39, 56 P. 201. The petition was to compel the board to issue to plaintiff an estimate on completion of his contract for grading and paving. It alleged the contract, the statutory proceedings by the board and city to give validity to the contract, performance by plaintiff and refusal by the board to issue the estimate which the contract required. 

Grand Co. v. Peo., 16 C. A. 215, 234, 64 P. 675. But the meaning was that since the law permitted the levy of but 1.50% in any year the complaint should show that that amount had not already been levied. 

This seems like requiring plaintiff to anticipate a defense. There is no presumption that the full levy has been already made.

§ 765. Mandamus, Allegations, continued: In an action to compel the state auditor to draw a warrant it is not necessary to allege that there is money in the treasury to meet it, at least if it is not drawn against a special fund,' and such an allegation is a conclusion of law. The alternate writ must. aver and prove all facts necessary to the duty of the treasurer to pay the warrants. In mandamus to permit the inspection by a stockholder of corporate books the writ need not specify the particular books to be inspected, but if it is purposed to also compel the issue of stock to plaintiff the complaint must allege compliance with the by-laws with reference to the transfer of stock. In mandamus to compel the issue of an execution on a judgment of record. The rendition of the judgment and that it is unsatisfied are the only necessary allegations."

§ 767. Mandamus, Defenses: The defense is usually one of law, not of fact. The question is: Is it the duty of respondent to do as the relator desires. It is no defense to say performance is impossible if the respondent created the impossibility,¹ and in an action to permit a stockholder to inspect the corporate books, it is no defense to say that plaintiff is acting in bad faith or on improper motives.2

In mandamus to compel delivery of irrigation water the defendant cannot have equitable relief, i.e., an order that the rate tendered is confiscatory, fixing a proper rate but must bring another action, and title to water cannot be litigated in mandamus.¹ 

But in mandamus as in other code actions the plaintiff may, if not mandamus, have such other relief as the facts pleaded and proved will justify.5

§ 768. Certiorari: The common law writ of certiorari was to review the action of an inferior court, which had exceeded its jurisdiction. It was addressed to the lower court and directed that court to send up its record for review. It was not a substitute for a writ of error, and it did not review the record as pertaining to the rights of the parties but only as to whether the court had kept within its jurisdiction. The code of Colorado, however, permits the review as to whether the lower court has "greatly abused the discretion of such tribunal ***" and there is no appeal nor in the judgment of the court any plain, speedy and adequate remedy. 

The code has no application to proceedings in the Supreme Court. They are there still controlled by the common law,2 and therefore that court considers only the question of jurisdiction.

of Parker's Ed.) with the clause "greatly abused the discretion, etc." added.

§ 771. Certiorari, Petition: In quo warranto the code provides for a complaint and so, inferentially, for answer and replication, but not so in certiorari. Indeed in certiorari such

pleadings are not appropriate, since the petition for the writ is, in limine, taken as true and the whole case is upon the record of the inferior tribunal.2 There is no issue of fact, so no pleading, properly so called, and no evidence except the record. If there is notice or an order to show cause, the petition may be attacked for insufficiency or any defense which shows there is no ground for the writ.2 

The petition³ must be "upon affidavit," and if it is sufficient the writ is granted. The writ is addressed to and served on the lower tribunal; returned with the record, which is reviewed, and the question of excess of jurisdiction determined therefrom. The allegations of the petition are not admitted by lack of answer.

§ 773. Prohibition, Nature: The code uses the term "pro hibition" but once and that only in the heading to Ch. XXIX. "Writ of Certiorari and Prohibition. It may be that this chapter was intended to control the proceeding called prohibition as well as certiorari, make them one; but they have been considered as distinct, and prohibition has followed partially the old practice. They might well be one. Each was to question the jurisdiction of a lower tribunal, prohibition before final judgment and certiorari after. Prohibition prevents action in want or in excess of jurisdiction, certiorari removes the consequences of it. Article VI, § 3 of the State

§ 774. Prohibition, When Proper: Like certiorari pro hibition is said to be proper only when a writ of error will not furnish full relief. The Supreme Court used to grant the writ of prohibition in case of an unauthorized change of venue, but later it established the practice of leaving such cases to writ of error. Since the writ is not of right but discretionary2 this practice was legal.

§ 775. Prohibition, Petition: The application for the writ is called the petition. The prayer is that the respondent tribunal be (restrained, enjoined and) prohibited from doing that which is claimed to be beyond its jurisdiction, or for an order to show cause why it should not be so prohibited, or for an alternative writ to that effect. In some jurisdictions a simple notice to show cause is served upon respondent, in others an alternative writ setting forth the cause of action, in which case the return of the writ constitutes the answer and with the writ constitutes the pleadings, as in mandamus. In

§ 783. In Capacity to Sue: A foreign corporation must do certain things before it may sue or defend in Colorado.¹ 2 The substance of an answer which stated the failure of a foreign plaintiff corporation to comply with this law is given in one case. It is not a matter of question that if the incapacity of the plaintiff does not appear in the complaint it must be pleaded in abatement.

In other cases it is said it must be "pleaded," and failure to do so waives the objection.* 

There are other cases."

The defenses of release and payment are sufficiently treated in Code 

Chaps. XXV and XXVI. 

2Int. Tr. Co. v. Lerschen & Sons Co., 41 C. 299, 801, 92 P. 727. It seems to the writer that the terms in which the plea is stated in the opinion would be quite sufficient in the pleading itself, where it was probably more prolix. 

³Arch. N. Pr. 159; I Chit. 448. Ill. S. M. Co. v. Harrison, 43 C. 362, 365, 96 P. 177. The opinion says "in bar of the action," but if plaintiff had no capacity to sue there could not be a bar to the cause of action, therefore the plea is in abatement. The same expression is used in Tabor v. G. P. Mfg. Co., 11 C. 419, 429, 18 P. 587, one of the cases cited in the opinion, but in the other case there cited, Utley v. The Clark-Gardner Co., 4 C. 369, 372, 376, the plea is shown to be in abatement. Judg Elbert's remark, "The plea to have availed, if at all, should have been in bar of the action." Evidently misled the later writers. What he meant was that incapacity to do business was a plea in bar and should have been so pleaded (remember they were pleading under the common law) and that the statute (then in force) did not limit capacity to sue. In other words incapacity to do business nullifies the contract and so the cause of action while incapacity to sue can only affect the action, not the cause of action.

§ 786. Statute of Frauds: We speak of "pleading the statute of frauds," but we mean pleading (alleging) the facts which show that the plaintiff's claim is subject to that statute.¹ 

The statute itself is not alleged. As we have shown, the defense of the statute of frauds is usually regarded as in confession and avoidance. So it cannot be made by objection to evidence. The contract alleged in the complaint is presumed to be in writing where writing is necessary, and consequently it is not necessary to allege in the complaint that the contract in suit is written, and the question cannot be raised by general demurrer. Ultra Vires: A corporation defendant sometimes defends an action ex contractu on the ground that the contract was beyond its powers. It would seem reasonable that this defense be regarded as evidential, in support of a denial of the making of the contract. If the corporation could not make it, it did not make it, and the allegation, therefore, that it could not make it is an argumentative denial. This question, however, we do not find raised in Colorado. It is doubtless prudent, though illogical, to plead it in confession and avoidance, and it should be sufficient to merely say that the contract is not within the powers of the defendant corporation.¹

The Colorado courts are ill-disposed toward this defense, and it is held, substantially, that it will not be allowed to do injustice.2 

The defense is not enforced against an executed contract.

§ 796. Statute of Limitations, In Actions Ex Contractu: A 

new promise within six years is a common reply to a plea of the statute in an action for breach of a contract to pay money. 

It is said that the new promise should be alleged in the complaint since it is the real basis of the action. It is proper, however, to allege it in the replication,2 and it may be stated in the complaint by amendment after demurrer sustained2 but the statute cannot be pleaded by amendment. If the new promise is conditional it must be so pleaded. It must be voluntary and must be shown to have been paid on the debt in question and so received by plaintiff. So where the payment was alleged in the complaint and denied, the issue tried was "payment on the note vel non," not payment vel non. 

1Buckingham v. Orr, 6 C. 587, 590; Richardson v. Bricker, 7 C. 58, 1 P. 433. It seems to the writer that the new promise (sometimes implied from a payment) is not the basis of the action but amounts to an acknowledgment of the original liability; this is shown by the rule that a bare acknowledgment, not amounting to a promise, will arrest the statute. Tidd's Pr. 22, Yost v. Irwin, 53 C. 269, 272, 125 P. 526, considers that the statute of limitations is no ground of demurrer; and so the rule that the plea of the statute is in confession and avoidance is right. Consistently, a demurrer on the ground of the statute will not lie to a complaint which shows a payment within the six years, Dubois v. First Natl. Bank, 43 C. 400, 403-4, 96 P. 169. 

2Yost v. Irwin, 53 C. 269, 272-3, 125 P. 526. The amendment was a special demurrer after a general demurrer was overruled.

§ 803. Laches, How Pleaded: The weight of authority in 

Colorado is that the defense of Laches is in confession and

SPECIFIC DEFENSES 

587 2 avoidance, and must be so pleaded, and that it is not a ground for demurrer. The court of appeals, however, said that as a general rule it was in confession and avoidance, and that it ought not ordinarily to be determined on demurrer, and the Supreme Court has said that the defense must be made by answer unless the facts are shown by the complaint, but it was later held that even though the laches appeared in the complaint a demurrer would not lie. Inconsistently with these propositions it is held that if a long time has passed, the complaint must show excuse for laches, and, contrary to them, that it need not be pleaded as a defense, and the Supreme Court dismissed a petition for certiorari because of laches although there was no plea thereof. Neither a stranger to plaintiff's title, nor one in possession for him can claim laches on his part. Laches is not a matter of time alone, the effect of delay on others must be considered.10 Laches is an equitable defense and a plaintiff cannot shift from equity to law to avoid it.¹ 10

§ 804. Another Suit Pending: This is a defense in abate ment'; not in bar, because it has no bearing on the merits, that is, plaintiff's substantial rights. A writ of error, without supersedeas, from a judgment of dismissal for want of jurisdiction, is not "another suit pending" unless it is in the same. jurisdiction. The suits must be upon the same subject matter,3 and between the same parties. An action to enjoin the opening of a road is no defense to a proceeding in eminent domain to open it, but a pending action by plaintiff and defendant for specific performance is a defense to an action for an accounting.

The question may be raised by demurrer or answer, but not by motion. Of course by demurrer when the pending suit appears on the face of the complaint but not otherwise.8 

The point is waived by failure to plead it.º

§ 805. Res Adjudicata: The plea of res adjudicata (the thing has been adjudged) is a species of estoppel by record.¹ 

It is a matter of confession and avoidance,² and may be used in the answer or the replication. 3 It is available only where the parties are the same and appear in the same character and capacity, and in such case there are three general conditions on which the plea is justified: 

1. Where the former judgment was upon the same cause of action; 2. Where in the former judgment an issue material in the present case, was determined in the pleador's favor; 

3. Where a ground of relief or defense is now set up which might have been, though it was not, set up in the former action.

2 Arch. Nisi Pr., 336, from which one would infer that at least on the question of title vel non the former judgment might be proved on that issue alone; and in Hughes v. Jones, 89 C. 455, 457, 3 P. (2d) 1074, a replication was stricken because it alleged matters which had been previously adjudicated in the same court of which the court took judicial notice. Counter-Claim, In General: Many questions in respect to counter-claim are not within the strict limits of our subject, which is pleading strictly so called, but it is convenient and perhaps of advantage to the student and prac-

titioner to give a rather full statement of the condition of the subject in Colorado.

The term, counter-claim, includes all the denotation of set off at common law and of cross-bill in chancery, and, in law actions, much more¹; the decisions, therefore, concerning its scope are usually interpretations of the code.

§ 814. Counter-claim, What May be Set Off: An equitable defense may be alleged against a suit on a note.¹

A claim on contract cannot be set off against an action for conversion²; payment made to a contractor or on his order may be set off against his assignee. In an action to cancel a forged deed the defendant answered that the plaintiff held the title in trust for him and asked to have his title quieted. 

The court held it was no defense and not a valid counter-claim because the action was not on a contract and the counterclaim did not arise out of the same transaction.* 

Where plaintiff sued on a contract for a deed to mining claims, defendant denied it and alleged a different contract on the same subject and counter-claimed on that, his damages were held to arise out of the same transaction." § 819. Counter-Claim, Equity: In chancery the defendant's claim to relief was called a cross-bill. The denotation of counter-claim includes the cross-bill' and that term is often used, also the term cross-complaint. Their convenience is obvious. So far as cross-bills in equity are concerned, the code § 63 is practically an enactment of chancery rules. The subject matter of a cross-complaint should be germain to the original complaint.2

Under the code an equitable cross-bill, though it requires new parties, is proper, and a cross-complaint is good against a co-defendant."

What would seem to be a counter-claim was pleaded as a sort of equitable satisfaction of a note, and was treated as a good plea."

CHAPTER 64. 

Supplemental Pleadings. 

Supplmental Complaint; Repetition. 

827. Not Amendment. 

§ 825. Nature: The purpose of supplemental pleadings is to bring before the court relevant, material facts which have occurred since the suit was begun,¹ and such facts may not be otherwise presented. The supplemental complaint corresponds to the supplemental bill in chancery and the supplemental answer to that in chancery or to the common law plea puis darrein continuance. Such a pleading is filed by leave of court,¹ and, it is said, in the court's discretion, and laches is of weight in denying the leave.³ 

¹Code, § 80. A supplemental complaint filed without leave was held properly stricken, Rogers v. Rogers, 57 C. 132, 140 P. 193. The complaint, however, was not supplemental but was an amendment. Yet it is held that leave is not necessary. Whitsett v. Clayton, 5 C. 476, 486. 

Sayre v. Sage, 47 C. 559, 108 P. 160. 

3Empire Co. v. Millett, 24 C. A. 464, 135 P. 127. 

§ 826. Supplemental Complaint; Repetition: A supple mental complaint need not state facts which already appear in the original. This is according to the fundamental rule that the whole record is a unit. This is illustrated by the rule that the whole is under consideration upon a demurrer for want of facts, and judgment must go accordingly.

It is unnecessary, and therefore improper, to repeat anything that already appears in the pleadings, except when in a new count, defense or reply. 

A complaint on a city warrant, payable out of a specific fund must allege that there is money in that fund to pay them.³

The sufficiency of the allegations on a contract to do assessment work is discussed.*

To allege more would be pleading evidence, McGonigle v. Kane, 20 C. 292, 298-9, 38 P. 367; (yet the court refers to evidential matter as if it strengthened the complaint). It follows that lack of proof of an ultimate fact is fatal, Costilla Co. v. Willis, 36 C. 339, 85 P. 428: 

Fishel v. Goddard, 30 C. 147, 156, 69 P. 607.

CONSTITUTIONAL QUESTIONS 

601 

Section. 

CHAPTER 65. 

Constitutional Questions. 

828. Pleading the Constitution. 

829. Pleading the Constitution, continued.

§ 828. Pleading and the Constitution: A constitutional question is whether a law is inconsistent with the constitution of the State or of the United States. In Colorado and in other states with like constitutions, these questions are of two kinds: 1. Whether the law in question is in substance inconsistent with the constitution; and, 2. Whether it has been passed in accordance with the constitution.¹ 

A question of the first kind is almost universally held to be for consideration at any time in any case whether raised by the pleadings or not, but the decisions with respect to the second kind have not been consistent,² and some of them are self-contradictory, with respect to other sections it is held that evidence cannot be taken to prove a law unconstitutional.* 

1 Const. Art. 5, § 22. 

3 

2In Colorado and So. R. Co. v. Davis, 21 C. A. 1, 4-5, 120 P. 1048, it was apparently held that either kind of question must be raised by the pleadings, which seems wrong, since it is equivalent to holding that whether a law is inconsistent with the constitution is a question of fact, but on the second point some Colorado cases seem to hold that the question whether the act was constitutionally passed is a question of fact, though not for the jury but for the court, and that the facts which show that it was not so passed must be alleged. 

Anderson v. Grand V. Irr. Dist., 35 C. 525, 85 P. 313; Vindicator Co. v. Firstbrook, 36 C. 498, 510, 86 P. 313; Peckham v. Peo., 32 C. 140, 75 P. 422; Nesbit v. Peo., 19 C. 441, 450, 36 P. 221; Rio G. S. Co. v. 

Catlin, 40 C. 450, 458-9, 94 P. 323. These cases, however, seem contrary to Ottawa v. Perkins, 94 U. S. 260, and to Post v. Supervisors, 105 U. S. 667. In Ottawa v. Perkins it is said "a question of fact respecting the existence or non-existence of a law is a question of law If a question of law, it should not be pleaded. This is made clear in Marean v. Stanley, 21 C. 43, 39 P. 1086, a case which for some reason is cited to the contrary, though all it holds is that evidence ought to show what was lacking in the passage of the law. 

The logical fault in requiring such facts to be pleaded is that they regard only the major premise of the legal syllogism, while pleadings should state only the facts which constitute the minor. See complaint and cause of action, Anderson v. Grand V. Irr. Co., cited in several cases, gives the point no support. Vindicator Co. v. Firstbrook does not definitely decide it. Peckham v. Peo., and Nesbit v. Peo., are not directly in point here because they are criminal cases. It would seem then, that the rule that the facts which show a law not to be constitutionally passed should be pleaded, has not a sound basis of authority.

Replies. 

At least one-fifth of the time of our District Courts is consumed in preliminary proceedings, mostly in respect to pleadings and in other later considerations of that subject. Several times as much time is thus spent under codes as under the practice at common law. The reason is that at common law the forms of pleadings had become fixed by long use, and so required no interpretation (even in equity the conditions were much the same) while under the code each pleader largely expresses his ideas as he thinks proper or convenient, and every pleading so expressed requires special interpretations. 

Such a system leads inevitably to verbosity, despite the requirement for conciseness, and so to the allegation of evidential matter, so that the issues are obscured and concealed. We even find the courts requiring such allegations on the ground that pleadings are to give notice. As we have shown elsewhere there is no logical way to limit pleadings in such a system and no limit to the verbosity of such pleading except the whim of the judge who happens to hear the demurrers and motions in the case, and so, insofar as courts have allowed that sort of pleading, justice has been delayed, and is delayed.

Neither the common law system, nor the chancery practice was free from this defect of delay though in modern days much superior in that respect to the code practice. The 

English, however, noticing this defect in their practice have taken the opposite course to overcome it. While we have turned pleaders loose, each to express himself as he may see fit, they have prescribed forms of complaint and answers in so many kinds of cases that the exceptions are negligible. 

These forms are not subject to demurrer or motion, so, while a pleader has the privilege of using his own language, the temptation to do so is removed and nearly every case goes directly to trial.¹

Since the code has thus far failed in its purpose to produce conciseness and directness in pleading and must continue to do so unless lawyers and courts shall develop customary forms.

of brevity and directness, which seems but remotely possible, it appears that the best course would be to adopt the English system; if not wholly at least partially, i.e., in all ordinary cases.

While England has thus reformed her court procedure the states in this country have sought to escape from the unsatisfactory procedure in their courts, first by the codes, and, now that they have proved ineffectual, superseding the courts, establishing administrative commissions with judicial powers, but unhampered by the procedure which prevails in the courts. 

One step toward a remedy for our defects in this respect is obedience to the code's requirements for conciseness and exclusion of immaterial allegations. The books of code forms, e.g., Estees, Boone, Bancroft, Abbott, are admirable, but their merits are more often unnoticed than regarded.2 

We do not attempt here, to give a complete set of forms, others have done that, but we give a few to illustrate our text and some of our citations.

The nearest approach to a demurrer is a notice, a part of the defense, (answer) that the defendant will object to the sufficiency of the statement (complaint). 

2The case of Hays v. Arbuckle, 72 C. 328, 211 P. 101, gives an example of conciseness which ought to be emulated. It almost equals the modern English forms in this respect. ᏢᎪᎡᎢ 1.
