Notary Public. 

Complaints are usually for convenience divided into numbered paragraphs. That the allegations are in the form of indirect discourse is a relic of the days of oral pleadings when the clerk recorded his notion of what counsel had said; in the present tense, however, as if when it was said. It is the logical form for a record, and the pleadings are a part of the record. 

If the defendant is a corporation the verification may read: "True to the best of his knowledge, information and belief." If the defendant is absent from the county where his attorney resides, or from some cause unable to verify the attorney may do it. Code, § 67.

The part in brackets may be omitted if nothing is stated on information and belief. The verification may be omitted unless it is desired to compel a verified answer.

Title. 

Form No. 3. 

Assault and Battery. 

The plaintiff complains and alleges: 

1. That at.. in said County, on the........day of 

19......, the defendant assaulted and beat the plaintiff (state method of assault) e.g., and struck him many times with a cane. 

2. (State the consequences of the assault) e.g., That plaintiff was thereby greatly hurt, bruised, and made sick, sore, lame and otherwise disordered, suffered great pain and was obliged to pay, and did pay, a large sum, to-wit: $100.00 for doctors and nurses, and other expenses to be cured of said hurts, all which is to his damage $..... 1 

Wherefore plaintiff demands judgment for.....................dollars.

The cause of action is stated in paragraph 1. It is the simplest of all causes. Everyone has a primary right to his person inviolate; an assault violates that right and creates a resulting right to a money compensation called damages. An allegation of an assault, therefore, shows a right to damages. For injury to property the relation of the plaintiff to the property must be shown, e.g., "owner" or "of the plaintiff."

Paragraph 2 shows the nature and extent of the damage, and the amount of the damages claimed. These are, illogically, held to be traversable in Tucker v. Parks, 7 C. 62, 1 P. 427. The court did not recollect the distinction between traversable and disputable. A traversable allegation is one the denial of which will defeat the action or defense. The nature of the damage and the amount of damages are always disputable but their disproof will not defeat the action; hence, at common law they were not traversed.

Form No. 17.

The allegation of this promise was necessary at common law but perhaps not under the code. Wilcox v. Jamieson, 20 C. 158, 160, 36 P. 902; Hays v. Arbuckle, 72 C. 328, 329, 211 P. 101. Note that in the action for money had and received there is never any allegation of the defendant's request so there is more reason for an allegation of the promise, yet the promise in such case is, more often than not, a pure conclusion of law, e.g., money received for converted personalty.

Form No. 28. 

Covenant of Seizin. 

The plaintiff complains and alleges: 1. That at......... on the............day of...... ...., 19......, the defendant, by his deed under his seal by him delivered to the

plaintiff, in consideration¹ of…......... dollars to him paid by the defendant purported to convey to the plaintiff the following described real property: 

(Description.) 

2. That by said deed the defendant covenanted and agreed among other things that (here state the covenant or covenants which the plaintiff claims have been broken) e.g., that he the said defendant was at the time of the delivery of said deed well seized of said premises as of a good and lawful estate of inheritance in fee simple.2

1Although the deed is sealed the allegation of consideration is necessary to show damages. 

2Here any other of the usual covenants in a warranty deed may be added, if it is relied on. 

It would seem that a breach of each of such covenants, seizin, quiet enjoyment against encumbrance, warranty, etc., would constitute a separate cause of action since it might be sued on alone, but they are usually treated as one: Hayden v. Patterson, 39 C. 15, 88 P. 437. All stated together and breach of each assigned. 

In the case of the covenant of seizin, since if broken at all, it is broken as soon as made, Hayden v. Patterson, 39 C. 15, 88 P. 437, no ouster need be alleged, but the breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment is ouster, so the complaint in such case should allege that A. B. had title by virtue of which and the judgment of..... ..Court the plaintiff had been evicted, or by virtue of which, on or about the ..day of............, he evicted the plaintiff. 

On breach of the covenant against encumbrances, the complaint should state the premises were not at the time of the execution of said deed free of encumbrance but were subject to..... (describe the encumbrance).

Form No. 51. 

Title of Defendant. 

19......, 4. The defendant says that on the............day of......... the plaintiff leased the said premises to him, the said defendant for one year, which term at the time of the said alleged trespass had not expired and pursuant to said lease the defendant entered said premises which is the trespass in said. complaint alleged.' 

11 Chit. Pl. 502-3, 5. Put. Pl. & Pr. 466. This plea was regarded as in confession and avoidance because it admits plaintiff's possession, which is enough to support the action against anyone without a better right, and alleges such better right; yet it seems that in such case the property is not "the close of the plaintiff" and, if so, the plea is an argumentative traverse; when, however, the defendant claims a superior right to the close in question, it is prudent, until our Supreme Court settles the matter, to add a defense alleging such right. 

This was required at common law, 1 Chit. Pl. 503-6, and any such right less than a freehold had to be alleged in detail, (Id. 505), with express color. As a reason for this, Mr. Chitty says: "But a special plea disclosing a possessory title in the defendant, as a leaseholder or termor, is openly at variance with, and directly contradicts the very gist of the plaintiff's action of trespass, and therefore should be pleaded in detail with express color."

This looks like a non sequitur. Is not a fact which is a direct contradiction of the very gist of the action good evidence in support of a general denial? Is not a superior right in the defendant evidence that the close is not the close of the plaintiff. 

Payne v. Williams, 62 C. 86, 160 P. 196, which we have cited so often, and which has been followed many times. (See also Sylvis v. 

Sylvis, 11 C. 319, 330, 17 P. 912; Gafner v. Nelson, 66 C. 586, 590, 185 P. 338), holds that "under a general denial the defendant may introduce any evidence that goes to controvert, without admitting them, the facts which the plaintiff is bound to establish in order to sustain his action." The plaintiff in trespass quare clausum is bound to establish his allegation "of the plaintiff," if there is a plea "not of the plaintiff" or a general denial. "Of the plaintiff" includes any and every possessory right that plaintiff may have (Foster v. Coffee, 71 C. 171, 173, 204 P. 900, and see Ownership). At least one of them he is bound to establish. Evidence of a superior right in defendant controverts it; not merely avoids its effect, but, if true, destroys it. 

Is there any escape from the conclusion that such evidence is competent to support such a denial? Compare 1 Chit. Pl. 527-9, where, with respect to trespass de bonis, this proposition is maintained.

Form No. 52. 

Conversion, Denial of Taking. 

The defendant says that he did not take¹ or convert¹ the (goods) in said complaint mentioned.

Since the taking is a species of conversion a denial of conversion ought to be sufficient without a denial of taking, and for the same reason a denial of the taking alone would not deny the conversion The old distinction between trespass de bonis and trover is gone.

Form No. 53. 

Denial of Conversion. 

The defendant says that he did not convert (to his own use) the (goods) in said complaint mentioned." "These words are usual, but logically unnecessary for the same reason that denial of taking is unnecessary. It is perhaps safer, however, to use them.

Under a denial of conversion to his own use the defendant ought to be permitted to show proper care of the chattel, e.g., bestowing it in a safe place, since such is not a conversion to his own use. Defences in discharge must, of course, be affirmatively stated. There can hardly be any other plea in confession and avoidance of a conversion. Gerard v. Jones, 78 Ind. 378.

Form No. 57. 

Contributory Negligence, Careless Use of Machine. 

Title.

Form No. 60. 

Ejectment, General Denial. 

The defendant answers the complaint and denies each and every allegation therein.¹

Confession and Avoidance. 

For a second defense defendant alleges (anything consistent with plaintiff's ownership but inconsistent with his right of possession²; e.g., a contract of purchase and possession thereunder with payment or accord and satisfaction of the purchase price).2

It is held that this will not deny defendant's possession. See Ejectment § 554. The issues then are: "Plaintiff owner vel non," and "defendant detains vel non." Since it may be omitted if detention is alleged, ouster cannot in such case, be a material allegation and so no issue can then be made upon it. "Defendant damaged the realty vel non" looks like an issue but is not, because its decision will not decide the case, since it is only collateral to the issues of ownership and ouster or detention, i.e., which ever way it may be decided the right of plaintiff to judgment is not decided, and if it were the only question the plaintiff would be entitled to a judgment for possession on general demurrer. If, however, ownership of plaintiff were the only question its decision, whichever way would decide the whole case and likewise of detention. Actually there can be but two issues: 1. Has plaintiff an interest which gives him a right of possession? and, 2. Does defendant detain? 

2Roller v. Smith, 76 C. 371, 231 P. 656. This case seems not wholly consistent with those cases which hold that the allegation "owner" permits proof of every sort of interest.

Form No. 64. 

Breach of Warranty of Title. 

And for a third and further defense, defendant alleges that said policy was issued pursuant to an application in writing signed by said plaintiff wherein and whereby he stated and warranted that his title to said house and the land on which it stood was a fee simple. 

2. That said policy was conditioned that if any of the warranties in said application were untrue the said policy should be void. 

3. That at the time of said application and at the issuance the said plaintiff had no title whatever to said house or the land wherein it stood.¹

If the plaintiff had title but less than a fee simple, draw this paragraph according to the fact, i.e., that at the time, etc., the plaintiff had not a title in fee simple to said property. Do not say what his title was, e.g., "but was an estate for his own life only." That is the evidence that it was not a fee simple and would make the defense equivalent to the common law special traverse which was an anomaly the code sought to eliminate and a denial of it would form no issue.

Form No. 74. 

1 

Statute of Frauds, Interest in Real Estate.

The defendant says that the said alleged contract was not nor was any note or memorandum thereof in writing. 

We speak of pleading the statute of frauds, but we mean alleging the facts which show that that statute governs the case. We never plead a statute. With care an answer under any other section of the statute may be drawn by analogy to these forms. Be careful not to deny any fact in the complaint necessary to the defense. 

Form No. 75. 

Another Form. 

The defendant says that neither the said contract nor any note or memorandum thereof in writing was signed by him. or by any one thereto authorized by him.¹ 

¹If there was unwritten authority add: "In writing," C. L. '21, § 5105. If the contract was a lease or agreement for a lease, allege that it was for a term exceeding one year, unless that fact already appears in the complaint, see note under Form No. 76.

Form No. 76. 

Sale of Goods. 

The defendant says that said contract was not by its terms to be performed within one year from the making thereof and no note or memorandum thereof was in writing or signed by him.¹ 

1C. L. '21, § 5111. If the complaint shows the time of performance, performance within one year need not be negatived.

1The complaint is usually verified, and so the full general denial may not ordinarily be used, but is proper, and may often be found advisable.

20r: Did not (on or before the........ ..day of.. ......, 19......, pay or tender, etc.). Defendant Willing to Comply.

Form No. 79. 

Limitations.

The defendant answers the complaint and says that the said supposed cause of action in said complaint mentioned did not accrue within (six)¹ years next before the commencement of this suit.2 

¹Insert the number of years according to the statute. 

2Sweet v. Barnard, 66 Colo. 526, 535, 182 P. 22; Adams v. Tucker, 6 C. A. 393, 396, 40 P. 783. Logically, this plea should be sufficient in any action at law; it accords with the literal terms of many sections, but the plea is often otherwise, e.g., on any simple contract, where assumpsit would lie at common law, the plea may be "did not promise within six years," etc. The pleas of the statutes of Limitation are so many and various that no form book attempts to embrace them all. 

The pleader should consider carefully the statute on which he relies and state briefly the facts which bring the case within its terms.

ᏢᎪᎡᎢ 5. REPLICATION.

Form No. 85. 

Skeleton Form.

The plaintiff replies to the answer of the defendent and for a first replication.¹

Denies :-1 

And for a second replication.¹

Alleges:-1

1The direct negative "not" is the better form of denial. See the notes to the skeleton forms of Answers.

Form No. 86. 

Title. 

Assault, General Denial. 

The plaintiff replies to the (second) defense in said answer and denies each and every allegation therein.

Form No. 87. 

Assault, Specific Denial. 

The plaintiff replies to the (second) defense in said answer and says that he did not assault the defendant.¹ 

And for a (second) replication to said (second) defense plaintiff says that he did not first assault the defendant.¹ 

For a (third) replication to said (second) defense plaintiff says that it was not necessary for defendant to assault the plaintiff to defend himself.2 

1These two replies are questionable. Plaintiff's assault vel non and plaintiff's first assault vel non look like true issues, but are not, because, although either, if decided in the negative, would give the plaintiff a victory, yet if decided in the affirmative would not give the defendant the victory unless plaintiff's assault was such as made defendant's assault necessary in self defense. The real issue, then, is in the third reply. Defendant's assault necessary in self defense vel non.

There is now the additional issue: Defendant's assault necessary in self defense vel non. This is a true issue because if it is the sole question, its determination would determine the case whichever way the jury went.

Form No. 88. 

Assault, Justification. 

For a (third) replication to said (second) defense plaintiff says that the plaintiff at said time was in possession of and residing in his house (No......................Street, Colo- rado), and the defendant with force and arms attempted to enter the same and the plaintiff therefore necessarily committed the alleged first assault to repel him.¹

To any of the pleas of justification there is usually no reply except denial. The usual reply at common law was de juria. The plaintiff, however, may justify his first assault, 1 Chit. Pl., 609, and this reply being automatically denied under Code, § 77, we have another issue: Were plaintiff's acts necessary to repel defendant from his house, or not? 

This, again, is a true issue, for the reasons above stated. To a plea of discharge, e.g., payment, accord and satisfaction, the replication may be a denial, fraud, mistake, duress and perhaps other matters.

The following are examples of defense. (Answer.) Note their simplicity; yet they tell all that more elaborate ones do. 

1. The defendant did not make the note. 

2. The defendant did not draw the check. 

3. Te defendant or (A. B.) did not indorse to the plaintiff

P. 1383. 

The defendant was induced to accept by the fraud of the drawer who indorsed to the plaintiff without consideration (or with notice of the fraud or after maturity.)

Particulars of the fraud are as follows:

The drawer on or about the....day of..........., falsely and fraudulently stated to the defendant that he had shipped 20 tons of pig iron for the defendant on board the (Ajax) which he had not done. P. 1383.

The defendant did not order the goods. P. 1384. 

The goods were not delivered to the defendant. P. 1384. 

The defendant or A. B. as agent satisfied the claim by payment before action to plaintiff (or, to C. D., the plaintiff's agent) on the.............day of.............. P. 1384. 

As to the whole (or at to.... parcel of the money claimed) the defendant made tender before action( or on the day it fell due) of £.…………………………………….., and has paid the same into court. .P. 1385.

The debt was barred by the Statute of Limitations (state which). P. 1385.

The defendant did not receive the plaintiff as a passenger to be carried as alleged. P. 1386. 

Form No. 102. Replies. 

The plaintiff says that:

As to the first paragraph of the defense he joins issue. 

P. 1390.

This is the substance of the common law similiter. 

Instead of a demurrer or as a demurrer, the defendant may add to his answer, e.g., "The defendant will object that the special damage stated is not sufficient in point of law to sustain the action." P. 1391.
